paragraphs: This paper explores how a single neuron might perform computations resembling those of a multilayer network. Its motivation comes from detailed models in which dendritic membrane nonlinearities create local processing elements before signals reach the cell body. These local elements can play a role analogous to hidden units.

The authors introduce the clusteron, an abstract neuron model incorporating sensitivity to the spatial clustering of synaptic inputs. They show that a Hebb-type learning rule can extract higher-order statistics from training patterns by changing the spatial ordering of synaptic connections along the dendritic tree. The arrangement of inputs is thus an explicit part of learning.

The paper then investigates the possible biological relevance of these statistics for nonlinear pattern discrimination using a full compartmental model of a neocortical pyramidal cell. That study uses 1,000 high-dimensional sparse random patterns. The work connects a simplified learning mechanism with detailed neuronal modeling to examine how dendritic organization could contribute to a single cell's computational capabilities.
summary.tldr: The clusteron learns higher-order pattern structure by rearranging synaptic inputs to exploit nonlinear interactions along dendrites.

title: The Clusteron: Toward a Simple Abstraction for a Complex Neuron

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a small, fixed neural network can learn nearly as well as the same network with optimal weights, given sufficiently long training. The distinction matters because earlier negative learning results considered what happens as the number of network nodes grows without bound. That setting does not directly answer the authors’ fixed-network question.

The analysis uses an agnostic refinement of probably approximately correct learning. Here, the learning target need not satisfy a predetermined structural assumption, training data may contain noise, and inputs and outputs can take non-Boolean values. Success therefore means approaching the best true error available within the chosen network, rather than necessarily eliminating error.

The authors give a positive answer in this framework and obtain a positive result for multilayer networks in the original PAC model as a special case. They also describe an efficient parallel implementation of their algorithm. The contribution is a learnability guarantee framed around prolonged training of a fixed analog network.
summary.tldr: For small fixed analog networks, the paper establishes learning guarantees that approach optimal-weight performance despite noise and unrestricted targets.

title: Agnostic PAC-Learning of Functions on Analog Neural Nets

abstract: The paradigm of Hebbian learning has recently received a novel in(cid:173) terpretation with the discovery of synaptic plasticity that depends on the relative timing of pre and post synaptic spikes. This paper derives a temporally dependent learning rule from the basic princi(cid:173) ple of mutual information maximization and studies its relation to the experimentally observed plasticity. We find that a supervised spike-dependent learning rule sharing similar structure with the ex(cid:173) perimentally observed plasticity increases mutual information to a stable near optimal level. Moreover, the analysis reveals how the temporal structure of time-dependent learning rules is determined by the temporal filter applied by neurons over their inputs. These results suggest experimental prediction as to the dependency of the learning rule on neuronal biophysical parameters

paragraphs: This paper seeks an information-theoretic explanation for synaptic changes that depend on the relative timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes. It starts from the principle of maximizing mutual information and derives a learning rule with temporal dependence. The resulting rule is then studied in relation to experimentally observed plasticity.

The authors find that a supervised, spike-dependent rule with a structure similar to the observed plasticity raises mutual information to a stable level near the optimum. This connects a specific learning objective with a timing-sensitive pattern of synaptic adaptation. The result concerns the derived supervised rule and its information behavior, while the structural similarity supplies the link to experimental observations.

The analysis also relates the timing structure of the learning rule to the temporal filter neurons apply to their inputs. This gives the model a connection to neuronal processing beyond spike timing alone. The authors suggest experimental predictions about how learning rules should depend on biophysical parameters, extending the account from an information objective to potentially testable dependencies.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information maximization yields a timing-dependent plasticity rule whose temporal structure is linked to neuronal input filtering.

title: Temporally Dependent Plasticity: An Information Theoretic Account

abstract: We present an information-geometric measure to systematically investigate neuronal firing patterns, taking account not only of the second-order but also of higher-order interactions. We begin with the case of two neurons for illustration and show how to test whether or not any pairwise correlation in one period is significantly different from that in the other period. In order to test such a hy(cid:173) pothesis of different firing rates, the correlation term needs to be singled out 'orthogonally' to the firing rates, where the null hypoth(cid:173) esis might not be of independent firing. This method is also shown to directly associate neural firing with behavior via their mutual information, which is decomposed into two types of information, conveyed by mean firing rate and coincident firing, respectively. Then, we show that these results, using the 'orthogonal' decompo(cid:173) sition, are naturally extended to the case of three neurons and n neurons in general.

paragraphs: Neural firing patterns contain information in both individual firing rates and relationships among neurons. This paper introduces an information-geometric measure for studying those relationships, including interactions beyond pairs. Its central concern is to separate different contributions so that a change in firing rate is not confused with a change in correlation.

For two neurons, the authors show how to test whether pairwise correlation differs significantly between two periods. Their construction isolates the correlation term orthogonally to firing-rate terms. This separation matters because the comparison need not assume independent firing under the null hypothesis: it can address differences in correlation while allowing a non-independent reference case.

The same framework links neural firing to behavior through mutual information. It decomposes that information into contributions conveyed by mean firing rates and by coincident firing. The authors then extend the orthogonal decomposition to three neurons and to general populations. The result is a systematic way to distinguish rate-related information from information associated with coordinated activity.
summary.tldr: An information-geometric decomposition separates firing-rate and interaction effects when testing neural correlations and relating activity to behavior.

title: Information-Geometric Decomposition in Spike Analysis

abstract: Many real-world domains are relational in nature, consisting of a set of objects related to each other in complex ways. This paper focuses on predicting the existence and the type of links between entities in such domains. We apply the relational Markov network framework of Taskar et al. to deﬁne a joint probabilis- tic model over the entire link graph — entity attributes and links. The application of the RMN algorithm to this task requires the deﬁnition of probabilistic patterns over subgraph structures. We apply this method to two new relational datasets, one involving university webpages, and the other a social network. We show that the collective classiﬁcation approach of RMNs, and the introduction of subgraph patterns over link labels, provide signiﬁcant improvements in accuracy over ﬂat classiﬁcation, which attempts to predict each link in isolation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict whether two entities are linked and what kind of link connects them. In relational data, these decisions occur within a larger network of objects and relationships. The authors therefore model link predictions jointly with entity attributes and the rest of the link graph.

Their approach uses relational Markov networks and defines probabilistic patterns over subgraph structures. These patterns allow the model to represent relationships among link labels, rather than treating each possible link as an isolated classification problem. Collective classification makes the surrounding relational structure part of the prediction process.

The method is applied to two datasets: university webpages and a social network. The reported results show significant accuracy improvements over flat classification, which predicts links independently. The findings support both the use of collective prediction and the inclusion of subgraph patterns over link labels. They show that, in these applications, modeling how relationships fit together supplies useful predictive information beyond a separate decision for each link.
summary.tldr: Joint relational models using subgraph patterns improve link prediction over independent classification on webpage and social-network data.

title: Link Prediction in Relational Data

abstract: To understand the brain mechanisms involved in reward prediction on different time scales, we developed a Markov decision task that requires prediction of both immediate and future rewards, and ana- lyzed subjects’ brain activities using functional MRI. We estimated the time course of reward prediction and reward prediction error on different time scales from subjects' performance data, and used them as the explanatory variables for SPM analysis. We found topog- raphic maps of different time scales in medial frontal cortex and striatum. The result suggests that different cortico-basal ganglia loops are specialized for reward prediction on different time scales.

paragraphs: The study asks how the brain predicts rewards arriving at different time scales. The researchers develop a Markov decision task that requires participants to consider both immediate and future rewards. They observe brain activity with functional MRI, connecting a task with multiple reward horizons to measurements of where related activity occurs.

Using participants’ performance, the authors estimate how reward predictions and reward-prediction errors change over time at different time scales. Those estimates become explanatory variables in the brain-imaging analysis. This connects observed brain activity to specific quantities derived from behavior, allowing the analysis to distinguish associations with different prediction horizons.

The researchers find spatial maps of time scales in the medial frontal cortex and striatum. They interpret this organization as suggesting that different loops connecting cortex and basal ganglia specialize in reward prediction over different horizons. The stated conclusion is suggestive: the observed mapping supports differentiated temporal roles for these circuits, without turning that interpretation into a demonstrated universal division of function.
summary.tldr: Brain-imaging maps suggest that different cortico-basal ganglia loops predict rewards over different time horizons.

title: Different Cortico-Basal Ganglia Loops Specialize in Reward Prediction at Different Time Scales

abstract: Although discriminatively trained classiﬁers are usually more accurate when labeled training data is abundant, previous work has shown that when training data is limited, generative classiﬁers can out-perform them. This paper describes a hybrid model in which a high-dimensional subset of the parameters are trained to maximize generative likelihood, and another, small, subset of parameters are discriminatively trained to maximize conditional likelihood. We give a sample complexity bound showing that in order to ﬁt the discriminative parameters well, the num- ber of training examples required depends only on the logarithm of the number of feature occurrences and feature set size. Experimental results show that hybrid models can provide lower test error and can produce better accuracy/coverage curves than either their purely generative or purely discriminative counterparts. We also discuss several advantages of hybrid models, and advocate further work in this area.

We also discuss several advantages of hybrid models, and advocate further work in this area.

paragraphs: Generative and discriminative classifiers can have different advantages depending on how much labeled data is available. The paper starts from evidence that discriminative training usually works better with abundant labels, while generative classifiers can perform better when training data is limited. It proposes combining the two training approaches within a single classification model.

The hybrid divides its parameters into two groups. A large, high-dimensional group is fitted by maximizing generative likelihood, while a small group is fitted by maximizing conditional likelihood. This reserves discriminative training for a restricted part of the model. A sample-complexity bound shows that fitting these discriminative parameters well requires a number of examples that depends only logarithmically on feature occurrences and feature-set size.

Experiments show that the hybrids can achieve lower test error and better accuracy-versus-coverage curves than either purely generative or purely discriminative counterparts. These results support the proposed division of training responsibilities. The theoretical bound concerns the discriminative parameter subset, while the empirical results establish that combining objectives can benefit classification in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Training most parameters generatively and a small subset discriminatively can improve classification while limiting the discriminative training data requirement.

title: Classification with Hybrid Generative/Discriminative Models

abstract: We study gender discrimination of human faces using a combination of psychophysical classiﬁcation and discrimination experiments together with methods from machine learning. We reduce the dimensionality of a set of face images using principal component analysis, and then train a set of linear classiﬁers on this reduced representation (linear support vec- tor machines (SVMs), relevance vector machines (RVMs), Fisher linear discriminant (FLD), and prototype (prot) classiﬁers) using human clas- siﬁcation data. Because we combine a linear preprocessor with linear classiﬁers, the entire system acts as a linear classiﬁer, allowing us to visu- alise the decision-image corresponding to the normal vector of the separ- ating hyperplanes (SH) of each classiﬁer. We predict that the female-to- maleness transition along the normal vector for classiﬁers closely mim- icking human classiﬁcation (SVM and RVM [1]) should be faster than the transition along any other direction. A psychophysical discrimina- tion experiment using the decision images as stimuli is consistent with this prediction.

paragraphs: The paper uses machine learning to investigate human judgments of gender from face images. It combines human classification data with psychophysical discrimination experiments. The purpose is to connect a fitted classifier's decision rule to the visual changes that influence people's perception in this task.

The authors first reduce the face images with principal component analysis and then train several linear classifiers, including support vector machines, relevance vector machines, Fisher linear discriminants, and prototype classifiers. Because both stages are linear, the complete decision rule can be visualized as a decision image. This image corresponds to the direction perpendicular to the classifier's separating boundary.

For the support vector and relevance vector classifiers, which closely mimic human classifications, the authors predict the fastest perceived transition from female to male appearance along that perpendicular direction. A psychophysical experiment using the decision images is consistent with this prediction. The finding supports the use of interpretable classifier directions to formulate and test hypotheses about visual judgments.
summary.tldr: Visualized linear classifiers generate predictions about perceived gender transitions in faces that are consistent with a psychophysical experiment.

title: Machine Learning Applied to Perception: Decision Images for Gender Classification

abstract: We introduce a computationally efficient method to estimate the validity of the BP method as a function of graph topology, the connectivity strength, frustration and network size. We present numerical results that demonstrate the correctness of our estimates for the uniform random model and for a real-world network (“C. Elegans”). Although the method is restricted to pair-wise interactions, no local evidence (zero “biases”) and binary variables, we believe that its predictions correctly capture the limitations of BP for inference and MAP estimation on arbitrary graphical models. Using this approach, we find that BP always performs better than MF. Especially for large networks with broad degree distributions (such as scale-free networks) BP turns out to significantly outperform MF.

We present numerical results that demonstrate the correctness of our estimates for the uniform random model and for a real-world network (“C. Elegans”). Although the method is restricted to pair-wise interactions, no local evidence (zero “biases”) and binary variables, we believe that its predictions correctly capture the limitations of BP for inference and MAP estimation on arbitrary graphical models. Using this approach, we find that BP always performs better than MF. Especially for large networks with broad degree distributions (such as scale-free networks) BP turns out to significantly outperform MF.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an efficient way to estimate when belief propagation is reliable on networks with loops. The estimates account for graph topology, connection strength, frustration, and network size. This makes reliability a property to examine through the structure and interactions of the network, rather than treating the inference algorithm in isolation.

The method is restricted to binary variables, pairwise interactions, and zero local biases. Numerical results on uniform random networks and a C. elegans network support the correctness of the estimates in the studied settings. The authors believe the predictions also capture limitations of belief propagation for inference and maximum a posteriori estimation in more general graphical models.

Within this approach, belief propagation is found to perform better than mean-field inference throughout the comparison. Its advantage is especially pronounced for large networks with broad degree distributions, including scale-free networks. The result links the relative usefulness of these approximations to network structure, while the proposed broader applicability remains the authors' stated expectation beyond the method's restricted formulation.
summary.tldr: An efficient reliability estimate for restricted binary networks favors belief propagation over mean field, especially on large networks with broad degree distributions.

title: Validity Estimates for Loopy Belief Propagation on Binary Real-world Networks

abstract: We describe a framework for learning an object classifier from a single example. This goal is achieved by emphasizing the relevant dimensions for classification using available examples of related classes. Learning to accurately classify objects from a single training example is often un- feasible due to overfitting effects. However, if the instance representa- tion provides that the distance between each two instances of the same class is smaller than the distance between any two instances from dif- ferent classes, then a nearest neighbor classifier could achieve perfect performance with a single training example. We therefore suggest a two stage strategy. First, learn a metric over the instances that achieves the distance criterion mentioned above, from available examples of other related classes. Then, using the single examples, define a nearest neigh- bor classifier where distance is evaluated by the learned class relevance metric. Finding a metric that emphasizes the relevant dimensions for classification might not be possible when restricted to linear projections. We therefore make use of a kernel based metric learning algorithm. Our setting encodes object instances as sets of locality based descriptors and adopts an appropriate image kernel for the class relevance metric learn- ing. The proposed framework for learning from a single example is demonstrated in a synthetic setting and on a character classification task.

paragraphs: This paper tackles object classification when only one example of a target class is available. Learning directly from so little data can overfit. The proposed solution uses examples from related classes to learn which aspects of an object representation should matter when measuring similarity.

The method follows two stages. First, it learns a distance metric from related classes. Then it applies nearest-neighbor classification to the single examples using that metric. The motivating condition is sufficient for perfect classification: every within-class distance must be smaller than every between-class distance. The framework seeks a metric that achieves this separation; the conditional argument does not establish that every learned metric will do so.

Because linear projections may be unable to emphasize the needed dimensions, the authors use kernel-based metric learning. Objects are represented as sets of local descriptors with an appropriate image kernel. Demonstrations on synthetic data and character classification illustrate the strategy of transferring a useful notion of similarity before learning from a single example.
summary.tldr: The framework learns a kernel-based similarity metric from related classes, then uses it for nearest-neighbor classification from single examples.

title: Object Classification from a Single Example Utilizing Class Relevance Metrics

abstract: Motor imagery attenuates EEG and rhythms over sensorimotor cortices. These amplitude changes are most successfully captured by the method of Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) and widely used in braincomputer interfaces (BCI). BCI methods based on amplitude information, however, have not incoporated the rich phase dynamics in the EEG rhythm. This study reports on a BCI method based on phase synchrony rate (SR). SR, computed from binarized phase locking value, describes the number of discrete synchronization events within a window. Statistical nonparametric tests show that SRs contain significant differences between 2 types of motor imageries. Classifiers trained on SRs consistently demonstrate satisfactory results for all 5 subjects. It is further observed that, for 3 subjects, phase is more discriminative than amplitude in the first 1.5-2.0 s, which suggests that phase has the potential to boost the information transfer rate in BCIs.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces can distinguish imagined movements using changes in EEG activity over sensorimotor cortex. The paper notes that widely used amplitude-based approaches, including Common Spatial Patterns, do not incorporate the richer phase dynamics of EEG rhythms. It investigates whether a measure of synchronization events can provide useful information for recognizing motor imagery.

The proposed feature is phase synchrony rate. It is calculated from a binarized phase-locking value and counts discrete synchronization events within a time window. Nonparametric statistical tests find significant differences in these rates between two kinds of motor imagery. Classifiers trained on the rates consistently produce results described as satisfactory across all five subjects.

For three subjects, phase information is more discriminative than amplitude during the first 1.5 to 2 seconds. This timing result suggests that phase could help improve information transfer rates in brain-computer interfaces. The conclusion is a possibility supported by early discrimination in those subjects, rather than a demonstrated increase in transfer rate for every participant.
summary.tldr: Phase synchrony rates distinguish two motor-imagery types, with early phase advantages in three of five subjects suggesting potential for faster BCI communication.

title: Phase Synchrony Rate for the Recognition of Motor Imagery in Brain-Computer Interface

abstract: We investigate the learning of the appearance of an object from a single image of it. Instead of using a large number of pictures of the object to recognize, we use a labeled reference database of pictures of other ob- jects to learn invariance to noise and variations in pose and illumination. This acquired knowledge is then used to predict if two pictures of new objects, which do not appear on the training pictures, actually display the same object. We propose a generic scheme called chopping to address this task. It relies on hundreds of random binary splits of the training set chosen to keep together the images of any given object. Those splits are extended to the complete image space with a simple learning algorithm. Given two images, the responses of the split predictors are combined with a Bayesian rule into a posterior probability of similarity. Experiments with the COIL-100 database and with a database of 150 de- graded LATEX symbols compare our method to a classical learning with several examples of the positive class and to a direct learning of the sim- ilarity.

paragraphs: This paper studies recognizing an object from a single image by learning useful variation from other objects. A labeled reference collection provides examples of changes in pose, illumination, and noise. The learned information is then used to judge whether two images depict the same new object, even though that object was absent from training.

The proposed chopping scheme makes hundreds of random binary divisions of the reference set. Each division keeps all images of a given object together. A simple learning algorithm extends each division to the wider image space, producing predictors that can respond to previously unseen images.

For a pair of images, the method combines those predictors' responses using a Bayesian rule to obtain a posterior probability of similarity. The authors evaluate the scheme on COIL-100 and a collection of 150 degraded LaTeX symbols. They compare it with learning from several positive examples and with learning similarity directly. The approach's central contribution is a mechanism for transferring knowledge about appearance variation into recognition from one example.
summary.tldr: Chopping learns random object-preserving partitions of reference images and combines them to judge similarity between images of unseen objects.

title: Pattern Recognition from One Example by Chopping

abstract: Semi-supervised inductive learning concerns how to learn a decision rule from a data set containing both labeled and unlabeled data. Several boosting algorithms have been extended to semi-supervised learning with various strategies. To our knowledge, however, none of them takes local smoothness constraints among data into account during ensemble learning. In this paper, we introduce a local smoothness regularizer to semi-supervised boosting algorithms based on the universal optimization framework of margin cost functionals. Our regularizer is applicable to existing semi-supervised boosting algorithms to improve their generalization and speed up their training. Comparative results on synthetic, benchmark and real world tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our local smoothness regularizer. We discuss relevant issues and relate our regularizer to previous work.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning builds a decision rule from both labeled and unlabeled examples. Boosting methods have been adapted to this setting, but the authors identify a missing ingredient in existing approaches: local smoothness constraints during ensemble learning. Such constraints express a preference for the decision rule to behave smoothly among nearby data.

The regularizer is designed to apply to existing semi-supervised boosting algorithms, providing a common way to incorporate this information during the construction of the ensemble.

The stated benefits are improved generalization and faster training. Comparisons on synthetic data, benchmark tasks, and real-world tasks demonstrate the regularizer's effectiveness. These results support using local relationships among examples as part of semi-supervised ensemble learning. The contribution is an adaptable regularization mechanism and empirical evidence for its value across the evaluated settings, together with a discussion of its relationship to previous work.
summary.tldr: A local smoothness regularizer can improve generalization and accelerate training in existing semi-supervised boosting algorithms.

title: Regularized Boost for Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Consider linear prediction models where the target function is a sparse linear combination of a set of basis functions. We are interested in the problem of identifying those basis functions with non-zero coefficients and reconstructing the target function from noisy observations. Two heuristics that are widely used in practice are forward and backward greedy algorithms. First, we show that neither idea is adequate. Second, we propose a novel combination that is based on the forward greedy algorithm but takes backward steps adaptively whenever beneficial. We prove strong theoretical results showing that this procedure is effective in learning sparse representations. Experimental results support our theory.

paragraphs: The paper considers prediction problems in which the target is a linear combination of only a few available basis functions. Learning has two connected goals: identify the functions with nonzero coefficients and reconstruct the target from noisy observations. Sparsity makes selecting the relevant functions a central part of the problem.

Two common strategies proceed greedily, either adding functions through forward steps or removing them through backward steps. The authors first show that neither idea alone is adequate for the problem they study. They then propose a forward-driven procedure that can also take backward steps, choosing those removals adaptively when they are beneficial.

The combination matters because selecting a function need not be a permanent commitment: subsequent backward steps can revise the developing representation. The authors prove strong theoretical results supporting the procedure’s effectiveness for sparse learning and report experiments consistent with that theory. The stated contribution is therefore both an adaptive algorithm and a mathematical justification for combining selection with selective removal.
summary.tldr: An adaptive greedy method learns sparse linear models by adding basis functions and selectively removing them when beneficial.

title: Adaptive Forward-Backward Greedy Algorithm for Sparse Learning with Linear Models

abstract: We analyse matching pursuit for kernel principal components analysis by proving that the sparse subspace it produces is a sample compression scheme. We show that this bound is tighter than the KPCA bound of Shawe-Taylor et al swck-05 and highly predictive of the size of the subspace needed to capture most of the variance in the data. We analyse a second matching pursuit algorithm called kernel matching pursuit (KMP) which does not correspond to a sample compression scheme. However, we give a novel bound that views the choice of subspace of the KMP algorithm as a compression scheme and hence provide a VC bound to upper bound its future loss. Finally we describe how the same bound can be applied to other matching pursuit related algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes matching pursuit methods through compression: whether a learned representation can be understood in terms of a compact selection from the data. For kernel principal components analysis, the authors prove that the sparse subspace produced by matching pursuit forms a sample compression scheme.

This characterization yields a bound tighter than an earlier kernel PCA bound. The authors also report that it is highly predictive of the subspace size needed to retain most of the data’s variance. The analysis therefore connects sparsity to a practical representation question: how large a subspace is needed to preserve the principal variation.

A second algorithm, kernel matching pursuit, does not itself form a sample compression scheme. The authors address this distinction by treating its subspace choice as a compression scheme instead. That leads to a VC bound on future loss. They also explain how the same bound can apply to related matching-pursuit algorithms, extending the analytical idea beyond the initial kernel PCA setting.
summary.tldr: Compression-based analyses give matching-pursuit bounds for retained variance and future loss, using different arguments for two kernel methods.

title: Theory of matching pursuit

abstract: There is a growing body of experimental evidence to suggest that the brain is capable of approximating optimal Bayesian inference in the face of noisy input stimuli. Despite this progress, the neural underpinnings of this computation are still poorly understood. In this paper we focus on the problem of Bayesian filtering of stochastic time series. In particular we introduce a novel neural network, derived from a line attractor architecture, whose dynamics map directly onto those of the Kalman Filter in the limit where the prediction error is small. When the prediction error is large we show that the network responds robustly to change-points in a way that is qualitatively compatible with the optimal Bayesian model. The model suggests ways in which probability distributions are encoded in the brain and makes a number of testable experimental predictions.

Despite this progress, the neural underpinnings of this computation are still poorly understood. In this paper we focus on the problem of Bayesian filtering of stochastic time series. In particular we introduce a novel neural network, derived from a line attractor architecture, whose dynamics map directly onto those of the Kalman Filter in the limit where the prediction error is small. When the prediction error is large we show that the network responds robustly to change-points in a way that is qualitatively compatible with the optimal Bayesian model. The model suggests ways in which probability distributions are encoded in the brain and makes a number of testable experimental predictions.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a neural network could carry out Bayesian filtering: updating an estimate of a changing process as noisy observations arrive. Evidence that people can approximate optimal inference motivates the question, but the authors focus on a possible computational mechanism rather than treating that behavioral evidence as an explanation of the mechanism.

They construct a network based on a line attractor architecture and analyze its dynamics. When prediction errors are small, those dynamics map directly onto the Kalman filter. This supplies a specific connection between a neural system's evolving activity and a familiar statistical filtering procedure, with the correspondence tied to the small-error limit.

For large prediction errors, the network responds robustly to change-points, where the observed process changes. Its response is qualitatively compatible with an optimal Bayesian model, a weaker claim than the direct small-error correspondence. The proposed model also suggests how the brain might represent probability distributions and generates testable experimental predictions. These contributions make it a candidate neural account of inference across both ordinary fluctuations and abrupt changes.
summary.tldr: A proposed neural network reproduces Kalman-filter dynamics for small prediction errors and responds robustly to abrupt changes.

title: A Neural Implementation of the Kalman Filter

abstract: In this work we use Branch-and-Bound (BB) to efficiently detect objects with deformable part models. Instead of evaluating the classifier score exhaustively over image locations and scales, we use BB to focus on promising image locations. The core problem is to compute bounds that accommodate part deformations; for this we adapt the Dual Trees data structure to our problem. We evaluate our approach using Mixture-of-Deformable Part Models. We obtain exactly the same results but are 10-20 times faster on average. We also develop a multiple-object detection variation of the system, where hypotheses for 20 categories are inserted in a common priority queue. For the problem of finding the strongest category in an image this results in up to a 100-fold speedup.

We also develop a multiple-object detection variation of the system, where hypotheses for 20 categories are inserted in a common priority queue. paragraphs: Detecting objects with deformable part models can require scoring many image positions and scales. This paper accelerates that search with branch-and-bound, which directs computation toward promising candidates. The central challenge is constructing valid bounds when an object's parts can move relative to one another.

The authors adapt a dual-tree data structure to handle those deformations when computing bounds. Evaluated with mixtures of deformable part models, the resulting search produces exactly the same detection results while running 10–20 times faster on average. The reported improvement therefore comes from organizing the search more efficiently while preserving its outcome.

A second version combines hypotheses for 20 object categories in a shared priority queue. This allows the search to prioritize candidates across categories. For the specific task of finding the strongest category in an image, the authors report speedups of up to 100 times. That larger figure concerns this cross-category task and is distinct from the average detection speedup.
summary.tldr: Dual-tree branch-and-bound preserves deformable-model detection results while delivering a reported average speedup of 10–20 times.

title: Rapid Deformable Object Detection using Dual-Tree Branch-and-Bound

abstract: Clustering is a popular problem with many applications. We consider the k-means problem in the situation where the data is too large to be stored in main memory and must be accessed sequentially, such as from a disk, and where we must use as little memory as possible. Our algorithm is based on recent theoretical results, with significant improvements to make it practical. Our approach greatly simpli(cid:173) fies a recently developed algorithm, both in design and in analysis, and eliminates large constant factors in the approximation guarantee, the memory requirements, and the running time. We then incorporate approximate nearest neighbor search to compute k-means in o(nk) (where n is the number of data points; note that com(cid:173) puting the cost, given a solution, takes 8(nk) time). We show that our algorithm compares favorably to existing algorithms - both theoretically and experimentally, thus providing state-of-the-art performance in both theory and practice.

paragraphs: This paper considers k-means clustering when the dataset cannot fit in main memory and must be read sequentially, for example from disk. The goal is to cluster effectively while using very little memory. That setting makes the practical costs of an algorithm central, because a theoretically attractive method may still require too much storage or computation.

Building on recent theoretical work, the authors simplify an existing algorithm in both its design and analysis. Their changes remove large constant factors from the approximation guarantee, memory requirements, and running time. These improvements address several practical obstacles together, connecting the quality of the resulting clustering with the resources needed to produce it.

The method additionally incorporates approximate nearest-neighbor search to obtain computation below the n-times-k scale, where n is the number of points and k is the number of clusters. The authors report favorable theoretical and experimental comparisons with existing methods. The contribution is an approach designed to retain strong clustering performance under sequential-access and memory constraints.
summary.tldr: A simplified, memory-efficient k-means algorithm combines theoretical improvements with approximate nearest-neighbor search for large sequentially accessed datasets.

title: Fast and Accurate k-means For Large Datasets

abstract: We present theoretical and empirical results for a framework that combines the benefits of apprenticeship and autonomous reinforcement learning. Our approach modifies an existing apprenticeship learning framework that relies on teacher demonstrations and does not necessarily explore the environment. The first change is replacing previously used Mistake Bound model learners with a recently proposed framework that melds the KWIK and Mistake Bound supervised learning protocols. The second change is introducing a communication of expected utility from the student to the teacher. The resulting system only uses teacher traces when the agent needs to learn concepts it cannot efficiently learn on its own.

Our approach modifies an existing apprenticeship learning framework that relies on teacher demonstrations and does not necessarily explore the environment. The first change is replacing previously used Mistake Bound model learners with a recently proposed framework that melds the KWIK and Mistake Bound supervised learning protocols. The second change is introducing a communication of expected utility from the student to the teacher. The resulting system only uses teacher traces when the agent needs to learn concepts it cannot efficiently learn on its own.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a reinforcement learning agent can combine learning from a teacher with learning through its own exploration. Its starting point is an apprenticeship learning framework that uses teacher demonstrations but does not necessarily explore the environment. The authors modify that framework so the student can use both sources of experience.

One change replaces the previous Mistake Bound model learners with a framework combining the KWIK and Mistake Bound supervised learning protocols. A second change adds communication of expected utility from the student to the teacher. Together, these changes make the student's own learning situation relevant to how teaching is used, rather than relying solely on demonstration traces.

The resulting system uses teacher traces only when the agent needs concepts that it cannot learn efficiently by itself. The authors present theoretical and empirical results for this combined framework. Its significance is the selective role assigned to teaching: demonstrations support concepts that are difficult for autonomous learning, while exploration remains part of the student's overall learning process.
summary.tldr: A combined apprenticeship and reinforcement learning framework uses teacher traces when the student cannot efficiently learn the needed concepts alone.

title: Blending Autonomous Exploration and Apprenticeship Learning

abstract: We develop a novel Bayesian nonparametric model for random bipartite graphs. The model is based on the theory of completely random measures and is able to handle a potentially infinite number of nodes. We show that the model has appealing properties and in particular it may exhibit a power-law behavior. We derive a posterior characterization, an Indian Buffet-like generative process for network growth, and a simple and efficient Gibbs sampler for posterior simulation. Our model is shown to be well fitted to several real-world social networks.
originalAbstract: We develop a novel Bayesian nonparametric model for random bipartite graphs. The model is based on the theory of completely random measures and is able to handle a potentially infinite number of nodes. We show that the model has appealing properties and in particular it may exhibit a power-law behavior. We derive a posterior characterization, an Indian Buffet-like generative process for network growth, and a simple and efficient Gibbs sampler for posterior simulation. Our model is shown to be well fitted to several real-world social networks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic model for bipartite graphs, whose connections run between two sets of nodes. Its Bayesian nonparametric construction can accommodate potentially infinitely many nodes. This gives the model a way to describe networks without committing to a fixed finite collection of possible nodes at the outset.

The construction uses completely random measures. Among its stated properties is the possibility of power-law behavior, meaning that this kind of uneven network structure can arise within the model. The authors also derive an Indian Buffet-like process for network growth, providing a generative account of how the graph can develop.

For inference, the paper characterizes the posterior distribution and supplies a simple, efficient Gibbs sampler. These pieces connect the mathematical model to the task of learning from observed networks. The authors report good fits to several real-world social networks. Those results support the model's practical relevance, while the power-law claim remains a capability of the model rather than a universal property of every graph it generates.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric bipartite-graph model accommodates potentially infinite networks and possible power-law behavior, with efficient posterior sampling.

title: Bayesian nonparametric models for bipartite graphs

abstract: We derive a novel norm that corresponds to the tightest convex relaxation of sparsity combined with an $\ell_2$ penalty. We show that this new norm provides a tighter relaxation than the elastic net, and is thus a good replacement for the Lasso or the elastic net in sparse prediction problems. But through studying our new norm, we also bound the looseness of the elastic net, thus shedding new light on it and providing justification for its use.
originalAbstract: We derive a novel norm that corresponds to the tightest convex relaxation of sparsity combined with an $\ell_2$ penalty. We show that this new norm provides a tighter relaxation than the elastic net, and is thus a good replacement for the Lasso or the elastic net in sparse prediction problems. But through studying our new norm, we also bound the looseness of the elastic net, thus shedding new light on it and providing justification for its use.

paragraphs: Sparse prediction seeks models that use relatively few variables while also controlling the size of their coefficients. The paper studies a mathematical representation of these two goals together: sparsity combined with an l2 penalty. It derives a new norm, the k-support norm, corresponding to the tightest convex relaxation of that combination.

A convex relaxation replaces a difficult constraint or penalty with a convex formulation that approximates its intended effect. Tightness describes how closely that formulation represents the original target. The authors show that their norm gives a tighter relaxation than the elastic net, providing a mathematical reason to consider it as a replacement for elastic-net or Lasso regularization in sparse prediction.

The comparison also clarifies the existing elastic net. By studying the new norm, the authors bound how loose the elastic-net relaxation can be, giving additional justification for its use. The contribution therefore offers both an alternative regularizer and a sharper understanding of an established one. Its stated advantage concerns the geometry of the relaxation.
summary.tldr: The k-support norm gives the tightest convex relaxation of sparsity with an l2 penalty and bounds the looseness of the elastic net.

title: Sparse Prediction with the $k$-Support Norm

abstract: Sampling inference methods are computationally difficult to scale for many models in part because global dependencies can reduce opportunities for parallel computation. Without strict conditional independence structure among variables, standard Gibbs sampling theory requires sample updates to be performed sequentially, even if dependence between most variables is not strong. Empirical work has shown that some models can be sampled effectively by going Hogwild'' and simply running Gibbs updates in parallel with only periodic global communication, but the successes and limitations of such a strategy are not well understood. As a step towards such an understanding, we study the Hogwild Gibbs sampling strategy in the context of Gaussian distributions. We develop a framework which provides convergence conditions and error bounds along with simple proofs and connections to methods in numerical linear algebra. In particular, we show that if the Gaussian precision matrix is generalized diagonally dominant, then any Hogwild Gibbs sampler, with any update schedule or allocation of variables to processors, yields a stable sampling process with the correct sample mean. "

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling updates variables using their relationships with other variables. Those dependencies often force standard updates to run sequentially, restricting parallel computation even when many relationships are weak. Hogwild sampling relaxes this coordination: processors update variables in parallel and communicate globally only periodically. The paper asks when this strategy remains well behaved.

The authors study Gaussian distributions and build a framework giving convergence conditions and error bounds. Connections to numerical linear algebra help explain the behavior and support relatively simple proofs. Focusing on this distribution family provides a concrete setting in which the consequences of reduced coordination can be analyzed.

A central result concerns Gaussian precision matrices that are generalized diagonally dominant. Under that sufficient condition, any Hogwild update schedule and any assignment of variables to processors produce a stable sampling process with the correct sample mean. The conclusion specifically establishes stability and mean accuracy; it does not equate these properties with exact recovery of the entire distribution. The result clarifies one substantial setting where aggressive parallelism has theoretical support.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian models satisfying a stated precision-matrix condition, Hogwild Gibbs sampling remains stable and preserves the correct mean.

title: Analyzing Hogwild Parallel Gaussian Gibbs Sampling

abstract: Most learning algorithms are not invariant to the scale of the signal that is being approximated. We propose to adaptively normalize the targets used in the learning updates. This is important in value-based reinforcement learning, where the magnitude of appropriate value approximations can change over time when we update the policy of behavior. Our main motivation is prior work on learning to play Atari games, where the rewards were clipped to a predetermined range. This clipping facilitates learning across many different games with a single learning algorithm, but a clipped reward function can result in qualitatively different behavior. Using adaptive normalization we can remove this domain-specific heuristic without diminishing overall performance.

Using adaptive normalization we can remove this domain-specific heuristic without diminishing overall performance.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms often behave differently when the magnitude of their target signal changes. In value-based reinforcement learning, this matters because appropriate value estimates can change scale as the agent’s behavior policy changes. The paper proposes adaptive normalization of the targets used in learning updates to address this moving scale.

The motivating application is learning to play Atari games with one algorithm. Earlier work clipped rewards to a fixed range, making learning across games easier. However, clipping changes the reward function and can produce qualitatively different behavior. The issue therefore concerns both the numerical scale encountered during learning and the behavior encouraged by the resulting rewards.

Adaptive normalization allows the authors to remove this domain-specific clipping heuristic without reducing overall performance. The finding supports adjusting the scale of learning targets as an alternative way to accommodate varying signal magnitudes in the studied setting. The reported outcome concerns overall performance; it does not assert an improvement on every individual game.
summary.tldr: Adaptive target normalization removes reward clipping in the studied reinforcement learning setting without reducing overall performance.

title: Learning values across many orders of magnitude

abstract: Matching users to the right items at the right time is a fundamental task in recommendation systems. As users interact with different items over time, users' and items' feature may evolve and co-evolve over time. Traditional models based on static latent features or discretizing time into epochs can become ineffective for capturing the fine-grained temporal dynamics in the user-item interactions. We propose a coevolutionary latent feature process model that accurately captures the coevolving nature of users' and items' feature. To learn parameters, we design an efficient convex optimization algorithm with a novel low rank space sharing constraints. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate significant improvements in user behavior prediction compared to state-of-the-arts.

To learn parameters, we design an efficient convex optimization algorithm with a novel low rank space sharing constraints. paragraphs: Recommendation depends on matching a user with an item at an appropriate time. The paper emphasizes that the hidden features describing users and items can change together as interactions occur. Fixed representations, or representations updated only within discrete time periods, can be ineffective at capturing the finer temporal structure of those interactions.

The proposed model represents user and item features as coevolving processes in continuous time. This makes their joint evolution part of the recommendation model itself. The modeling choice matters because changes on either side of an interaction can be relevant to predicting subsequent behavior, and the timing of those changes need not align with predefined epochs.

To estimate the parameters, the authors develop an efficient convex optimization algorithm with low-rank space-sharing constraints. Experiments across diverse real-world datasets show significant improvements in user behavior prediction over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The stated evidence supports modeling temporal coevolution as a useful ingredient in prediction, alongside an optimization procedure designed to make the model practical.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time model of jointly evolving user and item features improves behavior prediction in experiments on diverse real-world datasets.

title: Coevolutionary Latent Feature Processes for Continuous-Time User-Item Interactions

abstract: Experiments reveal that in the dorsal medial superior temporal (MSTd) and the ventral intraparietal (VIP) areas, where visual and vestibular cues are integrated to infer heading direction, there are two types of neurons with roughly the same number. One is “congruent” cells, whose preferred heading directions are similar in response to visual and vestibular cues; and the other is “opposite” cells, whose preferred heading directions are nearly “opposite” (with an offset of 180 degree) in response to visual vs. vestibular cues. Congruent neurons are known to be responsible for cue integration, but the computational role of opposite neurons remains largely unknown. Here, we propose that opposite neurons may serve to encode the disparity information between cues necessary for multisensory segregation. We build a computational model composed of two reciprocally coupled modules, MSTd and VIP, and each module consists of groups of congruent and opposite neurons. In the model, congruent neurons in two modules are reciprocally connected with each other in the congruent manner, whereas opposite neurons are reciprocally connected in the opposite manner. Mimicking the experimental protocol, our model reproduces the characteristics of congruent and opposite neurons, and demonstrates that in each module, the sisters of congruent and opposite neurons can jointly achieve optimal multisensory information integration and segregation. This study sheds light on our understanding of how the brain implements optimal multisensory integration and segregation concurrently in a distributed manner.

paragraphs: Brain areas involved in estimating heading from visual and vestibular signals contain two roughly equally numerous neuron types. Congruent neurons prefer similar headings for both cues, whereas opposite neurons prefer headings separated by about 180 degrees. While congruent cells have an established role in combining cues, the computational purpose of opposite cells is less clear.

The paper proposes that opposite neurons may encode disagreement between cues, supplying information needed to keep sensory signals separate. To explore this possibility, the authors construct a model with reciprocally coupled MSTd and VIP modules. Each module contains both neuron types, with connections between modules arranged in congruent or opposite patterns according to cell type.

Under a protocol modeled on experiments, the network reproduces characteristics of both populations. Within the model, the two types jointly support optimal integration and segregation in each module. This provides a computational explanation for how distributed populations could combine sensory evidence while also representing its discrepancies. The proposed biological role of opposite neurons remains a model-supported hypothesis.
summary.tldr: A computational model suggests that opposite neurons encode cue disagreement while congruent neurons support multisensory integration.

title: “Congruent” and “Opposite” Neurons: Sisters for Multisensory Integration and Segregation

abstract: Spike sorting is a critical first step in extracting neural signals from large-scale electrophysiological data. This manuscript describes an efficient, reliable pipeline for spike sorting on dense multi-electrode arrays (MEAs), where neural signals appear across many electrodes and spike sorting currently represents a major computational bottleneck. We present several new techniques that make dense MEA spike sorting more robust and scalable. Our pipeline is based on an efficient multi-stage ''triage-then-cluster-then-pursuit'' approach that initially extracts only clean, high-quality waveforms from the electrophysiological time series by temporarily skipping noisy or ''collided'' events (representing two neurons firing synchronously). This is accomplished by developing a neural network detection method followed by efficient outlier triaging. The clean waveforms are then used to infer the set of neural spike waveform templates through nonparametric Bayesian clustering. Our clustering approach adapts a ''coreset'' approach for data reduction and uses efficient inference methods in a Dirichlet process mixture model framework to dramatically improve the scalability and reliability of the entire pipeline. The ''triaged'' waveforms are then finally recovered with matching-pursuit deconvolution techniques. originalAbstract: Spike sorting is a critical first step in extracting neural signals from large-scale electrophysiological data. This manuscript describes an efficient, reliable pipeline for spike sorting on dense multi-electrode arrays (MEAs), where neural signals appear across many electrodes and spike sorting currently represents a major computational bottleneck. We present several new techniques that make dense MEA spike sorting more robust and scalable. Our pipeline is based on an efficient multi-stage ''triage-then-cluster-then-pursuit'' approach that initially extracts only clean, high-quality waveforms from the electrophysiological time series by temporarily skipping noisy or ''collided'' events (representing two neurons firing synchronously). This is accomplished by developing a neural network detection method followed by efficient outlier triaging. The clean waveforms are then used to infer the set of neural spike waveform templates through nonparametric Bayesian clustering. Our clustering approach adapts a ''coreset'' approach for data reduction and uses efficient inference methods in a Dirichlet process mixture model framework to dramatically improve the scalability and reliability of the entire pipeline. The ''triaged'' waveforms are then finally recovered with matching-pursuit deconvolution techniques. The proposed methods improve on the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy and stability on both real and biophysically-realistic simulated MEA data. Furthermore, the proposed pipeline is efficient, learning templates and clustering faster than real-time for a 500-electrode dataset, largely on a single CPU core.

paragraphs: YASS addresses spike sorting for dense multi-electrode recordings, where signals from neurons appear across many electrodes. A neural-network detector and outlier triaging initially set aside noisy waveforms and collisions caused by two neurons firing synchronously.

A coreset reduces the data handled during clustering, and efficient inference in a Dirichlet process mixture model improves scalability. Matching-pursuit deconvolution then recovers the waveforms that were temporarily excluded, so triaging is an intermediate step rather than permanent rejection.

The pipeline improves accuracy and stability over the state of the art on real and biophysically realistic simulated recordings. For a 500-electrode dataset, template learning and clustering run faster than real time, largely on one CPU core. That speed statement applies specifically to those stages. The results support separating clean-template discovery from subsequent recovery of more difficult events.
summary.tldr: YASS learns spike templates from clean events before recovering difficult waveforms, improving sorting accuracy, stability, and scalability.

title: YASS: Yet Another Spike Sorter

abstract: Bayesian models are established as one of the main successful paradigms for complex problems in machine learning. To handle intractable inference, research in this area has developed new approximation methods that are fast and effective. However, theoretical analysis of the performance of such approximations is not well developed. The paper furthers such analysis by providing bounds on the excess risk of variational inference algorithms and related regularized loss minimization algorithms for a large class of latent variable models with Gaussian latent variables. We strengthen previous results for variational algorithms by showing they are competitive with any point-estimate predictor. Unlike previous work, we also provide bounds on the risk of the \emph{Bayesian} predictor and not just the risk of the Gibbs predictor for the same approximate posterior. The bounds are applied in complex models including sparse Gaussian processes and correlated topic models. Theoretical results are complemented by identifying novel approximations to the Bayesian objective that attempt to minimize the risk directly. An empirical evaluation compares the variational and new algorithms shedding further light on their performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian models often require approximate inference because exact computation is intractable. Although such approximations can be fast and effective, their predictive performance needs theoretical justification. This paper supplies excess-risk bounds for variational inference and related regularized loss-minimization methods in a broad class of models whose latent variables are Gaussian.

The bounds strengthen earlier results by showing that variational algorithms are competitive with any point-estimate predictor. They also address the Bayesian predictor itself, extending analysis beyond the Gibbs predictor associated with the same approximate posterior. That distinction matters because a guarantee for one prediction rule does not automatically establish a guarantee for another, even when both use the same inferred distribution.

The authors apply their bounds to sparse Gaussian processes and correlated topic models. They also identify new approximations to the Bayesian objective intended to minimize predictive risk directly, and compare these with variational algorithms empirically. The work thus connects theoretical guarantees about prediction to alternative optimization objectives, with the experiments examining their performance rather than establishing a universal winner.
summary.tldr: New risk bounds justify variational prediction in latent Gaussian models and motivate approximations aimed directly at predictive risk.

title: Excess Risk Bounds for the Bayes Risk using Variational Inference in Latent Gaussian Models

abstract: We propose a data-efficient Gaussian process-based Bayesian approach to the semi-supervised learning problem on graphs. The proposed model shows extremely competitive performance when compared to the state-of-the-art graph neural networks on semi-supervised learning benchmark experiments, and outperforms the neural networks in active learning experiments where labels are scarce. Furthermore, the model does not require a validation data set for early stopping to control over-fitting. Our model can be viewed as an instance of empirical distribution regression weighted locally by network connectivity. We further motivate the intuitive construction of the model with a Bayesian linear model interpretation where the node features are filtered by an operator related to the graph Laplacian. The method can be easily implemented by adapting off-the-shelf scalable variational inference algorithms for Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Gaussian process approach to learning from graph data when only some nodes have labels. Its construction brings together node features and network connectivity within a Bayesian model. The aim is to make effective use of limited labels while accounting for the relationships represented by the graph.

The model has two complementary interpretations. One views it as regression on empirical distributions, with local graph connections determining how information is weighted. The other starts from a Bayesian linear model in which node features are filtered using an operator related to the graph Laplacian. These interpretations explain how graph structure enters the prediction process. Implementation can build on existing scalable variational inference methods for Gaussian processes.

On semi-supervised benchmarks, the model is highly competitive with leading graph neural networks. In active learning experiments with scarce labels, it outperforms those neural networks. It also avoids needing a separate validation dataset for early stopping to control overfitting, a useful property when labeled data are already limited.
summary.tldr: A graph Gaussian process combines node features and connectivity to learn efficiently from scarce labels.

title: Bayesian Semi-supervised Learning with Graph Gaussian Processes

abstract: Normalization techniques play an important role in supporting efficient and often more effective training of deep neural networks. While conventional methods explicitly normalize the activations, we suggest to add a loss term instead. This new loss term encourages the variance of the activations to be stable and not vary from one random mini-batch to the next. As we prove, this encourages the activations to be distributed around a few distinct modes. We also show that if the inputs are from a mixture of two Gaussians, the new loss would either join the two together, or separate between them optimally in the LDA sense, depending on the prior probabilities. Finally, we are able to link the new regularization term to the batchnorm method, which provides it with a regularization perspective. Our experiments demonstrate an improvement in accuracy over the batchnorm technique for both CNNs and fully connected networks.

paragraphs: Normalization methods help train deep networks by controlling their activations. This paper introduces a loss term that encourages activation variance to remain stable across randomly sampled mini-batches. The quantity being controlled is the variation between batch-level variance estimates, making consistency of those estimates a direct training objective.

The authors prove that this regularizer encourages activations to concentrate around a few distinct modes. They also analyze a specific setting in which the inputs follow a mixture of two Gaussian distributions. Depending on the prior probabilities, the loss either brings the two groups together or separates them optimally in the sense of linear discriminant analysis.

The paper connects the proposed term to batch normalization, providing a regularization interpretation of that method. Experiments report higher accuracy than batch normalization for both convolutional and fully connected networks. Together, the analysis and experiments link a constraint on batch-to-batch variance fluctuations to the shape of learned activation distributions and to improved accuracy in the evaluated networks.
summary.tldr: A loss that stabilizes activation variance across mini-batches encourages distinct modes and improves accuracy over batch normalization in reported experiments.

title: Regularizing by the Variance of the Activations' Sample-Variances

abstract: Frequency-specific patterns of neural activity are traditionally interpreted as sustained rhythmic oscillations, and related to cognitive mechanisms such as attention, high level visual processing or motor control. While alpha waves (8--12\,Hz) are known to closely resemble short sinusoids, and thus are revealed by Fourier analysis or wavelet transforms, there is an evolving debate that electromagnetic neural signals are composed of more complex waveforms that cannot be analyzed by linear filters and traditional signal representations. In this paper, we propose to learn dedicated representations of such recordings using a multivariate convolutional sparse coding (CSC) algorithm. Applied to electroencephalography (EEG) or magnetoencephalography (MEG) data, this method is able to learn not only prototypical temporal waveforms, but also associated spatial patterns so their origin can be localized in the brain. Our algorithm is based on alternated minimization and a greedy coordinate descent solver that leads to state-of-the-art running time on long time series. To demonstrate the implications of this method, we apply it to MEG data and show that it is able to recover biological artifacts. More remarkably, our approach also reveals the presence of non-sinusoidal mu-shaped patterns, along with their topographic maps related to the somatosensory cortex.

paragraphs: Electromagnetic brain activity is often studied through frequency-specific oscillations, but some neural waveforms may have more complex shapes than sinusoids. The paper proposes learning representations directly from recordings so that analysis can capture temporal structure beyond the patterns emphasized by traditional frequency-based representations.

Its multivariate convolutional sparse coding method learns both prototypical temporal waveforms and their associated spatial patterns across EEG or MEG measurements. Linking these two components makes it possible to characterize a waveform and localize its origin in the brain. The representation exposes structure that is relevant to interpreting the recording, while the efficient solver supports applying the approach to long sequences of measurements.
summary.tldr: Multivariate convolutional sparse coding learns brain-signal waveforms and spatial patterns, revealing non-sinusoidal structure in MEG recordings.

title: Multivariate Convolutional Sparse Coding for Electromagnetic Brain Signals

abstract: The widespread online misinformation could cause public panic and serious economic damages. The misinformation containment problem aims at limiting the spread of misinformation in online social networks by launching competing campaigns. Motivated by realistic scenarios, we present the first analysis of the misinformation containment problem for the case when an arbitrary number of cascades are allowed. This paper makes four contributions. First, we provide a formal model for multi-cascade diffusion and introduce an important concept called as cascade priority. Second, we show that the misinformation containment problem cannot be approximated within a factor of $\Omega(2^{\log^{1-\epsilon}n^4})$ in polynomial time unless $NP \subseteq DTIME(n^{\polylog{n}})$. Third, we introduce several types of cascade priority that are frequently seen in real social networks. Finally, we design novel algorithms for solving the misinformation containment problem. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is supported by encouraging experimental results.

paragraphs: Misinformation containment seeks to limit the spread of false information by launching competing campaigns in a social network. This paper examines the problem when an arbitrary number of information cascades can coexist. That setting makes interactions among campaigns central to deciding how a containment effort should operate.

The authors introduce a formal model of multi-cascade diffusion and a concept called cascade priority. They also describe several types of priority that they identify as common in real social networks. This gives the analysis a way to distinguish different forms of competition between spreading campaigns, rather than treating every cascade interaction as interchangeable.

The paper establishes a strong conditional hardness-of-approximation result for the general containment problem: the stated polynomial-time approximation is unavailable unless NP is contained in the specified quasipolynomial deterministic-time class. Alongside that theoretical obstacle, the authors develop algorithms and report encouraging experimental results. The two findings address different questions: the difficulty of broad computational guarantees and the observed effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.
summary.tldr: A multi-cascade model exposes strong conditional computational barriers to misinformation containment and supports algorithms with encouraging experimental results.

title: On Misinformation Containment in Online Social Networks

abstract: Recurrent networks of spiking neurons (RSNNs) underlie the astounding computing and learning capabilities of the brain. But computing and learning capabilities of RSNN models have remained poor, at least in comparison with ANNs. We address two possible reasons for that. One is that RSNNs in the brain are not randomly connected or designed according to simple rules, and they do not start learning as a tabula rasa network. Rather, RSNNs in the brain were optimized for their tasks through evolution, development, and prior experience. Details of these optimization processes are largely unknown. But their functional contribution can be approximated through powerful optimization methods, such as backpropagation through time (BPTT). A second major mismatch between RSNNs in the brain and models is that the latter only show a small fraction of the dynamics of neurons and synapses in the brain. We include neurons in our RSNN model that reproduce one prominent dynamical process of biological neurons that takes place at the behaviourally relevant time scale of seconds: neuronal adaptation. We denote these networks as LSNNs because of their Long short-term memory. The inclusion of adapting neurons drastically increases the computing and learning capability of RSNNs if they are trained and configured by deep learning (BPTT combined with a rewiring algorithm that optimizes the network architecture). In fact, the computational performance of these RSNNs approaches for the first time that of LSTM networks. In addition RSNNs with adapting neurons can acquire abstract knowledge from prior learning in a Learning-to-Learn (L2L) scheme, and transfer that knowledge in order to learn new but related tasks from very few examples. We demonstrate this for supervised learning and reinforcement learning.

The paper demonstrates this in supervised learning and reinforcement learning. These results connect richer neuronal dynamics with both memory and transferable learning, while treating powerful optimization as an approximation to the functional contribution of biological development and prior experience.
summary.tldr: Adapting neurons and deep optimization improve spiking networks' memory and enable transfer to related tasks from very few examples.

title: Long short-term memory and Learning-to-learn in networks of spiking neurons

abstract: In many supervised learning tasks, learning what changes do not affect the predic-tion target is as crucial to generalisation as learning what does. Data augmentationis a common way to enforce a model to exhibit an invariance: training data is modi-fied according to an invariance designed by a human and added to the training data.We argue that invariances should be incorporated the model structure, and learnedusing themarginal likelihood, which can correctly reward the reduced complexityof invariant models. We incorporate invariances in a Gaussian process, due to goodmarginal likelihood approximations being available for these models. Our maincontribution is a derivation for a variational inference scheme for invariant Gaussianprocesses where the invariance is described by a probability distribution that canbe sampled from, much like how data augmentation is implemented in practice
