paragraphs: This paper studies how a model can learn which changes to an input should leave its prediction unchanged. Such invariances are often imposed through data augmentation, where a person chooses transformations and adds modified examples to the training set. The authors argue for placing invariances within the model structure and learning them through marginal likelihood.

Their reasoning is that marginal likelihood can reward the reduction in model complexity that comes from invariance. They use Gaussian processes because suitable approximations to marginal likelihood are available for this model family. This connects the choice of invariance to a probabilistic learning criterion instead of treating the transformation rule only as an external training-data choice.

The main contribution is a variational inference scheme for invariant Gaussian processes. It handles invariance described through a probability distribution from which samples can be drawn, resembling the sampling mechanism used in practical data augmentation. The resulting formulation brings a familiar way of specifying transformations into structured probabilistic inference, making invariance part of the model being learned.
summary.tldr: A variational inference scheme incorporates sampled invariances into Gaussian processes and supports learning them through marginal likelihood.

title: Learning Invariances using the Marginal Likelihood

abstract: Time series clustering is an essential unsupervised technique in cases when category information is not available. It has been widely applied to genome data, anomaly detection, and in general, in any domain where pattern detection is important. Although feature-based time series clustering methods are robust to noise and outliers, and can reduce the dimensionality of the data, they typically rely on domain knowledge to manually construct high-quality features. Sequence to sequence (seq2seq) models can learn representations from sequence data in an unsupervised manner by designing appropriate learning objectives, such as reconstruction and context prediction. When applying seq2seq to time series clustering, obtaining a representation that effectively represents the temporal dynamics of the sequence, multi-scale features, and good clustering properties remains a challenge. How to best improve the ability of the encoder is still an open question. Here we propose a novel unsupervised temporal representation learning model, named Deep Temporal Clustering Representation (DTCR), which integrates the temporal reconstruction and K-means objective into the seq2seq model. This approach leads to improved cluster structures and thus obtains cluster-specific temporal representations. Also, to enhance the ability of encoder, we propose a fake-sample generation strategy and auxiliary classification task. Experiments conducted on extensive time series datasets show that DTCR is state-of-the-art compared to existing methods. The visualization analysis not only shows the effectiveness of cluster-specific representation but also shows the learning process is robust, even if K-means makes mistakes.

paragraphs: Clustering time series requires representations that preserve temporal patterns while making similar sequences easy to group. Handcrafted features can help, but they depend on domain knowledge. This paper proposes Deep Temporal Clustering Representation, or DTCR, to learn cluster-oriented features without category labels.

DTCR combines a sequence-to-sequence model's temporal reconstruction objective with a K-means objective. Reconstruction encourages the representation to retain information about the sequence, while the clustering objective encourages a structure suited to grouping sequences. The authors also introduce generated fake samples and an auxiliary classification task to strengthen the encoder. These additions provide another learning signal within the unsupervised representation-learning framework.

Across extensive time-series experiments, the authors report state-of-the-art performance relative to existing methods. Their visualizations support the usefulness of the cluster-specific representations and show a robust learning process even when K-means makes mistakes. The result suggests that jointly shaping representations and clusters can be effective, instead of assuming a representation learned for reconstruction alone will automatically have the desired clustering structure.
summary.tldr: DTCR jointly learns temporal reconstruction and clustering objectives to produce time-series representations suited to unsupervised grouping.

title: Learning Representations for Time Series Clustering

abstract: Deep neural network (DNN) based salient object detection in images based on high-quality labels is expensive. Alternative unsupervised approaches rely on careful selection of multiple handcrafted saliency methods to generate noisy pseudo-ground-truth labels. In this work, we propose a two-stage mechanism for robust unsupervised object saliency prediction, where the first stage involves refinement of the noisy pseudo labels generated from different handcrafted methods. Each handcrafted method is substituted by a deep network that learns to generate the pseudo labels. These labels are refined incrementally in multiple iterations via our proposed self-supervision technique. In the second stage, the refined labels produced from multiple networks representing multiple saliency methods are used to train the actual saliency detection network. We show that this self-learning procedure outperforms all the existing unsupervised methods over different datasets. Results are even comparable to those of fully-supervised state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Salient object detection identifies objects that stand out in an image. Training deep networks for this task with high-quality labels is expensive, so unsupervised approaches often obtain substitute labels from handcrafted saliency methods. Those substitutes contain noise, making the quality of the automatically generated supervision an important part of the learning problem.

DeepUSPS addresses this with two stages. First, a separate deep network learns to reproduce the pseudo labels from each handcrafted method. A self-supervision procedure then refines these labels incrementally over several iterations. Second, the refined outputs from the collection of networks become the training supervision for the final saliency detector.

This arrangement makes label refinement an explicit step before training the detector that will perform the task. Across the evaluated datasets, the authors report better performance than existing unsupervised methods, with results comparable to fully supervised state-of-the-art approaches. The findings show that iteratively improving noisy supervision can yield strong saliency predictions without the high-quality labels used by supervised methods.
summary.tldr: DeepUSPS iteratively refines automatically generated saliency labels before using them to train a strong unsupervised detector.

title: DeepUSPS: Deep Robust Unsupervised Saliency Prediction via Self-supervision

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Boosting (SGB) is a widely used approach to regularization of boosting models based on decision trees. It was shown that, in many cases, random sampling at each iteration can lead to better generalization performance of the model and can also decrease the learning time. Different sampling approaches were proposed, where probabilities are not uniform, and it is not currently clear which approach is the most effective. In this paper, we formulate the problem of randomization in SGB in terms of optimization of sampling probabilities to maximize the estimation accuracy of split scoring used to train decision trees.This optimization problem has a closed-form nearly optimal solution, and it leads to a new sampling technique, which we call Minimal Variance Sampling (MVS).The method both decreases the number of examples needed for each iteration of boosting and increases the quality of the model significantly as compared to the state-of-the art sampling methods. The superiority of the algorithm was confirmed by introducing MVS as a new default option for subsampling in CatBoost, a gradient boosting library achieving state-of-the-art quality on various machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient boosting trains successive decision trees using sampled data. Sampling can reduce training time and, in many cases, improve generalization, but examples need not all have the same probability of selection. This paper asks how to choose those probabilities according to the accuracy of the estimates used to select tree splits.

The authors formulate sampling as an optimization problem: maximize the estimation accuracy of split scores. They derive a closed-form, nearly optimal solution, leading to Minimal Variance Sampling. This connects the sampling rule directly to a calculation that determines how each decision tree is built, giving the rule a concrete statistical objective.

The paper reports that MVS reduces the number of examples required per boosting iteration while significantly improving model quality compared with leading sampling methods. It also reports adoption as a default subsampling option in CatBoost. The stated benefit is therefore a combination of using less data at each iteration and making those sampled examples more informative for the tree-building process.
summary.tldr: Minimal Variance Sampling chooses boosting samples to improve split-score estimates, reducing examples per iteration while improving reported model quality.

title: Minimal Variance Sampling in Stochastic Gradient Boosting

abstract: As deep learning applications continue to become more diverse, an interesting question arises: Can general problem solving arise from jointly learning several such diverse tasks? To approach this question, deep multi-task learning is extended in this paper to the setting where there is no obvious overlap between task architectures. The idea is that any set of (architecture,task) pairs can be decomposed into a set of potentially related subproblems, whose sharing is optimized by an efficient stochastic algorithm. The approach is first validated in a classic synthetic multi-task learning benchmark, and then applied to sharing across disparate architectures for vision, NLP, and genomics tasks. It discovers regularities across these domains, encodes them into sharable modules, and combines these modules systematically to improve performance in the individual tasks. The results confirm that sharing learned functionality across diverse domains and architectures is indeed beneficial, thus establishing a key ingredient for general problem solving in the future.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning seeks benefits from learning several tasks together. This paper extends that idea to tasks whose neural network architectures have no obvious overlap. The motivating question is whether models from very different domains can still share useful learned functionality, contributing toward more general problem-solving capabilities.

The approach decomposes architecture-and-task pairs into potentially related subproblems. An efficient stochastic algorithm then optimizes which parts should share functionality. Rather than requiring an obvious common architecture at the outset, the method discovers regularities, represents them as shareable modules, and combines those modules to support the individual tasks.

The authors first validate the approach on a standard synthetic multi-task benchmark, then apply it across vision, natural language processing, and genomics architectures. The reported results show that sharing modules across these domains improves individual task performance. This supports the feasibility of useful sharing across disparate architectures; the demonstrated contribution is a component relevant to future general problem solving, rather than a completed general-purpose solver.
summary.tldr: A modular sharing method improves tasks across vision, language, and genomics even when their architectures have no obvious overlap.

title: Modular Universal Reparameterization: Deep Multi-task Learning Across Diverse Domains

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely used in representation learning on graphs and achieved state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, most existing GNNs are designed to learn node representations on the fixed and homogeneous graphs. The limitations especially become problematic when learning representations on a misspecified graph or a heterogeneous graph that consists of various types of nodes and edges. In this paper, we propose Graph Transformer Networks (GTNs) that are capable of generating new graph structures, which involve identifying useful connections between unconnected nodes on the original graph, while learning effective node representation on the new graphs in an end-to-end fashion. Graph Transformer layer, a core layer of GTNs, learns a soft selection of edge types and composite relations for generating useful multi-hop connections so-call meta-paths. Our experiments show that GTNs learn new graph structures, based on data and tasks without domain knowledge, and yield powerful node representation via convolution on the new graphs. Without domain-specific graph preprocessing, GTNs achieved the best performance in all three benchmark node classification tasks against the state-of-the-art methods that require pre-defined meta-paths from domain knowledge.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly learn node representations while treating the supplied graph as fixed. That can be restrictive when its connections are poorly specified or when it contains multiple kinds of nodes and edges. Graph Transformer Networks address this by learning useful graph structures alongside the representations used for the prediction task.

Their central layer learns a soft selection over edge types and combinations of relations. These combinations create multi-hop connections, called meta-paths, that can connect nodes without a direct edge in the original graph. Convolution on the resulting graphs then learns node representations. Structure learning and representation learning operate together in an end-to-end system.

The experiments show that the model can discover useful structures from the data and task without domain-specific graph preprocessing. It achieves the best results on all three reported node-classification benchmarks against methods requiring manually predefined meta-paths. The finding supports learning which relational paths matter for a task, reducing reliance on domain knowledge to prescribe those paths before training.
summary.tldr: Graph Transformer Networks jointly learn useful multi-hop graph connections and node representations without requiring predefined meta-paths.

title: Graph Transformer Networks

abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of interest in combining deep learning models with reasoning in order to handle more sophisticated learning tasks. In many cases, a reasoning task can be solved by an iterative algorithm. This algorithm is often unrolled, and used as a specialized layer in the deep architecture, which can be trained end-to-end with other neural components. Although such hybrid deep architectures have led to many empirical successes, the theoretical foundation of such architectures, especially the interplay between algorithm layers and other neural layers, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we take an initial step towards an understanding of such hybrid deep architectures by showing that properties of the algorithm layers, such as convergence, stability, and sensitivity, are intimately related to the approximation and generalization abilities of the end-to-end model. Furthermore, our analysis matches closely our experimental observations under various conditions, suggesting that our theory can provide useful guidelines for designing deep architectures with reasoning modules (i.e., algorithm layers).

Although such hybrid systems have worked well empirically, the interaction between the algorithmic layer and the surrounding network has lacked a clear theoretical account.

This paper takes an initial step toward that account. It connects properties of the algorithm layer—its convergence, stability, and sensitivity—to the approximation and generalization abilities of the complete model. The analysis therefore treats the reasoning component's behavior as relevant to what the full architecture can represent and how its learned behavior extends beyond training examples.

The authors report that their analysis closely matches experimental observations under various conditions. This agreement suggests that algorithm-layer properties can inform architecture design, rather than leaving the reasoning module's selection entirely to empirical trial. The contribution is an initial theoretical framework with supporting experiments, and the stated implication is that it may provide useful design guidance for hybrid networks containing reasoning modules.
summary.tldr: Theoretical links between reasoning-layer behavior and whole-network approximation and generalization offer guidance for designing hybrid neural architectures.

title: Understanding Deep Architecture with Reasoning Layer

abstract: Ensembles of deep neural networks are known to achieve state-of-the-art performance in uncertainty estimation and lead to accuracy improvement. In this work, we focus on a classification problem and investigate the behavior of both non-calibrated and calibrated negative log-likelihood (CNLL) of a deep ensemble as a function of the ensemble size and the member network size. We indicate the conditions under which CNLL follows a power law w. r. t. ensemble size or member network size, and analyze the dynamics of the parameters of the discovered power laws. Our important practical finding is that one large network may perform worse than an ensemble of several medium-size networks with the same total number of parameters (we call this ensemble a memory split). Using the detected power law-like dependencies, we can predict (1) the possible gain from the ensembling of networks with given structure, (2) the optimal memory split given a memory budget, based on a relatively small number of trained networks.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks into an ensemble can improve classification accuracy and uncertainty estimation. This paper studies how ensemble quality changes with both the number of member networks and the size of each member. It examines negative log-likelihood before and after calibration, focusing on how the model assigns probabilities to labels.

The authors identify conditions under which calibrated negative log-likelihood follows a power law as ensemble size or member size changes. They also analyze how the parameters of these relationships behave. A practical finding is that several medium-sized networks can outperform one larger network with the same total number of parameters, an allocation they call a memory split.

The detected power-law-like patterns can help predict the benefit of adding ensemble members and the optimal memory split for a given budget. These predictions use a relatively small number of trained networks. The contribution therefore connects measured scaling behavior to model-allocation decisions, while preserving the conditional nature of the power laws and the possible advantage of an ensemble over a single network.
summary.tldr: Conditional power-law patterns help predict ensemble gains and how to divide a fixed parameter budget among networks.

title: On Power Laws in Deep Ensembles

abstract: Missing Not At Random (MNAR) values where the probability of having missing data may depend on the missing value itself, are notoriously difficult to account for in analyses, although very frequent in the data. One solution to handle MNAR data is to specify a model for the missing data mechanism, which makes inference or imputation tasks more complex. Furthermore, this implies a strong \textit{a priori} on the parametric form of the distribution. However, some works have obtained guarantees on the estimation of parameters in the presence of MNAR data, without specifying the distribution of missing data \citep{mohan2018estimation, tang2003analysis}. This is very useful in practice, but is limited to simple cases such as few self-masked MNAR variables in data generated according to linear regression models. We continue this line of research, but extend it to a more general MNAR mechanism, in a more general model of the probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA), \textit{i.e.}, a low-rank model with random effects. We prove identifiability of the PPCA parameters. We then propose an estimation of the loading coefficients, and a data imputation method. Both are based on estimators of means, variances and covariances of missing variables, for which consistency is discussed. These estimators have the great advantage of being calculated using only the observed information, leveraging the underlying low-rank structure of the data. We illustrate the relevance of the method with numerical experiments on synthetic data and also on two datasets, one collected from a medical register and the other one from a recommendation system.

This paper extends work on recovering information under such missingness without specifying its distribution, using probabilistic principal component analysis.

The result connects structural assumptions about the data to estimation despite value-dependent missingness.
summary.tldr: A low-rank probabilistic model supports parameter estimation and imputation when missingness depends on unseen values, without specifying the missingness distribution.

title: Estimation and Imputation in Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis with Missing Not At Random Data

abstract: This paper introduces Deep Statistical Solvers (DSS), a new class of trainable solvers for optimization problems, arising e.g., from system simulations. The key idea is to learn a solver that generalizes to a given distribution of problem instances. This is achieved by directly using as loss the objective function of the problem, as opposed to most previous Machine Learning based approaches, which mimic the solutions attained by an existing solver. Though both types of approaches outperform classical solvers with respect to speed for a given accuracy, a distinctive advantage of DSS is that they can be trained without a training set of sample solutions. Focusing on use cases of systems of interacting and interchangeable entities (e.g. molecular dynamics, power systems, discretized PDEs), the proposed approach is instantiated within a class of Graph Neural Networks. Under sufficient conditions, we prove that the corresponding set of functions contains approximations to any arbitrary precision of the actual solution of the optimization problem. The proposed approach is experimentally validated on large linear problems, demonstrating super-generalisation properties; And on AC power grid simulations, on which the predictions of the trained model have a correlation higher than 99.99% with the outputs of the classical Newton-Raphson method (known for its accuracy), while being 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Deep Statistical Solvers learn to solve optimization problems drawn from a particular distribution of instances. Their training loss is the optimization objective itself, so training does not require a collection of answers produced by an existing solver. This removes the need to generate sample solutions before learning can begin.

The paper develops this idea using graph neural networks for systems composed of interacting, interchangeable entities, including power systems and discretized physical equations. Under sufficient conditions, the authors prove that the resulting function class can approximate the actual optimization solution to arbitrary precision. This is a statement about what the function class can represent under those conditions, rather than a guarantee that every training run finds such an approximation.

Experiments cover large linear problems and AC power grid simulations. On the power grid tasks, predictions correlate above 99.99% with Newton–Raphson outputs while running two to three orders of magnitude faster. The reported correlation and speed illustrate the practical promise of learning a solver tailored to a distribution of problems.
summary.tldr: Deep Statistical Solvers train directly on optimization objectives, avoiding example solutions while achieving substantial reported speedups on power grid simulations.

title: Deep Statistical Solvers

abstract: Orthogonal Monte Carlo (OMC) is a very effective sampling algorithm imposing structural geometric conditions (orthogonality) on samples for variance reduction. Due to its simplicity and superior performance as compared to its Quasi Monte Carlo counterparts, OMC is used in a wide spectrum of challenging machine learning applications ranging from scalable kernel methods to predictive recurrent neural networks, generative models and reinforcement learning. However theoretical understanding of the method remains very limited. In this paper we shed new light on the theoretical principles behind OMC, applying theory of negatively dependent random variables to obtain several new concentration results. As a corollary, we manage to obtain first uniform convergence results for OMCs and consequently, substantially strengthen best known downstream guarantees for kernel ridge regression via OMCs. We also propose novel extensions of the method leveraging theory of algebraic varieties over finite fields and particle algorithms, called Near-Orthogonal Monte Carlo (NOMC). We show that NOMC is the first algorithm consistently outperforming OMC in applications ranging from kernel methods to approximating distances in probabilistic metric spaces.

paragraphs: Orthogonal Monte Carlo reduces sampling variance by imposing geometric structure on samples: their directions are orthogonal. Although the method has proved useful across machine learning applications, the paper identifies a gap between its practical success and its theoretical explanation. The authors investigate how dependence among these structured samples supports reliable estimates.

Their analysis uses the theory of negatively dependent random variables to establish new concentration results. Such results describe how estimates stay close to their targets. From these, the authors derive the first uniform convergence results for Orthogonal Monte Carlo and substantially strengthen existing guarantees for its use in kernel ridge regression. The contribution therefore connects sampling geometry to downstream learning guarantees.

The authors report that these extensions consistently outperform Orthogonal Monte Carlo across the applications examined, including kernel methods and distance approximation in probabilistic metric spaces. The work thus combines a stronger explanation of an established method with proposed improvements to its sampling strategy.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for Orthogonal Monte Carlo and introduces near-orthogonal extensions with better reported application performance.

title: Demystifying Orthogonal Monte Carlo and Beyond

abstract: Intelligent agents are continuously faced with the challenge of optimizing a policy based on what they can observe (see) and which actions they can take (do) in the environment where they are deployed. Most policies can be parametrized in terms of these two dimensions, i.e., as a function of what can be seen and done given a certain situation, which we call a mixed policy. In this paper, we investigate several properties of the class of mixed policies and provide an efficient and effective characterization, including optimality and non-redundancy. Specifically, we introduce a graphical criterion to identify unnecessary contexts for a set of actions, leading to a natural characterization of non-redundancy of mixed policies. We then derive sufficient conditions under which one strategy can dominate the other with respect to their maximum achievable expected rewards (optimality). This characterization leads to a fundamental understanding of the space of mixed policies and a possible refinement of the agent's strategy so that it converges to the optimum faster and more robustly. One surprising result of the causal characterization is that the agent following a more standard approach --- intervening on all intervenable variables and observing all available contexts --- may be hurting itself, and will never achieve an optimal performance.

paragraphs: An agent's strategy depends both on what it can observe and on which parts of its environment it can change. This paper studies these choices together as mixed policies. The central question is how the available observations and interventions affect the best expected reward a strategy can achieve.

The authors introduce a graphical criterion for identifying contexts that are unnecessary for a given set of actions. This provides a characterization of policies without redundant context. They also derive sufficient conditions for one strategy to dominate another in maximum achievable expected reward. Sufficient conditions establish cases where dominance holds without claiming to capture every possible case.

A striking consequence is that intervening on every available variable while observing every available context can, in some settings, prevent optimal performance. More extensive intervention is therefore not automatically a better strategy. The characterization offers a possible route to refining an agent's choices so learning reaches an optimum faster and more robustly. That improvement is presented as a potential consequence of the analysis, rather than a universal convergence result.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes useful observations and interventions, showing that acting on every available variable can sometimes prevent optimal performance.

title: Characterizing Optimal Mixed Policies: Where to Intervene and What to Observe

abstract: Decision trees with binary splits are popularly constructed using Classification and Regression Trees (CART) methodology. For regression models, this approach recursively divides the data into two near-homogenous daughter nodes according to a split point that maximizes the reduction in sum of squares error (the impurity) along a particular variable. This paper aims to study the statistical properties of regression trees constructed with CART methodology. In doing so, we find that the training error is governed by the Pearson correlation between the optimal decision stump and response data in each node, which we bound by constructing a prior distribution on the split points and solving a nonlinear optimization problem. We leverage this connection between the training error and Pearson correlation to show that CART with cost-complexity pruning achieves an optimal complexity/goodness-of-fit tradeoff when the depth scales with the logarithm of the sample size. Data dependent quantities, which adapt to the dimensionality and latent structure of the regression model, are seen to govern the convergence rates of the prediction error.

paragraphs: CART regression trees repeatedly split data into two groups, selecting a variable and split point that most reduce squared-error impurity. This paper studies the statistical behavior of that familiar procedure. It asks what controls training error and how tree construction and pruning can balance model complexity against fit.

The analysis links training error to the Pearson correlation between the response and the best single-split predictor within each node. To bound that correlation, the authors construct a prior distribution over split points and solve a nonlinear optimization problem. This connection translates the quality of local splits into a tool for understanding the tree’s overall fit.

Using that relationship, the paper shows that CART with cost-complexity pruning achieves an optimal complexity-versus-fit tradeoff when depth scales logarithmically with sample size. Prediction-error convergence rates are governed by data-dependent quantities that adapt to dimensionality and hidden regression structure. The result explains how the statistical behavior of CART can reflect the structure of the particular learning problem.
summary.tldr: A correlation-based analysis explains CART’s training error and establishes an optimal pruning tradeoff when tree depth scales logarithmically with sample size.

title: Sparse Learning with CART

abstract: Goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) is a promising approach for scaling up reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. However, it often suffers from training inefficiency as the action space of the high-level, i.e., the goal space, is often large. Searching in a large goal space poses difficulties for both high-level subgoal generation and low-level policy learning. In this paper, we show that this problem can be effectively alleviated by restricting the high-level action space from the whole goal space to a k-step adjacent region of the current state using an adjacency constraint. We theoretically prove that the proposed adjacency constraint preserves the optimal hierarchical policy in deterministic MDPs, and show that this constraint can be practically implemented by training an adjacency network that can discriminate between adjacent and non-adjacent subgoals. Experimental results on discrete and continuous control tasks show that incorporating the adjacency constraint improves the performance of state-of-the-art HRL approaches in both deterministic and stochastic environments.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning divides decision-making between a high-level policy that chooses subgoals and a low-level policy that pursues them. When the high-level policy can choose from a very large goal space, both selecting goals and learning to reach them become difficult. This paper addresses that search burden by restricting which subgoals are considered.

The proposed adjacency constraint limits high-level choices to a region reachable within k steps of the current state. A learned adjacency network distinguishes nearby subgoals from non-adjacent ones, making the restriction practical to implement. This narrows the high-level action space and simplifies the subgoal choices presented to the low-level learner.

The authors prove that the restriction preserves an optimal hierarchical policy in deterministic Markov decision processes. Experiments on discrete and continuous control tasks show improved performance when the constraint is added to leading hierarchical methods. Those empirical gains occur in both deterministic and stochastic environments; the policy-preservation theorem specifically applies to the deterministic setting. The results connect a smaller search space with more effective hierarchical learning.
summary.tldr: Restricting hierarchical subgoals to a learned k-step neighborhood improves learning and preserves optimal hierarchical policies in deterministic environments.

title: Generating Adjacency-Constrained Subgoals in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Contemporary coding education often presents students with the task of developing programs that have user interaction and complex dynamic systems, such as mouse based games. While pedagogically compelling, there are no contemporary autonomous methods for providing feedback. Notably, interactive programs are impossible to grade by traditional unit tests. In this paper we formalize the challenge of providing feedback to interactive programs as a task of classifying Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Each student's program fully specifies an MDP where the agent needs to operate and decide, under reasonable generalization, if the dynamics and reward model of the input MDP should be categorized as correct or broken. We demonstrate that by designing a cooperative objective between an agent and an autoregressive model, we can use the agent to sample differential trajectories from the input MDP that allows a classifier to determine membership: Play to Grade. Our method enables an automatic feedback system for interactive code assignments. We release a dataset of 711,274 anonymized student submissions to a single assignment with hand-coded bug labels to support future research.

The proposed method, Play to Grade, combines an agent with an autoregressive model through a cooperative objective. The agent interacts with the submitted program to collect differential trajectories: sequences of behavior that help a classifier distinguish the relevant categories. This connects the choice of interactions to the grading decision, so the system gathers behavioral evidence by playing the program.

The authors demonstrate that this design enables automatic feedback for interactive code assignments. They also release 711,274 anonymized student submissions with manually assigned bug labels. All submissions come from a single assignment, giving the research community a large dataset within that particular educational setting. The contribution combines a formal view of interactive grading with a method for collecting evidence and a resource for further study.
summary.tldr: Play to Grade learns to interact with student programs and use their resulting behavior to classify them as correct or broken.

title: Play to Grade: Testing Coding Games as Classifying Markov Decision Process

abstract: Machine learning has successfully framed many sequential decision making problems as either supervised prediction, or optimal decision-making policy identification via reinforcement learning. In data-constrained offline settings, both approaches may fail as they assume fully optimal behavior or rely on exploring alternatives that may not exist. We introduce an inherently different approach that identifies "dead-ends" of a state space. We focus on patient condition in the intensive care unit, where a "medical dead-end" indicates that a patient will expire, regardless of all potential future treatment sequences. We postulate "treatment security" as avoiding treatments with probability proportional to their chance of leading to dead-ends, present a formal proof, and frame discovery as an RL problem. We then train three independent deep neural models for automated state construction, dead-end discovery and confirmation. Our empirical results discover that dead-ends exist in real clinical data among septic patients, and further reveal gaps between secure treatments and those administered.

The paper's defining shift is to learn about routes toward unavoidable failure, rather than making optimal treatment-policy identification the central objective.
summary.tldr: The paper learns to identify medical dead-ends and treatments that risk reaching them, finding gaps between secure and administered treatments in sepsis data.

title: Medical Dead-ends and Learning to Identify High-Risk States and Treatments

abstract: Recent advances in deep neural networks allowed artificial agents to derive their own emergent languages that promote interaction, coordination, and collaboration within a group. Just as we humans have succeeded in creating a shared language that allows us to interact within a large group, can the emergent communication within an artificial group converge to a shared, agreed language? This research provides an analytical study of the shared emergent language within the group communication settings of different sizes and connectivities. As the group size increases up to hundreds, agents start to speak dissimilar languages, but the rate at which they successfully communicate is maintained. We observe the emergence of different dialects when we restrict the group communication to have local connectivities only. Finally, we provide optimization results of group communication graphs when the number of agents one can communicate with is restricted or when we penalize communication between distant agent pairs. The optimized communication graphs show superior communication success rates compared to graphs with same number of links as well as the emergence of hub nodes and scale-free networks.

paragraphs: Artificial agents can develop communication systems that help them coordinate. This paper asks whether a larger community of agents converges on a shared language, and how the pattern of permitted communication affects that outcome. It studies both group size and the connectivity of the communication network.

As groups grow to hundreds of agents, their languages become less similar, yet their rate of successful communication is maintained. Restricting interactions to local connections produces distinct dialects. These observations separate two outcomes that might otherwise seem interchangeable: using a common language and communicating successfully within a group.

The authors also optimize communication networks when each agent has a limited number of contacts or communication between distant pairs carries a penalty. The optimized networks achieve better communication success than comparison networks with the same number of links. Hub nodes and scale-free network structures emerge in these results, connecting the organization of agent interactions with the effectiveness of their learned communication.
summary.tldr: Agent communities can maintain successful communication despite diverging languages, while connectivity shapes dialects and the benefits of network optimization.

title: Emergent Communication under Varying Sizes and Connectivities

abstract: Most prior methods for learning navigation policies require access to simulation environments, as they need online policy interaction and rely on ground-truth maps for rewards. However, building simulators is expensive (requires manual effort for each and every scene) and creates challenges in transferring learned policies to robotic platforms in the real-world, due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this paper, we pose a simple question: Do we really need active interaction, ground-truth maps or even reinforcement-learning (RL) in order to solve the image-goal navigation task? We propose a self-supervised approach to learn to navigate from only passive videos of roaming. Our approach, No RL, No Simulator (NRNS), is simple and scalable, yet highly effective. NRNS outperforms RL-based formulations by a significant margin. We present NRNS as a strong baseline for any future image-based navigation tasks that use RL or Simulation.

paragraphs: Learning image-goal navigation often relies on a simulator where a policy can interact with an environment and receive rewards derived from ground-truth maps. Building those simulators requires manual work for individual scenes. Differences between simulated and real environments also complicate transferring learned navigation policies to robots.

This paper asks whether those training requirements are necessary for the image-goal task. Its method, No RL, No Simulator, or NRNS, learns through a self-supervised approach using only passive videos of roaming. The training information therefore comes from recorded movement, without requiring the learning policy to actively collect interactions, access ground-truth maps, or train through reinforcement learning.

The authors describe NRNS as simple and scalable and report that it outperforms reinforcement-learning-based formulations by a significant margin. They propose it as a strong baseline for future image-based navigation research using RL or simulation. The finding establishes passive video learning as a competitive approach in the studied setting and challenges the assumed need for interactive simulator training.
summary.tldr: NRNS learns image-goal navigation from passive roaming videos and reports substantial gains over reinforcement-learning-based approaches.

title: No RL, No Simulation: Learning to Navigate without Navigating

abstract: We address the novel task of jointly reconstructing the 3D shape, texture, and motion of an object from a single motion-blurred image. While previous approaches address the deblurring problem only in the 2D image domain, our proposed rigorous modeling of all object properties in the 3D domain enables the correct description of arbitrary object motion. This leads to significantly better image decomposition and sharper deblurring results. We model the observed appearance of a motion-blurred object as a combination of the background and a 3D object with constant translation and rotation. Our method minimizes a loss on reconstructing the input image via differentiable rendering with suitable regularizers. This enables estimating the textured 3D mesh of the blurred object with high fidelity. Our method substantially outperforms competing approaches on several benchmarks for fast moving objects deblurring. Qualitative results show that the reconstructed 3D mesh generates high-quality temporal super-resolution and novel views of the deblurred object.

paragraphs: A single motion-blurred photograph mixes information about an object's appearance and its movement. This paper attempts to recover the object's three-dimensional shape, texture, and motion together. Modeling these properties in three dimensions provides a way to explain the blurred observation through the moving object that produced it.

The method represents the image as a combination of a background and a three-dimensional object undergoing constant translation and rotation. It uses differentiable rendering to reconstruct the input image, then adjusts the estimated object and motion to minimize reconstruction loss with regularization. The constant-motion model is a stated assumption of this reconstruction procedure.

The authors report high-fidelity textured meshes and substantially better fast-object deblurring than competing approaches on several benchmarks. The three-dimensional representation also supports outputs beyond a sharper version of the original photograph. Qualitative results show novel viewpoints and temporal super-resolution, producing views of the recovered object at finer temporal intervals. These findings demonstrate how explaining blur through geometry and motion can improve image decomposition while enabling additional renderings of the object.
summary.tldr: The method fits a moving textured 3D object to one blurred image, improving deblurring and enabling new views.

title: Shape from Blur: Recovering Textured 3D Shape and Motion of Fast Moving Objects

abstract: Equivariant networks capture the inductive bias about the symmetry of the learning task by building those symmetries into the model. In this paper, we study how equivariance relates to generalization error utilizing PAC Bayesian analysis for equivariant networks, where the transformation laws of feature spaces are deter- mined by group representations. By using perturbation analysis of equivariant networks in Fourier domain for each layer, we derive norm-based PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. The bound characterizes the impact of group size, and multiplicity and degree of irreducible representations on the generalization error and thereby provide a guideline for selecting them. In general, the bound indicates that using larger group size in the model improves the generalization error substantiated by extensive numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks build assumptions about symmetry directly into their architecture: transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation in its features. This paper asks how that architectural choice relates to generalization, meaning performance beyond the training data. It studies networks whose feature transformations are specified through mathematical group representations.

The authors analyze how perturbations affect each layer in the Fourier domain and use this analysis to derive norm-based PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. These bounds connect generalization error to several design choices: the size of the symmetry group, the dimensions of its irreducible representations, and how many times those representations appear in the network.

The resulting theory offers guidance for choosing how a network represents symmetry, rather than treating equivariance as a single architectural switch. In general, the bound favors larger groups, and numerical experiments support that tendency. The finding is a relationship expressed through the bound and supported empirically, rather than an unconditional promise that increasing symmetry always improves every model.
summary.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian analysis connects equivariant networks’ generalization to symmetry-group size and representation choices.

title: A PAC-Bayesian Generalization Bound for Equivariant Networks

abstract: Self-supervised models are increasingly prevalent in machine learning (ML) since they reduce the need for expensively labeled data. Because of their versatility in downstream applications, they are increasingly used as a service exposed via public APIs. At the same time, these encoder models are particularly vulnerable to model stealing attacks due to the high dimensionality of vector representations they output. Yet, encoders remain undefended: existing mitigation strategies for stealing attacks focus on supervised learning. We introduce a new dataset inference defense, which uses the private training set of the victim encoder model to attribute its ownership in the event of stealing. The intuition is that the log-likelihood of an encoder's output representations is higher on the victim's training data than on test data if it is stolen from the victim, but not if it is independently trained. We compute this log-likelihood using density estimation models. As part of our evaluation, we also propose measuring the fidelity of stolen encoders and quantifying the effectiveness of the theft detection without involving downstream tasks; instead, we leverage mutual information and distance measurements. Our extensive empirical results in the vision domain demonstrate that dataset inference is a promising direction for defending self-supervised models against model stealing.

paragraphs: Self-supervised encoders produce vector representations that can support many downstream applications. When exposed through public APIs, those rich outputs also make the encoders vulnerable to copying. This paper proposes a dataset inference defense that uses an encoder owner's private training data to help attribute ownership of a suspected stolen model.

The proposed signal is a difference between representations of training and test examples. The authors' intuition is that a stolen encoder assigns higher representation log-likelihood to the original encoder's training data than to test data, whereas an independently trained encoder does not show that same pattern. Density estimation models provide the likelihood estimates used to investigate this distinction.

The paper also proposes evaluating copying fidelity and theft detection directly at the representation level. It uses mutual information and distance measurements, avoiding the need to choose downstream tasks for these evaluations. Experiments in vision support dataset inference as a promising defense direction. The contribution concerns detecting and attributing copying through a training-data signature, with the reported support coming from empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Dataset inference uses representation likelihoods on an owner's private training data to help identify stolen self-supervised encoders.

title: Dataset Inference for Self-Supervised Models

abstract: Prediction failures of machine learning models often arise from deficiencies in training data, such as incorrect labels, outliers, and selection biases. However, such data points that are responsible for a given failure mode are generally not known a priori, let alone a mechanism for repairing the failure. This work draws on the Bayesian view of continual learning, and develops a generic framework for both, identifying training examples which have given rise to the target failure, and fixing the model through erasing information about them. This framework naturally allows leveraging recent advances in continual learning to this new problem of model repairment, while subsuming the existing works on influence functions and data deletion as specific instances. Experimentally, the proposed approach outperforms the baselines for both identification of detrimental training data and fixing model failures in a generalisable manner.

paragraphs: A model's prediction failures can originate in its training data, including wrong labels, unusual examples, or selection bias. Repair is difficult because the examples responsible for a particular failure are usually unknown. The paper addresses identification and correction together: it seeks the training examples behind a target failure and then removes their influence from the model.

The framework draws on a Bayesian view of continual learning, which studies how models retain and update information across learning experiences. Here, that perspective is used to erase information associated with detrimental examples. This creates a connection between techniques for managing learned information over time and techniques for repairing an already trained network.

The authors show that existing approaches based on influence functions and data deletion fit within the framework as special cases. Experiments outperform the compared baselines both in identifying harmful training examples and in correcting model failures in a generalizable way. The stated findings support addressing the training-data source of a failure as part of the repair procedure itself.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian continual-learning framework repairs model failures by identifying detrimental training examples and erasing information about them.

title: Repairing Neural Networks by Leaving the Right Past Behind

abstract: Designing physical artifacts that serve a purpose---such as tools and other functional structures---is central to engineering as well as everyday human behavior. Though automating design using machine learning has tremendous promise, existing methods are often limited by the task-dependent distributions they were exposed to during training. Here we showcase a task-agnostic approach to inverse design, by combining general-purpose graph network simulators with gradient-based design optimization. This constitutes a simple, fast, and reusable approach that solves high-dimensional problems with complex physical dynamics, including designing surfaces and tools to manipulate fluid flows and optimizing the shape of an airfoil to minimize drag. This framework produces high-quality designs by propagating gradients through trajectories of hundreds of steps, even when using models that were pre-trained for single-step predictions on data substantially different from the design tasks. In our fluid manipulation tasks, the resulting designs outperformed those found by sampling-based optimization techniques. In airfoil design, they matched the quality of those obtained with a specialized solver. Our results suggest that despite some remaining challenges, machine learning-based simulators are maturing to the point where they can support general-purpose design optimization across a variety of fluid-structure interaction domains.

This paper combines general-purpose graph network simulators with gradient-based optimization to design objects involved in fluid interactions. summary.tldr: Graph network simulators guide gradient-based design of fluid-interacting structures, with strong results beyond their original training tasks.

title: Inverse Design for Fluid-Structure Interactions using Graph Network Simulators

abstract: Accurately predicting the relevance of items to users is crucial to the success of many social platforms. Conventional approaches train models on logged historical data; but recommendation systems, media services, and online marketplaces all exhibit a constant influx of new content---making relevancy a moving target, to which standard predictive models are not robust. In this paper, we propose a learning framework for relevance prediction that is robust to changes in the data distribution. Our key observation is that robustness can be obtained by accounting for \emph{how users causally perceive the environment}. We model users as boundedly-rational decision makers whose causal beliefs are encoded by a causal graph, and show how minimal information regarding the graph can be used to contend with distributional changes. Experiments in multiple settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Predicting which items users find relevant becomes difficult when a platform continually receives new content. A model trained on historical interactions faces a changing distribution of items and responses. The paper addresses this instability in settings such as recommendation systems, media services, and online marketplaces.

Its central idea is to account for how users believe their environment works causally. The framework represents users as boundedly rational decision makers and encodes their causal beliefs in a graph. The graph therefore concerns the user’s perception of causal relationships, which becomes part of the relevance prediction model.

The authors show how even limited information about this graph can help address changes in the data distribution. The proposed route to robustness is to incorporate information about the process behind users’ judgments, rather than relying entirely on historical predictive relationships. Experiments in multiple settings demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness, supporting causal user modeling as a useful ingredient for relevance prediction under changing content.
summary.tldr: Modeling users’ causal beliefs helps relevance predictors cope with changes in the content and data they encounter.

title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Robust Prediction with Causal User Modeling

abstract: While neural architecture search (NAS) has enabled automated machine learning (AutoML) for well-researched areas, its application to tasks beyond computer vision is still under-explored. As less-studied domains are precisely those where we expect AutoML to have the greatest impact, in this work we study NAS for efficiently solving diverse problems. Seeking an approach that is fast, simple, and broadly applicable, we fix a standard convolutional network (CNN) topology and propose to search for the right kernel sizes and dilations its operations should take on. This dramatically expands the model's capacity to extract features at multiple resolutions for different types of data while only requiring search over the operation space. To overcome the efficiency challenges of naive weight-sharing in this search space, we introduce DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that computes the mixture-of-operations using the Fourier diagonalization of convolution, achieving both a better asymptotic complexity and an up-to-10x search time speedup in practice. We evaluate DASH on ten tasks spanning a variety of application domains such as PDE solving, protein folding, and heart disease detection. DASH outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML methods in aggregate, attaining the best-known automated performance on seven tasks. Meanwhile, on six of the ten tasks, the combined search and retraining time is less than 2x slower than simply training a CNN backbone that is far less accurate.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates choices about a network’s design, but its use beyond well-studied vision tasks remains comparatively limited. This paper seeks a simple search strategy for diverse problems. It fixes the overall structure of a convolutional network and searches over the kernel sizes and dilations of its operations.

Those choices change the resolutions at which the network can extract features without requiring a search over its entire topology. The proposed algorithm, DASH, makes this operation search more efficient by using Fourier diagonalization of convolution to compute mixtures of candidate operations. These results support targeted operation search as an efficient route to adapting networks across domains.
summary.tldr: DASH efficiently searches convolution sizes and dilations, achieving strong automated performance across ten diverse tasks.

title: Efficient Architecture Search for Diverse Tasks

abstract: As the curation of data for machine learning becomes increasingly automated, dataset tampering is a mounting threat. Backdoor attackers tamper with training data to embed a vulnerability in models that are trained on that data. This vulnerability is then activated at inference time by placing a "trigger'' into the model's input. Typical backdoor attacks insert the trigger directly into the training data, although the presence of such an attack may be visible upon inspection. In contrast, the Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack achieves poisoning without placing a trigger into the training data at all. However, this hidden trigger attack is ineffective at poisoning neural networks trained from scratch. We develop a new hidden trigger attack, Sleeper Agent, which employs gradient matching, data selection, and target model re-training during the crafting process. Sleeper Agent is the first hidden trigger backdoor attack to be effective against neural networks trained from scratch. We demonstrate its effectiveness on ImageNet and in black-box settings. Our implementation code can be found at: https://github.com/hsouri/Sleeper-Agent.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks tamper with training data so that a model later exhibits a vulnerability when a trigger appears in its input. Conventional attacks place the trigger directly in training examples, where inspection may reveal it. Hidden-trigger attacks seek to create the vulnerability without putting that trigger into the training data.

The paper addresses a weakness of an existing hidden-trigger approach: it does not effectively poison networks trained from scratch. The proposed attack, Sleeper Agent, combines gradient matching, data selection, and retraining of the target model during the crafting process. These components are used together to create poisoned data that affect the eventual trained network.

The authors report that Sleeper Agent is the first effective hidden-trigger backdoor attack against networks trained from scratch. They demonstrate effectiveness on ImageNet and in black-box settings. The finding expands the demonstrated reach of hidden-trigger poisoning: the absence of the eventual trigger from training examples does not prevent such a vulnerability from being learned in the settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: Sleeper Agent demonstrates hidden-trigger backdoor poisoning against neural networks trained from scratch, including ImageNet and black-box settings.

title: Sleeper Agent: Scalable Hidden Trigger Backdoors for Neural Networks Trained from Scratch

abstract: We study reward-free reinforcement learning (RL) under general non-linear function approximation, and establish sample efficiency and hardness results under various standard structural assumptions. On the positive side, we propose the RFOLIVE (Reward-Free OLIVE) algorithm for sample-efficient reward-free exploration under minimal structural assumptions, which covers the previously studied settings of linear MDPs (Jin et al., 2020b), linear completeness (Zanette et al., 2020b) and low-rank MDPs with unknown representation (Modi et al., 2021). Our analyses indicate that the explorability or reachability assumptions, previously made for the latter two settings, are not necessary statistically for reward-free exploration. On the negative side, we provide a statistical hardness result for both reward-free and reward-aware exploration under linear completeness assumptions when the underlying features are unknown, showing an exponential separation between low-rank and linear completeness settings.
originalAbstract: We study reward-free reinforcement learning (RL) under general non-linear function approximation, and establish sample efficiency and hardness results under various standard structural assumptions. On the positive side, we propose the RFOLIVE (Reward-Free OLIVE) algorithm for sample-efficient reward-free exploration under minimal structural assumptions, which covers the previously studied settings of linear MDPs (Jin et al., 2020b), linear completeness (Zanette et al., 2020b) and low-rank MDPs with unknown representation (Modi et al., 2021). Our analyses indicate that the explorability or reachability assumptions, previously made for the latter two settings, are not necessary statistically for reward-free exploration. paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning studies exploration without using a reward objective to guide the data collection. This paper examines its sample requirements with general nonlinear function approximation. The focus is on which structural assumptions permit efficient exploration and which leave the problem statistically difficult.

Their analysis shows that previously used explorability or reachability assumptions are not statistically necessary in the latter two settings. This removes particular requirements from the sample-efficiency account.

In that case, the authors establish statistical difficulty for both reward-free and reward-aware exploration, yielding an exponential separation from the low-rank setting. Together, the results show that closely related structural descriptions can imply very different data requirements, and that knowing the features matters to how these guarantees should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: RFOLIVE broadens sample-efficient reward-free exploration, while hardness results separate unknown-feature linear completeness from low-rank models.

title: On the Statistical Efficiency of Reward-Free Exploration in Non-Linear RL

abstract: The Transformer architecture has achieved remarkable success in a number of domains including natural language processing and computer vision. However, when it comes to graph-structured data, transformers have not achieved competitive performance, especially on large graphs. In this paper, we identify the main deficiencies of current graph transformers: (1) Existing node sampling strategies in Graph Transformers are agnostic to the graph characteristics and the training process. (2) Most sampling strategies only focus on local neighbors and neglect the long-range dependencies in the graph. We conduct experimental investigations on synthetic datasets to show that existing sampling strategies are sub-optimal. To tackle the aforementioned problems, we formulate the optimization strategies of node sampling in Graph Transformer as an adversary bandit problem, where the rewards are related to the attention weights and can vary in the training procedure. Meanwhile, we propose a hierarchical attention scheme with graph coarsening to capture the long-range interactions while reducing computational complexity. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets to demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing graph transformers and popular GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph transformers must choose which nodes to consider, especially when graphs are large. This paper identifies two weaknesses in existing choices: sampling often ignores graph characteristics and changes during training, and it tends to concentrate on nearby nodes. Synthetic-data experiments show that these sampling strategies can be suboptimal.

The proposed method treats node sampling as an adversarial bandit problem. Rewards depend on attention weights and can change as training progresses, allowing sampling decisions to respond to the learning process. A second component introduces hierarchical attention with graph coarsening, representing the graph at a coarser level to capture interactions over longer distances while reducing computational complexity.

Experiments on real-world datasets show the method outperforming the evaluated graph transformers and popular graph neural networks. Its contribution combines adaptive selection with a hierarchy for distant interactions. These components address complementary issues: which nodes receive attention during learning, and how the model can represent relationships that extend beyond a local neighborhood.
summary.tldr: Adaptive node sampling and hierarchical attention improve graph transformer performance while supporting longer-range interactions at lower computational complexity.

title: Hierarchical Graph Transformer with Adaptive Node Sampling

abstract: We introduce a novel paradigm for offline Video Instance Segmentation (VIS), based on the hypothesis that explicit object-oriented information can be a strong clue for understanding the context of the entire sequence. To this end, we propose VITA, a simple structure built on top of an off-the-shelf Transformer-based image instance segmentation model. Specifically, we use an image object detector as a means of distilling object-specific contexts into object tokens. VITA accomplishes video-level understanding by associating frame-level object tokens without using spatio-temporal backbone features. By effectively building relationships between objects using the condensed information, VITA achieves the state-of-the-art on VIS benchmarks with a ResNet-50 backbone: 49.8 AP, 45.7 AP on YouTube-VIS 2019 & 2021, and 19.6 AP on OVIS. Moreover, thanks to its object token-based structure that is disjoint from the backbone features, VITA shows several practical advantages that previous offline VIS methods have not explored - handling long and high-resolution videos with a common GPU, and freezing a frame-level detector trained on image domain. Code is available at the link.

paragraphs: Video instance segmentation requires understanding individual objects across a sequence. VITA approaches this by asking whether condensed, object-specific information can provide the context needed for offline video analysis. It builds on an existing transformer-based image instance segmentation model, using its detector to produce object tokens for each frame.

VITA associates those frame-level tokens to build relationships across the video. Its video-level processing does not use spatio-temporal backbone features. This separates sequence understanding from the detailed features produced by the image backbone and concentrates it on the object information distilled by the detector.

With a ResNet-50 backbone, VITA reports state-of-the-art results of 49.8 AP on YouTube-VIS 2019, 45.7 AP on YouTube-VIS 2021, and 19.6 AP on OVIS. The token-based design also supports long, high-resolution videos on a common GPU and allows the frame-level detector trained on images to remain frozen. These findings support object-token association as both an effective representation for video understanding and a useful architectural separation for practical processing.
summary.tldr: VITA links object tokens across frames to achieve strong video instance segmentation results while supporting long, high-resolution videos.

title: VITA: Video Instance Segmentation via Object Token Association

abstract: Although a number of studies are devoted to novel category discovery, most of them assume a static setting where both labeled and unlabeled data are given at once for finding new categories. In this work, we focus on the application scenarios where unlabeled data are continuously fed into the category discovery system. We refer to it as the {\bf Continuous Category Discovery} ({\bf CCD}) problem, which is significantly more challenging than the static setting. A common challenge faced by novel category discovery is that different sets of features are needed for classification and category discovery: class discriminative features are preferred for classification, while rich and diverse features are more suitable for new category mining. This challenge becomes more severe for dynamic setting as the system is asked to deliver good performance for known classes over time, and at the same time continuously discover new classes from unlabeled data. To address this challenge, we develop a framework of {\bf Grow and Merge} ({\bf GM}) that works by alternating between a growing phase and a merge phase: in the growing phase, it increases the diversity of features through a continuous self-supervised learning for effective category mining, and in the merging phase, it merges the grown model with a static one to ensure satisfying performance for known classes. Our extensive studies verify that the proposed GM framework is significantly more effective than the state-of-the-art approaches for continuous category discovery.

paragraphs: Category discovery becomes harder when unlabeled examples arrive continuously instead of being available together at the start. The system must recognize known categories while continuing to find new ones. The authors emphasize a representation conflict: features useful for distinguishing familiar classes may be less suitable for discovering categories that have not yet been identified.

Grow and Merge addresses this conflict by alternating between two phases. During growth, continuous self-supervised learning expands feature diversity to support discovery. During merging, the grown model is combined with a static model to maintain performance on known classes. These phases give discovery and familiar-category recognition distinct roles within the same ongoing learning process.

The authors report that extensive studies find this framework significantly more effective than state-of-the-art approaches for continuous category discovery. The finding supports deliberately balancing feature diversity with established classification ability as new data arrives. The contribution also makes the continuous setting explicit, drawing attention to a task that static category-discovery evaluations do not capture.
summary.tldr: Grow and Merge alternates feature expansion and model merging to discover new categories continuously while maintaining recognition of known ones.

title: Grow and Merge: A Unified Framework for Continuous Categories Discovery

abstract: Many potential applications of reinforcement learning (RL) are stymied by the large numbers of samples required to learn an effective policy. This is especially true when applying RL to real-world control tasks, e.g. in the sciences or robotics, where executing a policy in the environment is costly. In popular RL algorithms, agents typically explore either by adding stochasticity to a reward-maximizing policy or by attempting to gather maximal information about environment dynamics without taking the given task into account. In this work, we develop a method that allows us to plan for exploration while taking both the task and the current knowledge about the dynamics into account. The key insight to our approach is to plan an action sequence that maximizes the expected information gain about the optimal trajectory for the task at hand. We demonstrate that our method learns strong policies with 2x fewer samples than strong exploration baselines and 200x fewer samples than model free methods on a diverse set of low-to-medium dimensional control tasks in both the open-loop and closed-loop control settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require many interactions before an agent learns an effective policy, making it expensive for robotics and scientific control tasks. Common exploration strategies inject randomness into reward-seeking behavior or collect information about the environment's dynamics. The latter can spend effort learning details without considering how they relate to the task.

This paper proposes planning exploration around uncertainty about the optimal trajectory: the sequence of states and actions that would best accomplish the task. The method selects an action sequence to maximize expected information gain about that trajectory. Its choices therefore depend both on the task being pursued and on what the agent currently knows about the environment's dynamics.

Across diverse low-to-medium dimensional control tasks, the authors report learning strong policies with two times fewer samples than strong exploration baselines and 200 times fewer than model-free methods. The evaluation covers both open-loop and closed-loop control. These findings support the value of targeting exploration toward information about successful task execution in the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Planning actions to learn about the task's optimal trajectory reduces the interactions needed to learn strong policies in tested control tasks.

title: Exploration via Planning for Information about the Optimal Trajectory

abstract: We propose a new method for object pose estimation without CAD models. The previous feature-matching-based method OnePose has shown promising results under a one-shot setting which eliminates the need for CAD models or object-specific training. However, OnePose relies on detecting repeatable image keypoints and is thus prone to failure on low-textured objects. We propose a keypoint-free pose estimation pipeline to remove the need for repeatable keypoint detection. Built upon the detector-free feature matching method LoFTR, we devise a new keypoint-free SfM method to reconstruct a semi-dense point-cloud model for the object. Given a query image for object pose estimation, a 2D-3D matching network directly establishes 2D-3D correspondences between the query image and the reconstructed point-cloud model without first detecting keypoints in the image. Experiments show that the proposed pipeline outperforms existing one-shot CAD-model-free methods by a large margin and is comparable to CAD-model-based methods on LINEMOD even for low-textured objects. We also collect a new dataset composed of 80 sequences of 40 low-textured objects to facilitate future research on one-shot object pose estimation. The supplementary material, code and dataset are available on the project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/onepose_plus_plus/.
