paragraphs: OnePose++ estimates an object's pose without requiring a CAD model. It addresses a weakness in the earlier OnePose approach, whose one-shot setting avoids CAD models and object-specific training but depends on repeatedly detecting the same image keypoints. Low-textured objects make those repeatable detections difficult, creating a potential failure point.

The new pipeline removes the need to detect keypoints. Building on the detector-free matching method LoFTR, it uses a keypoint-free structure-from-motion procedure to reconstruct a semi-dense point cloud of the object. For a query image, a matching network directly connects image locations to points in that reconstructed three-dimensional model.

Experiments show a large improvement over existing one-shot methods that do not use CAD models. On LINEMOD, the pipeline is comparable to CAD-based approaches even for low-textured objects. These results support removing repeatable keypoint detection as a useful design choice for this setting. The authors also introduce a dataset containing 80 sequences of 40 low-textured objects, providing material for further research on one-shot object pose estimation.
summary.tldr: OnePose++ uses keypoint-free reconstruction and image-to-point-cloud matching to improve CAD-free pose estimation, including for low-textured objects.

title: OnePose++: Keypoint-Free One-Shot Object Pose Estimation without CAD Models

abstract: Directed Evolution (DE), a landmark wet-lab method originated in 1960s, enables discovery of novel protein designs via evolving a population of candidate sequences. Recent advances in biotechnology has made it possible to collect high-throughput data, allowing the use of machine learning to map out a protein's sequence-to-function relation. There is a growing interest in machine learning-assisted DE for accelerating protein optimization. Yet the theoretical understanding of DE, as well as the use of machine learning in DE, remains limited.In this paper, we connect DE with the bandit learning theory and make a first attempt to study regret minimization in DE. We propose a Thompson Sampling-guided Directed Evolution (TS-DE) framework for sequence optimization, where the sequence-to-function mapping is unknown and querying a single value is subject to costly and noisy measurements. TS-DE updates a posterior of the function based on collected measurements. It uses a posterior-sampled function estimate to guide the crossover recombination and mutation steps in DE. In the case of a linear model, we show that TS-DE enjoys a Bayesian regret of order $\tilde O(d^{2}\sqrt{MT})$, where $d$ is feature dimension, $M$ is population size and $T$ is number of rounds. This regret bound is nearly optimal, confirming that bandit learning can provably accelerate DE. It may have implications for more general sequence optimization and evolutionary algorithms.

paragraphs: Directed evolution searches for useful protein sequences by repeatedly changing a population of candidates. Measuring how well each sequence works can be expensive and noisy, so choosing candidates carefully matters. This paper connects that process to bandit learning, which studies how to make decisions while learning from uncertain measurements.

The proposed Thompson Sampling-guided Directed Evolution framework maintains a posterior distribution over the unknown relationship between sequence and function. As measurements arrive, it updates that distribution. It then samples a possible function and uses that sampled estimate to guide both crossover recombination and mutation. Uncertainty about sequence quality therefore directly influences how the next candidates are produced.

For a linear model, the authors prove a nearly optimal Bayesian regret bound of order d squared times the square root of MT, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is feature dimension, M is population size, and T is the number of rounds. This conditional result provides theoretical support for accelerating directed evolution with bandit learning, with possible implications for broader sequence optimization.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling guides evolutionary sequence search, with a nearly optimal Bayesian regret guarantee for the linear-model case.

title: Bandit Theory and Thompson Sampling-Guided Directed Evolution for Sequence Optimization

abstract: We study off-policy evaluation (OPE) for partially observable MDPs (POMDPs) with general function approximation. Existing methods such as sequential importance sampling estimators and fitted-Q evaluation suffer from the curse of horizon in POMDPs. To circumvent this problem, we develop a novel model-free OPE method by introducing future-dependent value functions that take future proxies as inputs. Future-dependent value functions play similar roles as classical value functions in fully-observable MDPs. We derive a new off-policy Bellman equation for future-dependent value functions as conditional moment equations that use history proxies as instrumental variables. We further propose a minimax learning method to learn future-dependent value functions using the new Bellman equation. We obtain the PAC result, which implies our OPE estimator is close to the true policy value as long as futures and histories contain sufficient information about latent states, and the Bellman completeness. Our code is available at https://github.com/aiueola/neurips2023-future-dependent-ope

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy's value using data collected under another policy. In partially observable environments, the underlying state is hidden, making this task especially difficult over long horizons. The paper develops a model-free approach intended to avoid the horizon-related difficulties of existing importance-sampling and fitted-Q methods.

Its key construction is a future-dependent value function that accepts future observations serving as proxies for hidden states. These functions play a role analogous to ordinary value functions in fully observed environments. The authors derive an off-policy Bellman equation as conditional moment equations, using historical proxies as instrumental variables, and then introduce a minimax procedure for learning the functions.

The theoretical result gives a probabilistic guarantee that the estimated policy value is close to its true value under stated conditions. Future and historical information must be sufficiently informative about latent states, and Bellman completeness must hold for the function class. These requirements are central: the guarantee explains when observable sequences can support reliable evaluation despite hidden states, rather than establishing reliability for arbitrary partially observed data.
summary.tldr: Future-dependent value functions enable off-policy evaluation with guarantees when observed histories and futures sufficiently reveal hidden-state information.

title: Future-Dependent Value-Based Off-Policy Evaluation in POMDPs

abstract: Accurately depicting the complex traffic scene is a vital component for autonomous vehicles to execute correct judgments. However, existing benchmarks tend to oversimplify the scene by solely focusing on lane perception tasks. Observing that human drivers rely on both lanes and traffic signals to operate their vehicles safely, we present OpenLane-V2, the first dataset on topology reasoning for traffic scene structure. The objective of the presented dataset is to advance research in understanding the structure of road scenes by examining the relationship between perceived entities, such as traffic elements and lanes. Leveraging existing datasets, OpenLane-V2 consists of 2,000 annotated road scenes that describe traffic elements and their correlation to the lanes. It comprises three primary sub-tasks, including the 3D lane detection inherited from OpenLane, accompanied by corresponding metrics to evaluate the model’s performance. We evaluate various state-of-the-art methods, and present their quantitative and qualitative results on OpenLane-V2 to indicate future avenues for investigating topology reasoning in traffic scenes.

paragraphs: An autonomous vehicle needs to understand how parts of a road scene relate to one another. Detecting lanes provides only part of that picture, because traffic elements and their relationships to lanes also inform driving decisions. OpenLane-V2 creates a benchmark centered on this structural understanding, described as topology reasoning.

Built from existing datasets, OpenLane-V2 contains 2,000 annotated road scenes describing traffic elements and their associations with lanes. It defines three main subtasks, including 3D lane detection inherited from OpenLane, and provides corresponding evaluation metrics. The annotations make relationships among perceived entities an explicit part of what models must understand.

The authors evaluate several state-of-the-art methods and present both numerical results and qualitative examples. These evaluations provide reference points for investigating road-scene reasoning and identifying directions for further research. The benchmark's contribution is to bring lane perception and scene relationships into a shared evaluation setting, making structural interpretation a visible component of model performance.
summary.tldr: OpenLane-V2 evaluates road-scene understanding through 3D lanes, traffic elements, and the relationships connecting them.

title: OpenLane-V2: A Topology Reasoning Benchmark for Unified 3D HD Mapping

abstract: We propose a novel approach to learning the generative neural fields represented by linear combinations of implicit basis networks. Our algorithm learns basis networks in the form of implicit neural representations and their coefficients in a latent space by either conducting meta-learning or adopting auto-decoding paradigms. The proposed method easily enlarges the capacity of generative neural fields by increasing the number of basis networks while maintaining the size of a network for inference to be small through their weighted model averaging. Consequently, sampling instances using the model is efficient in terms of latency and memory footprint. Moreover, we customize denoising diffusion probabilistic model for a target task to sample latent mixture coefficients, which allows our final model to generate unseen data effectively. Experiments show that our approach achieves competitive generation performance on diverse benchmarks for images, voxel data, and NeRF scenes without sophisticated designs for specific modalities and domains.

paragraphs: The paper builds generative neural fields from combinations of smaller implicit neural networks. These basis networks provide reusable components, while latent coefficients determine how they are combined for a particular instance. The method learns both the basis networks and the coefficients, using either meta-learning or an auto-decoding approach.

A central design goal is to increase the capacity of the generative model without enlarging the network needed at inference. Adding basis networks expands the available components, while weighted model averaging keeps the inference network small. This separation makes sampling efficient in latency and memory footprint, according to the abstract, while allowing the learned collection of basis networks to grow.

To generate new instances, the authors adapt a denoising diffusion probabilistic model to sample the latent mixture coefficients. Those sampled coefficients then specify a new neural field. Experiments report competitive generation across images, voxel data, and NeRF scenes without elaborate designs for each modality. The results support the combination framework as a shared approach across several kinds of visual data.
summary.tldr: Mixtures of implicit basis networks enable generative neural fields with expandable capacity and compact inference, using diffusion to sample mixture coefficients.

title: Generative Neural Fields by Mixtures of Neural Implicit Functions

abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithms (MORL) extend standard reinforcement learning (RL) to scenarios where agents must optimize multiple---potentially conflicting---objectives, each represented by a distinct reward function. To facilitate and accelerate research and benchmarking in multi-objective RL problems, we introduce a comprehensive collection of software libraries that includes: (i) MO-Gymnasium, an easy-to-use and flexible API enabling the rapid construction of novel MORL environments. It also includes more than 20 environments under this API. This allows researchers to effortlessly evaluate any algorithms on any existing domains; (ii) MORL-Baselines, a collection of reliable and efficient implementations of state-of-the-art MORL algorithms, designed to provide a solid foundation for advancing research. Notably, all algorithms are inherently compatible with MO-Gymnasium; and(iii) a thorough and robust set of benchmark results and comparisons of MORL-Baselines algorithms, tested across various challenging MO-Gymnasium environments. These benchmarks were constructed to serve as guidelines for the research community, underscoring the properties, advantages, and limitations of each particular state-of-the-art method.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning studies agents that must pursue several goals, potentially with competing demands. Each goal has its own reward function, so evaluating an algorithm involves more than optimizing a single reward. This paper introduces a coordinated software toolkit to make research and comparisons in this setting easier to carry out.

The first component, MO-Gymnasium, provides a common interface for building environments and includes more than 20 environments. The second, MORL-Baselines, supplies implementations of established multi-objective learning algorithms. These implementations are compatible with MO-Gymnasium, connecting the environments and algorithms through a shared foundation rather than requiring separate integration for each comparison.

The third component is a collection of benchmark results across challenging environments. These comparisons are intended to clarify the properties, strengths, and limitations of the included methods. Together, the libraries and benchmarks provide both reusable experimental infrastructure and reference results. The contribution is a practical foundation for studying how different algorithms handle multiple objectives and for evaluating new approaches within the same framework.
summary.tldr: A coordinated toolkit combines multi-objective reinforcement learning environments, compatible algorithm implementations, and benchmark comparisons.

title: A Toolkit for Reliable Benchmarking and Research in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The brittleness of these models, particularly when executing long chains of reasoning, currently seems to be an inevitable price to pay for their advanced capabilities of coherently synthesizing knowledge, pragmatics, and abstract thought. Towards making sense of this fundamentally unsolved problem, this work identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of _attention glitches_, in which the Transformer architecture's inductive biases intermittently fail to capture robust reasoning. To isolate the issue, we introduce _flip-flop language modeling_ (FFLM), a parametric family of synthetic benchmarks designed to probe the extrapolative behavior of neural language models. This simple generative task requires a model to copy binary symbols over long-range dependencies, ignoring the tokens in between. We find that Transformer FFLMs suffer from a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors, some of which we can eliminate using various regularization techniques. Our preliminary mechanistic analyses show why the remaining errors may be very difficult to diagnose and resolve. We hypothesize that attention glitches account for (some of) the closed-domain hallucinations in natural LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper studies intermittent reasoning failures in Transformers through a deliberately simple language-modeling task. The authors call the failures attention glitches: situations in which the architecture’s built-in tendencies do not support robust reasoning. title: Exposing Attention Glitches with Flip-Flop Language Modeling

abstract: We introduce WordScape, a novel pipeline for the creation of cross-disciplinary, multilingual corpora comprising millions of pages with annotations for document layout detection. Relating visual and textual items on document pages has gained further significance with the advent of multimodal models. Various approaches proved effective for visual question answering or layout segmentation. However, the interplay of text, tables, and visuals remains challenging for a variety of document understanding tasks. In particular, many models fail to generalize well to diverse domains and new languages due to insufficient availability of training data. WordScape addresses these limitations. Our automatic annotation pipeline parses the Open XML structure of Word documents obtained from the web, jointly providing layout-annotated document images and their textual representations. In turn, WordScape offers unique properties as it (1) leverages the ubiquity of the Word file format on the internet, (2) is readily accessible through the Common Crawl web corpus, (3) is adaptive to domain-specific documents, and (4) offers culturally and linguistically diverse document pages with natural semantic structure and high-quality text. Together with the pipeline, we will additionally release 9.5M urls to word documents which can be processed using WordScape to create a dataset of over 40M pages. Finally, we investigate the quality of text and layout annotations extracted by WordScape, assess the impact on document understanding benchmarks, and demonstrate that manual labeling costs can be substantially reduced.

paragraphs: Document understanding requires connecting text, tables, and visual elements on a page. Models can struggle with unfamiliar domains and languages when training data lacks sufficient variety. WordScape addresses this data problem through a pipeline for creating large, multilingual collections of document images, text, and layout annotations from Word files available on the web.

The pipeline parses the files’ Open XML structure to obtain textual representations and annotated document images together. It draws on the widespread availability of Word documents through Common Crawl and can be adapted to domain-specific material. Using the structure already present in these files provides a route to naturally organized, linguistically and culturally varied pages without manually labeling every document.

The authors describe a planned release of 9.5 million document URLs that can be processed into more than 40 million pages. They also evaluate extracted text and layout annotations, assess effects on document-understanding benchmarks, and demonstrate substantial reductions in manual labeling costs. The contribution is both a scalable extraction method and evidence that its automatically produced annotations can reduce annotation effort.
summary.tldr: WordScape turns web-hosted Word documents into multilingual text and layout-annotated page datasets, substantially reducing manual labeling costs.

title: WordScape: a Pipeline to extract multilingual, visually rich Documents with Layout Annotations from Web Crawl Data

abstract: Computational lithography provides algorithmic and mathematical support for resolution enhancement in optical lithography, which is the critical step in semiconductor manufacturing. The time-consuming lithography simulation and mask optimization processes limit the practical application of inverse lithography technology (ILT), a promising solution to the challenges of advanced-node lithography. Although various machine learning methods for ILT have shown promise for reducing the computational burden, this field is in lack of a dataset that can train the models thoroughly and evaluate the performance comprehensively. To boost the development of AI-driven computational lithography, we present the LithoBench dataset, a collection of circuit layout tiles for deep-learning-based lithography simulation and mask optimization. LithoBench consists of more than 120k tiles that are cropped from real circuit designs or synthesized according to the layout topologies of famous ILT testcases. The ground truths are generated by a famous lithography model in academia and an advanced ILT method. Based on the data, we provide a framework to design and evaluate deep neural networks (DNNs) with the data. The framework is used to benchmark state-of-the-art models on lithography simulation and mask optimization. We hope LithoBench can promote the research and development of computational lithography. LithoBench is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lithobench-APPL.

Machine-learning approaches have shown promise for reducing this burden, but the paper identifies a shortage of data for thorough training and comprehensive evaluation.

The tiles come from real circuit designs or are synthesized using the layout topologies of established inverse-lithography test cases. Reference outputs are generated using an academic lithography model and an advanced inverse-lithography method, supplying targets for the benchmark's learning tasks.

The accompanying framework supports the design and evaluation of deep neural networks, and the authors use it to benchmark leading models on both tasks. The contribution is a shared dataset and evaluation framework for studying AI-assisted computational lithography. It gives researchers a common basis for investigating whether learned simulation and optimization methods can reduce the computational obstacles motivating the work.
summary.tldr: LithoBench supplies over 120,000 circuit-layout tiles and a framework for evaluating learned lithography simulation and mask optimization.

title: LithoBench: Benchmarking AI Computational Lithography for Semiconductor Manufacturing

abstract: To generate evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled medical devices, AI models need to be evaluated on a diverse population of patient cases, some of which may not be readily available. We propose an evaluation approach for testing medical imaging AI models that relies on in silico imaging pipelines in which stochastic digital models of human anatomy (in object space) with and without pathology are imaged using a digital replica imaging acquisition system to generate realistic synthetic image datasets. Here, we release M-SYNTH, a dataset of cohorts with four breast fibroglandular density distributions imaged at different exposure levels using Monte Carlo x-ray simulations with the publicly available Virtual Imaging Clinical Trial for Regulatory Evaluation (VICTRE) toolkit. We utilize the synthetic dataset to analyze AI model performance and find that model performance decreases with increasing breast density and increases with higher mass density, as expected. As exposure levels decrease, AI model performance drops with the highest performance achieved at exposure levels lower than the nominal recommended dose for the breast type.

paragraphs: Evaluating medical imaging AI requires diverse cases, including combinations of patient and imaging characteristics that may be difficult to obtain. This paper proposes generating such cases through simulated imaging pipelines. Digital anatomical models, with and without disease, are passed through a digital replica of an imaging system to produce realistic synthetic images.

The authors release M-SYNTH, a mammography dataset covering four distributions of breast fibroglandular density and multiple exposure levels. The images are generated with Monte Carlo x-ray simulation using the VICTRE toolkit. This construction supports comparative evaluation across controlled variations in anatomy, lesion characteristics, and imaging exposure.

In the synthetic evaluation, AI performance decreases as breast density rises and improves as mass density rises. Lower exposure levels also reduce performance, while the highest observed performance occurs below the nominal recommended dose for the breast type. These are findings about model behavior in the simulated evaluation. The dataset's contribution is to make such systematic comparisons possible when corresponding patient cases are not readily available.
summary.tldr: M-SYNTH uses simulated mammography to evaluate how AI performance varies with breast density, mass density, and imaging exposure.

title: Knowledge-based in silico models and dataset for the comparative evaluation of mammography AI for a range of breast characteristics, lesion conspicuities and doses

abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) can be dramatically accelerated by spatial grid representations. However, they do not explicitly reason about scale and so introduce aliasing artifacts when reconstructing scenes captured at different camera distances. Mip-NeRF and its extensions propose scale-aware renderers that project volumetric frustums rather than point samples. But such approaches rely on positional encodings that are not readily compatible with grid methods. We propose a simple modification to grid-based models by training model heads at different spatial grid resolutions. At render time, we simply use coarser grids to render samples that cover larger volumes. Our method can be easily applied to existing accelerated NeRF methods and significantly improves rendering quality (reducing error rates by 20–90% across synthetic and unbounded real-world scenes) while incurring minimal performance overhead (as each model head is quick to evaluate). Compared to Mip-NeRF, we reduce error rates by 20% while training over 60x faster.

paragraphs: Spatial grids make neural radiance fields faster, but they can produce aliasing artifacts when images capture a scene from different distances. The problem is that these representations do not explicitly account for the spatial scale covered by a rendering sample. PyNeRF adds scale awareness to accelerated grid-based models through a simple change in their structure.

The method trains model heads at several grid resolutions. During rendering, samples covering larger volumes use coarser grids. This matches the detail level of the representation to the sample's spatial extent. The approach provides a way to handle scale within grid methods, where the positional encodings used by Mip-NeRF and its extensions are not readily compatible.

The authors report error reductions of 20% to 90% across synthetic and unbounded real-world scenes, with minimal performance overhead because the model heads are quick to evaluate. Compared with Mip-NeRF, they report 20% lower error and training more than 60 times faster. These results support adding multiple resolution-specific heads as an effective modification to existing accelerated NeRF methods.
summary.tldr: PyNeRF improves grid-based rendering by using model heads at different resolutions and choosing coarser grids for larger-volume samples.

title: PyNeRF: Pyramidal Neural Radiance Fields

abstract: In this work, we aim to characterize the statistical complexity of realizable regression both in the PAC learning setting and the online learning setting. Previous work had established the sufficiency of finiteness of the fat shattering dimension for PAC learnability and the necessity of finiteness of the scaled Natarajan dimension, but little progress had been made towards a more complete characterization since the work of Simon 1997 (SICOMP '97). To this end, we first introduce a minimax instance optimal learner for realizable regression and propose a novel dimension that both qualitatively and quantitatively characterizes which classes of real-valued predictors are learnable. We then identify a combinatorial dimension related to the graph dimension that characterizes ERM learnability in the realizable setting. Finally, we establish a necessary condition for learnability based on a combinatorial dimension related to the DS dimension, and conjecture that it may also be sufficient in this context. Additionally, in the context of online learning we provide a dimension that characterizes the minimax instance optimal cumulative loss up to a constant factor and design an optimal online learner for realizable regression, thus resolving an open question raised by Daskalakis and Golowich in STOC '22.

paragraphs: This paper studies the statistical complexity of realizable regression, where the predictor class can represent the target relationship. It considers both PAC learning and online learning. The objective is to identify mathematical properties of predictor classes that determine whether learning is possible and how difficult it is.

For PAC learning, the authors introduce a minimax instance-optimal learner and a new dimension that characterizes learnability both qualitatively and quantitatively. They also give a graph-related combinatorial dimension characterizing learnability through empirical risk minimization. A separate DS-related dimension supplies a necessary condition; its sufficiency remains a conjecture. Keeping these results distinct matters because a necessary condition alone does not establish learnability.

For online regression, the paper introduces a dimension that characterizes minimax instance-optimal cumulative loss within a constant factor and constructs an optimal learner. This resolves the stated open question for that setting. Together, the results sharpen the relationship between the combinatorial structure of real-valued predictor classes and the best achievable learning performance.
summary.tldr: New combinatorial dimensions and optimal learners characterize realizable regression in PAC and online settings, while one proposed sufficiency condition remains conjectural.

title: Optimal Learners for Realizable Regression: PAC Learning and Online Learning

abstract: The local search methods have been widely used to solve the clustering problems. In practice, local search algorithms for clustering problems mainly adapt the single-swap strategy, which enables them to handle large-scale datasets and achieve linear running time in the data size. However, compared with multi-swap local search algorithms, there is a considerable gap on the approximation ratios of the single-swap local search algorithms. Although the current multi-swap local search algorithms provide small constant approximation, the proposed algorithms tend to have large polynomial running time, which cannot be used to handle large-scale datasets. In this paper, we propose a multi-swap local search algorithm for the $k$-means problem with linear running time in the data size. Given a swap size $t$, our proposed algorithm can achieve a $(50(1+\frac{1}{t})+\epsilon)$-approximation, which improves the current best result 509 (ICML 2019) with linear running time in the data size. Our proposed method, compared with previous multi-swap local search algorithms, is the first one to achieve linear running time in the data size. To obtain a more practical algorithm for the problem with better clustering quality and running time, we propose a sampling-based method which accelerates the process of clustering cost update during swaps. Besides, a recombination mechanism is proposed to find potentially better solutions. Empirical experiments show that our proposed algorithms achieve better performances compared with branch and bound solver (NeurIPS 2022) and other existing state-of-the-art local search algorithms on both small and large datasets.

paragraphs: Local-search algorithms improve a clustering by swapping selected centers. Single-swap methods can scale linearly with dataset size, but their approximation guarantees are weaker than those available from multi-swap methods. Previously proposed multi-swap algorithms achieve stronger guarantees at polynomial running times that make large datasets difficult to handle.

This paper introduces a multi-swap k-means algorithm whose running time is linear in data size. For swap size t, its approximation factor is 50(1 + 1/t) + ε, improving the previously stated linear-time factor of 509. The guarantee bounds clustering cost relative to the optimum; increasing the swap size improves the stated factor toward 50 + ε.

The authors also develop practical additions: sampling speeds up clustering-cost updates during swaps, and recombination searches for potentially better solutions. Experiments on small and large datasets report better performance than a branch-and-bound solver and leading local-search alternatives. The work thus combines a stronger theoretical guarantee with mechanisms intended to improve practical clustering quality and runtime.
summary.tldr: A multi-swap k-means algorithm achieves linear scaling in dataset size with a stronger approximation guarantee and practical search improvements.

title: Linear Time Algorithms for k-means with Multi-Swap Local Search

abstract: The egocentric and exocentric viewpoints of a human activity look dramatically different, yet invariant representations to link them are essential for many potential applications in robotics and augmented reality. Prior work is limited to learning view-invariant features from paired synchronized viewpoints. We relax that strong data assumption and propose to learn fine-grained action features that are invariant to the viewpoints by aligning egocentric and exocentric videos in time, even when not captured simultaneously or in the same environment. To this end, we propose AE2, a self-supervised embedding approach with two key designs: (1) an object-centric encoder that explicitly focuses on regions corresponding to hands and active objects; (2) a contrastive-based alignment objective that leverages temporally reversed frames as negative samples. For evaluation, we establish a benchmark for fine-grained video understanding in the ego-exo context, comprising four datasets---including an ego tennis forehand dataset we collected, along with dense per-frame labels we annotated for each dataset. On the four datasets, our AE2 method strongly outperforms prior work in a variety of fine-grained downstream tasks, both in regular and cross-view settings.

paragraphs: An activity looks very different through the participant's camera and through an outside observer's camera. Linking these views requires representations that retain fine-grained action information despite the visual change. Earlier approaches relied on synchronized video pairs. This paper learns from videos that need not share a recording time or environment.

The AE2 method uses temporal alignment to connect first-person and third-person activity sequences. Its encoder focuses explicitly on hands and the objects being used. A contrastive alignment objective treats temporally reversed frames as negative examples, making action order part of the learning signal. These designs combine attention to the relevant interaction with sensitivity to how it unfolds.

The authors create a four-dataset benchmark for fine-grained understanding across these viewpoints, including a collected first-person tennis forehand dataset and dense frame labels for evaluation. AE2 strongly outperforms prior work across multiple downstream tasks in both regular and cross-view settings. The findings support learning detailed shared action features while relaxing the need for synchronized training recordings.
summary.tldr: AE2 learns fine-grained action representations across first-person and third-person videos through temporal alignment without synchronized recordings.

title: Learning Fine-grained View-Invariant Representations from Unpaired Ego-Exo Videos via Temporal Alignment

abstract: By universal formulas we understand parameterized analytic expressions that have a fixed complexity, but nevertheless can approximate any continuous function on a compact set. There exist various examples of such formulas, including some in the form of neural networks. In this paper we analyze the essential structural elements of these highly expressive models. We introduce a hierarchy of expressiveness classes connecting the global approximability property to the weaker property of infinite VC dimension, and prove a series of classification results for several increasingly complex functional families. In particular, we introduce a general family of polynomially-exponentially-algebraic functions that, as we prove, is subject to polynomial constraints. As a consequence, we show that fixed-size neural networks with not more than one layer of neurons having transcendental activations (e.g., sine or standard sigmoid) cannot in general approximate functions on arbitrary finite sets. On the other hand, we give examples of functional families, including two-hidden-layer neural networks, that approximate functions on arbitrary finite sets, but fail to do that on the whole domain of definition.

paragraphs: A universal formula is a parameterized expression of fixed complexity that can approximate any continuous function on a compact set. Some neural-network constructions have this property. This paper investigates which structural ingredients make such expressiveness possible and how weaker forms of expressive power relate to full approximation over a domain.

The authors introduce a hierarchy connecting global approximation with infinite VC dimension, a weaker measure of capacity. They classify several increasingly complex function families. In particular, they define a general family of polynomially-exponentially-algebraic functions and prove that it obeys polynomial constraints, providing a mathematical route to limits on expressiveness.

One consequence is that fixed-size networks with at most one layer of neurons using transcendental activations, such as sine or standard sigmoid, cannot generally approximate functions on arbitrary finite sets. Conversely, the paper gives families, including two-hidden-layer networks, that can approximate functions on arbitrary finite sets but fail across the whole domain. These results distinguish fitting any finite collection of values from having genuine global approximation power.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of expressiveness reveals structural limits and separates arbitrary finite-set approximation from universal approximation across a domain.

title: Structure of universal formulas

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the exact skeleton of general discrete Bayesian networks from potentially corrupted data. Building on distributionally robust optimization and a regression approach, we propose to optimize the most adverse risk over a family of distributions within bounded Wasserstein distance or KL divergence to the empirical distribution. The worst-case risk accounts for the effect of outliers. The proposed approach applies for general categorical random variables without assuming faithfulness, an ordinal relationship or a specific form of conditional distribution. We present efficient algorithms and show the proposed methods are closely related to the standard regularized regression approach. Under mild assumptions, we derive non-asymptotic guarantees for successful structure learning with logarithmic sample complexities for bounded-degree graphs. Numerical study on synthetic and real datasets validates the effectiveness of our method.

The worst-case risk accounts for the effect of outliers. The proposed approach applies for general categorical random variables without assuming faithfulness, an ordinal relationship or a specific form of conditional distribution. We present efficient algorithms and show the proposed methods are closely related to the standard regularized regression approach. paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the skeleton of a discrete Bayesian network from potentially corrupted data. The skeleton records which variables are connected without recovering the directions of those connections. The goal is exact recovery despite the possibility that outliers distort the empirical distribution used for learning.

The proposed method combines regression with distributionally robust optimization. Instead of optimizing risk only on the observed distribution, it considers the worst risk among distributions within a bounded Wasserstein distance or KL divergence of it. This makes possible distributional changes part of the objective. The approach handles general categorical variables without requiring faithfulness, an ordering of categories, or a specified conditional-distribution form.

The authors provide efficient algorithms and relate their methods to standard regularized regression. Under stated mild assumptions, they establish finite-sample guarantees for successful structure recovery, with logarithmic sample complexities for bounded-degree graphs. Studies on synthetic and real datasets support the method’s effectiveness. The theoretical result is conditional, while its practical motivation is to make structural learning less vulnerable to contamination in the data.
summary.tldr: The paper uses distributionally robust regression to recover discrete Bayesian-network skeletons from potentially corrupted data, with conditional finite-sample guarantees.

title: Distributionally Robust Skeleton Learning of Discrete Bayesian Networks

abstract: Knowledge distillation with unlabeled examples is a powerful training paradigm for generating compact and lightweight student models in applications where the amount of labeled data is limited but one has access to a large pool of unlabeled data. In this setting, a large teacher model generates "soft" pseudo-labels for the unlabeled dataset which are then used for training the student model. Despite its success in a wide variety of applications, a shortcoming of this approach is that the teacher's pseudo-labels are often noisy, leading to impaired student performance. In this paper, we present a principled method for knowledge distillation with unlabeled examples that we call Student-Label Mixing (SLaM) and we show that it consistently improves over prior approaches by evaluating it on several standard benchmarks. Finally, we show that SLaM comes with theoretical guarantees; along the way we give an algorithm improving the best-known sample complexity for learning halfspaces with margin under random classification noise, and provide the first convergence analysis for so-called ``forward loss-adjustment" methods.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation can train a compact student model using predictions from a larger teacher on unlabeled examples. Those predictions provide soft pseudo-labels when real labels are scarce. The difficulty is that teacher-generated targets can be noisy, allowing their errors to impair the student's performance even when plenty of unlabeled data is available.

Student-Label Mixing, or SLaM, is proposed as a principled method for this distillation setting. The authors evaluate it on several standard benchmarks and report consistent improvements over earlier approaches. The practical contribution is therefore better student training in the presence of imperfect teacher supervision, with performance evidence spanning multiple benchmark settings.

The paper also develops theoretical guarantees. Its analysis includes an algorithm improving the best-known sample complexity for learning halfspaces with a margin under random classification noise, and the first convergence analysis of forward loss-adjustment methods. These mathematical results complement the distillation experiments by advancing understanding of learning with noisy labels, while applying to the specific theoretical settings stated.
summary.tldr: SLaM improves distillation from noisy teacher labels and contributes theoretical results for learning under label noise.

title: SLaM: Student-Label Mixing for Distillation with Unlabeled Examples

abstract: We study the optimal control of multiple-input and multiple-output dynamical systems via the design of neural network-based controllers with stability and output tracking guarantees. While neural network-based nonlinear controllers have shown superior performance in various applications, their lack of provable guarantees has restricted their adoption in high-stake real-world applications. This paper bridges the gap between neural network-based controllers and the need for stabilization guarantees. Using equilibrium-independent passivity, a property present in a wide range of physical systems, we propose neural Proportional-Integral (PI) controllers that have provable guarantees of stability and zero steady-state output tracking error. The key structure is the strict monotonicity on proportional and integral terms, which is parameterized as gradients of strictly convex neural networks (SCNN). We construct SCNN with tunable softplus-$\beta$ activations, which yields universal approximation capability and is also useful in incorporating communication constraints. In addition, the SCNNs serve as Lyapunov functions, giving us end-to-end performance guarantees. Experiments on traffic and power networks demonstrate that the proposed approach improves both transient and steady-state performances, while unstructured neural networks lead to unstable behaviors.

This paper designs neural proportional-integral controllers for dynamical systems with multiple inputs and outputs. The guarantees rely on equilibrium-independent passivity, a property the authors identify in a broad range of physical systems.

Networks built with tunable softplus-β activations provide universal approximation capability and support communication constraints. title: Structured Neural-PI Control with End-to-End Stability and Output Tracking Guarantees

abstract: We present a novel learning-based framework for reconstructing 3D structures from tilt-series cryo-Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) data. Cryo-ET is a powerful imaging technique that can achieve near-atomic resolutions. Still, it suffers from challenges such as missing-wedge acquisition, large data size, and high noise levels. Our framework addresses these challenges by using an adaptive tensorial-based representation for the 3D density field of the scanned sample. First, we optimize a quadtree structure to partition the volume of interest. Then, we learn a vector-matrix factorization of the tensor representing the density field in each node. Moreover, we use a loss function that combines a differentiable tomographic formation model with three regularization terms: total variation, boundary consistency constraint, and an isotropic Fourier prior. Our framework allows us to query the density at any location using the learned representation and obtain a high-quality 3D tomogram. We demonstrate the superiority of our framework over existing methods using synthetic and real data. Thus, our framework boosts the quality of the reconstruction while reducing the computation time and the memory footprint. The code is available at https://github.com/yuanhaowang1213/adaptivetensordf.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron tomography reconstructs three-dimensional structures from a series of tilted observations. Although the imaging technique can achieve near-atomic resolution, reconstruction faces missing acquisition angles, large datasets, and substantial noise. This paper develops a learned density-field representation to address these difficulties while reducing computational and memory demands.

The method first optimizes a quadtree partition of the volume of interest. Within each node, it learns a vector-matrix factorization of the tensor describing density. Training combines a differentiable model of tomographic image formation with total variation, a boundary consistency constraint, and an isotropic Fourier prior. These regularization terms supplement the fit to the observed measurements.

The resulting representation allows density to be queried at arbitrary locations to construct a three-dimensional tomogram. On synthetic and real data, the authors report better reconstruction quality than existing methods alongside lower computation time and memory use. The contribution links an adaptive, factorized representation with a measurement-based training objective, allowing reconstruction quality and resource efficiency to improve together in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Adaptive factorized density fields improve cryo-ET reconstruction quality while reducing computation time and memory use in reported evaluations.

title: Learning Adaptive Tensorial Density Fields for Clean Cryo-ET Reconstruction

abstract: Deep predictive models of neuronal activity have recently enabled several new discoveries about the selectivity and invariance of neurons in the visual cortex.These models learn a shared set of nonlinear basis functions, which are linearly combined via a learned weight vector to represent a neuron's function.Such weight vectors, which can be thought as embeddings of neuronal function, have been proposed to define functional cell types via unsupervised clustering.However, as deep models are usually highly overparameterized, the learning problem is unlikely to have a unique solution, which raises the question if such embeddings can be used in a meaningful way for downstream analysis.In this paper, we investigate how stable neuronal embeddings are with respect to changes in model architecture and initialization. We find that $L_1$ regularization to be an important ingredient for structured embeddings and develop an adaptive regularization that adjusts the strength of regularization per neuron. This regularization improves both predictive performance and how consistently neuronal embeddings cluster across model fits compared to uniform regularization.To overcome overparametrization, we propose an iterative feature pruning strategy which reduces the dimensionality of performance-optimized models by half without loss of performance and improves the consistency of neuronal embeddings with respect to clustering neurons.Our results suggest that to achieve an objective taxonomy of cell types or a compact representation of the functional landscape, we need novel architectures or learning techniques that improve identifiability. The code is available https://github.com/pollytur/readout_reproducibility.

The code is available https://github.com/pollytur/readout_reproducibility.

paragraphs: Models of neuronal activity can represent each neuron through weights that combine shared nonlinear features. Researchers have proposed clustering these weight vectors to identify functional cell types. However, highly overparameterized models can admit different solutions, raising the question of whether the resulting neuronal groupings remain consistent across model fits.

The paper examines embedding stability under changes in architecture and initialization. It finds that L1 regularization helps produce structured embeddings and introduces a method that adapts regularization strength separately for each neuron. Compared with uniform regularization, this improves both predictive performance and the consistency of clustering across fits.

The authors also develop iterative feature pruning that halves the dimensionality of performance-optimized models without reducing predictive performance, while further improving clustering consistency. These findings show that representation reproducibility can improve alongside compactness and prediction quality. They also motivate the authors' broader conclusion that better identifiability through new architectures or learning techniques is needed to support an objective cell-type taxonomy or a compact map of neuronal function.
summary.tldr: Neuron-specific regularization and feature pruning improve the reproducibility of neuronal embeddings used to cluster mouse visual-cortex cells.

title: Reproducibility of predictive networks for mouse visual cortex

abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies enable the exploration of cellular heterogeneity and facilitate the construction of cell atlases. However, scRNA-seq data often contain a large portion of missing values (false zeros) or noisy values, hindering downstream analyses. To recover these false zeros, propagation-based imputation methods have been proposed using $k$-NN graphs. However they model only associating relationships among genes within a cell, while, according to well-known genetic evidence, there are both associating and dissociating relationships among genes. To apply this genetic evidence to gene-gene relationship modeling, this paper proposes a novel imputation method that newly employs dissociating relationships in addition to associating relationships. Our method constructs a $k$-NN graph to additionally model dissociating relationships via the negation of a given cell-gene matrix. Moreover, our method standardizes the value distribution (mean and variance) of each gene to have standard distributions regardless of the gene. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves exceptional performance gains over state-of-the-art methods in both cell clustering and gene expression recovery across six scRNA-seq datasets, validating the significance of using complete gene-gene relationships in accordance with genetic evidence. The source code is available at https://github.com/daehoum1/scCR.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing measures gene expression across individual cells, but its data can contain noisy values and false zeros. These errors can interfere with identifying cell groups or recovering expression patterns. Existing propagation-based imputation methods use nearest-neighbor graphs to fill in missing signal, yet the paper argues that their gene-relationship modeling is incomplete.

The proposed method incorporates both associating and dissociating relationships between genes, following the genetic evidence described by the authors. It constructs an additional nearest-neighbor graph using the negated cell-by-gene matrix to capture dissociating relationships. It also standardizes each gene’s value distribution in terms of mean and variance, placing different genes on a common distributional footing for the method.

Experiments across six single-cell RNA sequencing datasets evaluate both cell clustering and gene-expression recovery. The authors report substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods on these tasks. The findings support the value of modeling dissociating relationships alongside associating ones when repairing these data. Their significance extends beyond filling matrix entries: improved imputation also benefits the tested downstream grouping of cells.
summary.tldr: Modeling both associating and dissociating gene relationships improves single-cell expression imputation and cell clustering across six tested datasets.

title: Gene-Gene Relationship Modeling Based on Genetic Evidence for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Imputation

abstract: Modality differences have led to the development of heterogeneous architectures for vision and language models. While images typically require 2D non-causal modeling, texts utilize 1D causal modeling. This distinction poses significant challenges in constructing unified multi-modal models. This paper explores the feasibility of representing images using 1D causal modeling. We identify an "over-focus" issue in existing 1D causal vision models, where attention overly concentrates on a small proportion of visual tokens. The issue of "over-focus" hinders the model's ability to extract diverse visual features and to receive effective gradients for optimization. To address this, we propose De-focus Attention Networks, which employ learnable bandpass filters to create varied attention patterns. During training, large and scheduled drop path rates, and an auxiliary loss on globally pooled features for global understanding tasks are introduced. These two strategies encourage the model to attend to a broader range of tokens and enhance network optimization. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating that 1D causal visual representation can perform comparably to 2D non-causal representation in tasks such as global perception, dense prediction, and multi-modal understanding. Code shall be released.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether images can be modeled effectively as one-dimensional causal sequences, an approach associated with language modeling. Vision systems usually use two-dimensional, non-causal processing, and this architectural difference complicates unified multimodal models. The authors investigate a specific obstacle to bringing visual representations into the causal sequence setting.

They identify an over-focus problem: attention concentrates too heavily on a small subset of visual tokens. This restricts feature diversity and weakens useful training gradients. De-focus Attention Networks use learnable bandpass filters to produce varied attention patterns. Training also includes large, scheduled drop-path rates and, for global understanding tasks, an auxiliary loss on globally pooled features.

These mechanisms encourage attention to cover more tokens and improve optimization. Experiments show that the resulting one-dimensional causal representations can perform comparably to two-dimensional non-causal representations on global perception, dense prediction, and multimodal understanding tasks. The findings support the feasibility of this modeling approach across the tested tasks and identify attention concentration as an actionable problem in making it work.
summary.tldr: De-focus Attention Networks spread attention across visual tokens, enabling competitive one-dimensional causal image representations in the tested tasks.

title: Learning 1D Causal Visual Representation with De-focus Attention Networks

abstract: The deep equilibrium model (DEQ) generalizes the conventional feedforward neural network by fixing the same weights for each layer block and extending the number of layers to infinity. This novel model directly finds the fixed points of such a forward process as features for prediction. Despite empirical evidence showcasing its efficacy compared to feedforward neural networks, a theoretical understanding for its separation and bias is still limited. In this paper, we take a stepby proposing some separations and studying the bias of DEQ in its expressive power and learning dynamics. The results include: (1) A general separation is proposed, showing the existence of a width-$m$ DEQ that any fully connected neural networks (FNNs) with depth $O(m^{\alpha})$ for $\alpha \in (0,1)$ cannotapproximate unless its width is sub-exponential in $m$; (2) DEQ with polynomially bounded size and magnitude can efficiently approximate certain steep functions (which has very large derivatives) in $L^{\infty}$ norm, whereas FNN with bounded depth and exponentially bounded width cannot unless its weights magnitudes are exponentially large; (3) The implicit regularization caused by gradient flow from a diagonal linear DEQ is characterized, with specific examples showing the benefits brought by such regularization. From the overall study, a high-level conjecture from our analysis and empirical validations is that DEQ has potential advantages in learning certain high-frequency components.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models use the fixed point of a repeatedly applied, shared-weight transformation as their predictive representation. This paper studies what that construction can express and which solutions its learning dynamics favor. It aims to give theoretical explanations for advantages that have previously been observed empirically.

The authors establish separations between equilibrium models and fully connected feedforward networks under specified restrictions on depth, width, and parameter magnitudes. One result concerns a width-m equilibrium model and feedforward approximations of depth O(m^alpha), for alpha between zero and one. Another shows efficient approximation of certain steep functions by equilibrium models, while the compared bounded-depth feedforward networks require exponentially large weight magnitudes.

The paper also characterizes the implicit regularization produced by gradient flow in a diagonal linear equilibrium model, with examples illustrating its benefits. These results distinguish representational efficiency from the preferences introduced by training. Based on the analysis and empirical validation, the authors conjecture potential advantages for learning certain high-frequency components; they present that broader interpretation as a conjecture rather than a general theorem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional expressivity advantages and learning biases of deep equilibrium models, suggesting possible benefits for certain high-frequency functions.

title: Separation and Bias of Deep Equilibrium Models on Expressivity and Learning Dynamics

abstract: This paper introduces the notion of upper-linearizable/quadratizable functions, a class that extends concavity and DR-submodularity in various settings, including monotone and non-monotone cases over different types of convex sets. A general meta-algorithm is devised to convert algorithms for linear/quadratic maximization into ones that optimize upper-linearizable/quadratizable functions, offering a unified approach to tackling concave and DR-submodular optimization problems. The paper extends these results to multiple feedback settings, facilitating conversions between semi-bandit/first-order feedback and bandit/zeroth-order feedback, as well as between first/zeroth-order feedback and semi-bandit/bandit feedback. Leveraging this framework, new algorithms are derived using existing results as base algorithms for convex optimization, improving upon state-of-the-art results in various cases. Dynamic and adaptive regret guarantees are obtained for DR-submodular maximization, marking the first algorithms to achieve such guarantees in these settings. Notably, the paper achieves these advancements with fewer assumptions compared to existing state-of-the-art results, underscoring its broad applicability and theoretical contributions to non-convex optimization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for reusing simpler optimization algorithms on a broader family of objectives. It introduces upper-linearizable and upper-quadratizable functions, extending concavity and diminishing-returns submodularity across several settings. The treatment includes monotone and non-monotone objectives over different kinds of convex sets.

A general meta-algorithm converts methods for linear or quadratic maximization into methods for these broader function classes. The framework also supports conversions between feedback settings, including first-order information and zeroth-order observations, as well as semi-bandit and bandit feedback. This makes the approach useful when both the objective’s structure and the available information vary.

By using existing convex-optimization results as building blocks, the authors derive algorithms that improve prior results in several cases. They obtain the first dynamic and adaptive regret guarantees for the DR-submodular maximization settings considered, addressing performance as conditions change and over different portions of an online sequence. The paper reports these advances with fewer assumptions than previous results, making algorithm conversion the central source of its theoretical gains.
summary.tldr: A general conversion framework turns linear and quadratic optimization methods into algorithms for broader objectives and feedback settings.

title: From Linear to Linearizable Optimization: A Novel Framework with Applications to Stationary and Non-stationary DR-submodular Optimization

abstract: Visual object tracking aims to locate a targeted object in a video sequence based on an initial bounding box. Recently, Vision-Language~(VL) trackers have proposed to utilize additional natural language descriptions to enhance versatility in various applications. However, VL trackers are still inferior to State-of-The-Art (SoTA) visual trackers in terms of tracking performance. We found that this inferiority primarily results from their heavy reliance on manual textual annotations, which include the frequent provision of ambiguous language descriptions. In this paper, we propose ChatTracker to leverage the wealth of world knowledge in the Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to generate high-quality language descriptions and enhance tracking performance. To this end, we propose a novel reflection-based prompt optimization module to iteratively refine the ambiguous and inaccurate descriptions of the target with tracking feedback. To further utilize semantic information produced by MLLM, a simple yet effective VL tracking framework is proposed and can be easily integrated as a plug-and-play module to boost the performance of both VL and visual trackers. Experimental results show that our proposed ChatTracker achieves a performance comparable to existing methods.

paragraphs: Visual tracking follows a target through a video after receiving its initial bounding box. Language descriptions can provide additional information about the target, but the paper identifies ambiguous manual descriptions as a major reason vision-language trackers can trail strong visual trackers. ChatTracker addresses the quality of this language guidance.

It uses a multimodal large language model to generate descriptions informed by its world knowledge. A reflection-based prompt optimization module then revises ambiguous or inaccurate descriptions using feedback from tracking. This creates an iterative connection between describing the target and observing how well the tracker follows it, allowing the language guidance to be refined.

The paper also introduces a vision-language tracking framework that uses the resulting semantic information. It can be integrated as a plug-and-play module with either visual or vision-language trackers, making the approach applicable to both types of system. The experiments report performance comparable to existing methods. The stated finding therefore supports the usefulness of generated and refined descriptions without establishing that ChatTracker universally surpasses other trackers.
summary.tldr: ChatTracker uses tracking feedback to refine multimodal-model descriptions that guide an existing object tracker.

title: ChatTracker: Enhancing Visual Tracking Performance via Chatting with Multimodal Large Language Model

abstract: Humans judge perceptual similarity according to diverse visual attributes, including scene layout, subject location, and camera pose. Existing vision models understand a wide range of semantic abstractions but improperly weigh these attributes and thus make inferences misaligned with human perception. While vision representations have previously benefited from human preference alignment in contexts like image generation, the utility of perceptually aligned representations in more general-purpose settings remains unclear. Here, we investigate how aligning vision model representations to human perceptual judgments impacts their usability in standard computer vision tasks. We finetune state-of-the-art models on a dataset of human similarity judgments for synthetic image triplets and evaluate them across diverse computer vision tasks. We find that aligning models to perceptual judgments yields representations that improve upon the original backbones across many downstream tasks, including counting, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, instance retrieval, and retrieval-augmented generation. In addition, we find that performance is widely preserved on other tasks, including specialized out-of-distribution domains such as in medical imaging and 3D environment frames. Our results suggest that injecting an inductive bias about human perceptual knowledge into vision models can make them better representation learners.

The setup tests whether perceptual supervision contributes broadly useful information to the representation, extending investigation beyond settings such as image generation where human preference alignment has already been useful.

Aligned representations improve over the original backbones on many tasks, including counting, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, instance retrieval, and retrieval-augmented generation. Performance is also widely preserved on other tasks, including specialized out-of-distribution medical images and frames from 3D environments. These results suggest that human perceptual knowledge can provide a useful inductive bias for general representation learning, with benefits across several tasks rather than a claim of improvement on every task.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning vision models on human similarity judgments improves several downstream tasks while widely preserving performance elsewhere.

title: When does perceptual alignment benefit vision representations?

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are recognized for their strong performance across various applications, with the backpropagation (BP) algorithm playing a central role in the development of most GNN models. However, despite its effectiveness, BP has limitations that challenge its biological plausibility and affect the efficiency, scalability and parallelism of training neural networks for graph-based tasks. While several non-backpropagation (non-BP) training algorithms, such as the direct feedback alignment (DFA), have been successfully applied to fully-connected and convolutional network components for handling Euclidean data, directly adapting these non-BP frameworks to manage non-Euclidean graph data in GNN models presents significant challenges. These challenges primarily arise from the violation of the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption in graph data and the difficulty in accessing prediction errors for all samples (nodes) within the graph. To overcome these obstacles, in this paper we propose DFA-GNN, a novel forward learning framework tailored for GNNs with a case study of semi-supervised learning. The proposed method breaks the limitations of BP by using a dedicated forward training mechanism. Specifically, DFA-GNN extends the principles of DFA to adapt to graph data and unique architecture of GNNs, which incorporates the information of graph topology into the feedback links to accommodate the non-Euclidean characteristics of graph data. Additionally, for semi-supervised graph learning tasks, we developed a pseudo error generator that spreads residual errors from training data to create a pseudo error for each unlabeled node. These pseudo errors are then utilized to train GNNs using DFA. Extensive experiments on 10 public benchmarks reveal that our learning framework outperforms not only previous non-BP methods but also the standard BP methods, and it exhibits excellent robustness against various types of noise and attacks.

They also report robustness to several kinds of noise and attacks. The findings support adapting feedback alignment to the dependencies and incomplete labeling of graph data, rather than simply transferring the existing training procedure unchanged.
summary.tldr: DFA-GNN adapts direct feedback alignment to graph structure and unlabeled nodes, outperforming comparison training methods in ten benchmarks.

title: DFA-GNN: Forward Learning of Graph Neural Networks by Direct Feedback Alignment

abstract: The typical training of neural networks using large stepsize gradient descent (GD) under the logistic loss often involves two distinct phases, where the empirical risk oscillates in the first phase but decreases monotonically in the second phase. We investigate this phenomenon in two-layer networks that satisfy a near-homogeneity condition. We show that the second phase begins once the empirical risk falls below a certain threshold, dependent on the stepsize. Additionally, we show that the normalized margin grows nearly monotonically in the second phase, demonstrating an implicit bias of GD in training non-homogeneous predictors. If the dataset is linearly separable and the derivative of the activation function is bounded away from zero, we show that the average empirical risk decreases, implying that the first phase must stop in finite steps. Finally, we demonstrate that by choosing a suitably large stepsize, GD that undergoes this phase transition is more efficient than GD that monotonically decreases the risk. Our analysis applies to networks of any width, beyond the well-known neural tangent kernel and mean-field regimes.

paragraphs: Large gradient-descent steps can produce an initial period of oscillating training loss followed by steady decreases. This paper analyzes that transition for two-layer networks satisfying a near-homogeneity condition and trained with logistic loss. It seeks to explain when the apparently unstable early behavior gives way to more orderly progress.

The analysis shows that the second phase starts once empirical risk falls below a threshold that depends on the step size. During this phase, the normalized margin grows nearly monotonically, revealing an implicit preference in how gradient descent shapes the predictor. Under the additional assumptions of linearly separable data and an activation derivative bounded away from zero, decreasing average risk ensures that the first phase ends after finitely many steps.

The authors also show that an appropriately large step size, allowing this phase transition, can optimize more efficiently than gradient descent constrained to decrease risk monotonically. The analysis covers networks of any width within its assumptions. The result gives a conditional mathematical explanation for why temporary loss oscillation can accompany faster optimization and improving classification margins.
summary.tldr: Under stated network and data conditions, large gradient steps can transition from oscillating loss to efficient optimization with improving margins.

title: Large Stepsize Gradient Descent for Non-Homogeneous Two-Layer Networks: Margin Improvement and Fast Optimization

abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning is a powerful way to control an AI agent's behavior at runtime. That said, popular goal representations, e.g., target states or natural language, are either limited to Markovian tasks or rely on ambiguous task semantics. We propose representing temporal goals using compositions of deterministic finite automata (cDFAs) and use cDFAs to guide RL agents. cDFAs balance the need for formal temporal semantics with ease of interpretation: if one can understand a flow chart, one can understand a cDFA. On the other hand, cDFAs form a countably infinite concept class with Boolean semantics, and subtle changes to the automaton can result in very different tasks, making them difficult to condition agent behavior on. To address this, we observe that all paths through a DFA correspond to a series of reach-avoid tasks and propose pre-training graph neural network embeddings on "reach-avoid derived" DFAs. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that the proposed pre-training method enables zero-shot generalization to various cDFA task classes and accelerated policy specialization without the myopic suboptimality of hierarchical methods.

paragraphs: Controlling an agent through goals becomes difficult when success depends on the order of events. A target state can miss that temporal structure, while a natural-language instruction may leave its meaning ambiguous. This paper represents temporal goals using compositions of deterministic finite automata, giving tasks explicit rules that can be understood through a flow-chart-like structure.

The challenge is making those structures useful to a learned policy. There are infinitely many possible composed automata, and a small structural change can substantially alter the task. The authors observe that paths through an automaton can be understood as sequences of reach-avoid tasks. They use automata derived from these tasks to pretrain graph neural network embeddings.

Empirical evaluations show that the resulting embeddings support zero-shot generalization to several classes of composed-automaton tasks and faster specialization of policies. The authors also report avoiding the shortsighted suboptimality associated with hierarchical methods. The approach matters because it connects precise temporal instructions to learned representations that agents can use across different tasks.
summary.tldr: Pretraining graph embeddings of automata helps reinforcement-learning agents follow precise temporal goals and generalize to new task classes.

title: Compositional Automata Embeddings for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained models is a popular approach in machine learning for solving complex tasks with moderate data. However, fine-tuning the entire pre-trained model is ineffective in federated data scenarios where local data distributions are diversely skewed. To address this, we explore integrating federated learning with a more effective prompt-tuning method, optimizing for a small set of input prefixes to reprogram the pre-trained model's behavior. Our approach transforms federated learning into a distributed set modeling task, aggregating diverse sets of prompts to globally fine-tune the pre-trained model. We benchmark various baselines based on direct adaptations of existing federated model aggregation techniques and introduce a new probabilistic prompt aggregation method that substantially outperforms these baselines. Our reported results on a variety of computer vision datasets confirm that the proposed method is most effective to combat extreme data heterogeneity in federated learning.
