paragraphs: Retrieving information before generating an answer can help a language model access external knowledge, but a fixed retrieval step may be insufficient for complex questions. Information needs can change as reasoning unfolds, especially when questions are ambiguous or require several linked steps. InForage treats retrieval as an adaptive process carried out during reasoning.

Inspired by Information Foraging Theory, the framework uses reinforcement learning to train information-seeking behavior. It explicitly rewards the quality of intermediate retrievals, encouraging the model to gather and integrate useful information throughout the task. A human-guided dataset of iterative search and reasoning trajectories supports training on complex, real-world web questions.

Evaluations cover general question answering, multi-hop reasoning, and a newly developed real-time web question-answering dataset. The authors report better performance than baseline methods and describe the resulting agents as robust, adaptive, and efficient. These findings support making the usefulness of intermediate searches an explicit training signal when developing models that reason with external information.
summary.tldr: InForage rewards useful intermediate searches to train language models that retrieve and reason adaptively throughout a task.

title: Scent of Knowledge: Optimizing Search-Enhanced Reasoning with Information Foraging

abstract: We study the parameter complexity of robust memorization for ReLU networks: the number of parameters required to interpolate any dataset with $\epsilon$-separation between differently labeled points, while ensuring predictions remain consistent within a $\mu$-ball around each training example. We establish upper and lower bounds on the parameter count as a function of the robustness ratio $\rho = \mu / \epsilon$. Unlike prior work, we provide a fine-grained analysis across the entire range $\rho \in (0,1)$ and obtain tighter upper and lower bounds that improve upon existing results. Our findings reveal that the parameter complexity of robust memorization matches that of non-robust memorization when $\rho$ is small, but grows with increasing $\rho$. As a special case, when the input dimension is comparable to or exceeds the dataset size, our bounds become tight (up to logarithmic factors) across the entire range of $\rho$.

paragraphs: Memorizing training examples requires a network to predict their labels correctly. Robust memorization adds a local requirement: predictions must remain consistent within a specified neighborhood around each example. This paper asks how many parameters a ReLU network needs to meet that requirement for datasets whose differently labeled points have a specified separation.

The analysis tracks the ratio between the robustness radius and the separation scale. The authors establish tighter upper and lower parameter-count bounds throughout the ratio range from zero to one. Upper bounds describe sufficient network capacity, while lower bounds describe capacity requirements. Considering both helps characterize how the cost of robustness changes as the requested neighborhood becomes larger relative to separation.

The bounds show that small robustness ratios have the same parameter complexity as ordinary memorization, while larger ratios increase the cost. When input dimension is comparable to or greater than dataset size, the bounds agree up to logarithmic factors throughout the analyzed range. This gives a particularly precise characterization in that setting of how local prediction consistency changes the capacity needed for memorization.
summary.tldr: Tighter bounds characterize how ReLU-network parameter requirements grow as robust memorization demands larger neighborhoods relative to label separation.

title: The Cost of Robustness: Tighter Bounds on Parameter Complexity for Robust Memorization in ReLU Nets

abstract: We study policy optimization in Stackelberg mean field games (MFGs), a hierarchical framework for modeling the strategic interaction between a single leader and an infinitely large population of homogeneous followers. The objective can be formulated as a structured bi-level optimization problem, in which the leader needs to learn a policy maximizing its reward, anticipating the response of the followers. Existing methods for solving these (and related) problems often rely on restrictive independence assumptions between the leader’s and followers’ objectives, use samples inefficiently due to nested-loop algorithm structure, and lack finite-time convergence guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose AC-SMFG, a single-loop actor-critic algorithm that operates on continuously generated Markovian samples. The algorithm alternates between (semi-)gradient updates for the leader, a representative follower, and the mean field, and is simple to implement in practice. We establish the finite-time and finite-sample convergence of the algorithm to a stationary point of the Stackelberg objective. To our knowledge, this is the first Stackelberg MFG algorithm with non-asymptotic convergence guarantees. Our key assumption is a "gradient alignment" condition, which requires that the full policy gradient of the leader can be approximated by a partial component of it, relaxing the existing leader-follower independence assumption. Simulation results in a range of well-established economics environments demonstrate that AC-SMFG outperforms existing multi-agent and MFG learning baselines in policy quality and convergence speed.

paragraphs: Stackelberg mean field games model a leader interacting with an infinitely large population of homogeneous followers. The leader must improve its own policy while anticipating how the followers respond. This produces a two-level optimization problem, with existing approaches facing restrictive assumptions, inefficient nested training loops, or missing finite-time guarantees.

The proposed AC-SMFG algorithm uses a single actor-critic loop operating on continuously generated Markovian samples. It alternates updates for the leader, a representative follower, and the mean field describing the population. This structure addresses the sampling inefficiency associated with repeatedly solving an inner optimization problem.

The authors prove convergence to a stationary point within finite-time and finite-sample analyses. Their key gradient-alignment assumption allows part of the leader’s gradient to approximate its full policy gradient, relaxing prior leader-follower independence requirements. This is a conditional stationary-point guarantee, not a claim of global optimality. Simulations in established economics environments also show better policy quality and convergence speed than the evaluated multi-agent and mean-field learning baselines.
summary.tldr: AC-SMFG learns leader-follower policies in one loop with finite-sample stationary-point guarantees under a gradient-alignment assumption.

title: Learning in Stackelberg Mean Field Games: A Non-Asymptotic Analysis

abstract: We propose module graphical lasso (MGL), an aggressive dimensionality reduction and network estimation technique for a high-dimensional Gaussian graphical model (GGM). MGL achieves scalability, interpretability and robustness by exploiting the modularity property of many real-world networks. Variables are organized into tightly coupled modules and a graph structure is estimated to determine the conditional independencies among modules. MGL iteratively learns the module assignment of variables, the latent variables, each corresponding to a module, and the parameters of the GGM of the latent variables. In synthetic data experiments, MGL outperforms the standard graphical lasso and three other methods that incorporate latent variables into GGMs. When applied to gene expression data from ovarian cancer, MGL outperforms standard clustering algorithms in identifying functionally coherent gene sets and predicting survival time of patients. The learned modules and their dependencies provide novel insights into cancer biology as well as identifying possible novel drug targets.

paragraphs: Estimating a network among many variables can become difficult to compute and interpret. Module graphical lasso addresses this by exploiting modularity: variables are organized into tightly connected groups, and the model estimates relationships among those groups. It combines substantial dimensionality reduction with network estimation in a Gaussian graphical model.

The method iteratively learns which variables belong to each module, a latent variable representing each module, and the parameters of the graphical model over those latent variables. The resulting graph describes conditional independencies among modules. Learning these components together makes the grouping and network structure parts of one estimation procedure rather than unrelated outputs.

On synthetic data, the method outperforms standard graphical lasso and three alternatives that incorporate latent variables. On ovarian cancer gene expression data, it outperforms standard clustering methods in identifying functionally coherent gene groups and predicting patient survival time. The authors also report biological insights and possible new drug targets from the learned modules and dependencies. These targets are proposed possibilities, not experimentally established treatments.
summary.tldr: Module graphical lasso jointly learns variable groups and their dependency network, improving reported synthetic and ovarian cancer data results.

title: Efficient Dimensionality Reduction for High-Dimensional Network Estimation

abstract: In this article, we describe a method for optimizing control policies, with guaranteed monotonic improvement. By making several approximations to the theoretically-justified scheme, we develop a practical algorithm, called Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO). This algorithm is effective for optimizing large nonlinear policies such as neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate its robust performance on a wide variety of tasks: learning simulated robotic swimming, hopping, and walking gaits; and playing Atari games using images of the screen as input. Despite its approximations that deviate from the theory, TRPO tends to give monotonic improvement, with little tuning of hyperparameters.

paragraphs: A control policy determines how an agent acts, and policy optimization seeks to improve its performance. This paper begins with a theoretically justified optimization method that guarantees monotonic improvement. The goal is to translate that dependable improvement principle into a practical algorithm capable of training large nonlinear policies, including neural networks.

The practical method, Trust Region Policy Optimization or TRPO, is obtained through several approximations to the theoretical scheme. This distinction is central to interpreting the result: the guarantee belongs to the underlying method, while the implemented algorithm departs from its theory. The paper reports that practical TRPO nevertheless tends to improve monotonically.

Experiments cover simulated robotic swimming, hopping, and walking, as well as Atari games using screen images as input. Across these tasks, TRPO shows robust performance with little hyperparameter tuning. The results support the usefulness of the approximations for demanding policy-learning problems, while presenting monotonic improvement in the practical algorithm as an observed tendency rather than an unconditional guarantee.
summary.tldr: TRPO approximates a policy-optimization scheme with guaranteed improvement and empirically learns large policies robustly with little tuning.

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization

abstract: As deep nets are increasingly used in applications suited for mobile devices, a fundamental dilemma becomes apparent: the trend in deep learning is to grow models to absorb ever-increasing data set sizes; however mobile devices are designed with very little memory and cannot store such large models. We present a novel network architecture, HashedNets, that exploits inherent redundancy in neural networks to achieve drastic reductions in model sizes. HashedNets uses a low-cost hash function to randomly group connection weights into hash buckets, and all connections within the same hash bucket share a single parameter value. These parameters are tuned to adjust to the HashedNets weight sharing architecture with standard backprop during training. Our hashing procedure introduces no additional memory overhead, and we demonstrate on several benchmark data sets that HashedNets shrink the storage requirements of neural networks substantially while mostly preserving generalization performance.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can demand more storage than memory-constrained mobile devices can provide. HashedNets addresses this mismatch by reducing the number of distinct parameters stored in a network. The approach exploits redundancy among connection weights, allowing many connections to reuse a parameter while retaining the network's collection of connections.

A low-cost hash function assigns connection weights to groups called buckets. Every connection assigned to the same bucket uses the same parameter value. The shared values are trained with standard backpropagation, so learning adjusts them within the weight-sharing arrangement. The hashing procedure determines which connections share values without introducing additional memory overhead for that procedure.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show substantial reductions in storage requirements while mostly preserving generalization performance. The qualification matters: the result is strong compression with much of the predictive performance retained, rather than a guarantee of identical performance. The paper's contribution is a simple architecture in which parameter sharing is built into training and directly addresses the cost of storing neural networks.
summary.tldr: HashedNets compresses neural networks by hashing connections into shared parameters, substantially reducing storage while mostly preserving generalization.

title: Compressing Neural Networks with the Hashing Trick

abstract: We study the problem of imitation learning from demonstrations of multiple coordinating agents. One key challenge in this setting is that learning a good model of coordination can be difficult, since coordination is often implicit in the demonstrations and must be inferred as a latent variable. We propose a joint approach that simultaneously learns a latent coordination model along with the individual policies. In particular, our method integrates unsupervised structure learning with conventional imitation learning. We illustrate the power of our approach on a difficult problem of learning multiple policies for fine-grained behavior modeling in team sports, where different players occupy different roles in the coordinated team strategy. We show that having a coordination model to infer the roles of players yields substantially improved imitation loss compared to conventional baselines.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations becomes more complicated when several agents act together. An individual action can depend on the agent’s role within a shared strategy, yet demonstrations may never explicitly identify those roles. This paper treats coordination as hidden structure that must be inferred alongside the behavior of each agent.

The proposed approach jointly learns a latent coordination model and individual policies. It combines unsupervised structure learning, which discovers the hidden organization of the demonstrations, with conventional imitation learning, which learns how agents behave. Joint learning makes the inferred coordination part of the same modeling process as the policies it is meant to support.

The authors demonstrate the approach in team sports, where players occupy different roles within a coordinated strategy and fine-grained behavior is difficult to model. Inferring player roles through the coordination model substantially improves imitation loss compared with conventional baselines. This finding supports the value of modeling hidden roles when learning demonstrated team behavior; the reported measure concerns imitation quality.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning hidden coordination and individual policies improves imitation of team-sport behavior in the reported experiments.

title: Coordinated Multi-Agent Imitation Learning

abstract: PixelCNN achieves state-of-the-art results in density estimation for natural images. Although training is fast, inference is costly, requiring one network evaluation per pixel; O(N) for N pixels. This can be sped up by caching activations, but still involves generating each pixel sequentially. In this work, we propose a parallelized PixelCNN that allows more efficient inference by modeling certain pixel groups as conditionally independent. Our new PixelCNN model achieves competitive density estimation and orders of magnitude speedup – O(log N) sampling instead of O(N) – enabling the practical generation of 512x512 images. We evaluate the model on class-conditional image generation, text-to-image synthesis, and action-conditional video generation, showing that our model achieves the best results among non-pixel-autoregressive density models that allow efficient sampling.

Although training is fast, inference is costly, requiring one network evaluation per pixel; O(N) for N pixels. This can be sped up by caching activations, but still involves generating each pixel sequentially. In this work, we propose a parallelized PixelCNN that allows more efficient inference by modeling certain pixel groups as conditionally independent. paragraphs: PixelCNN can model natural-image distributions effectively, but generating an image requires sequential pixel predictions. Even caching intermediate activations leaves this ordering intact. The paper targets that generation bottleneck by changing which pixel predictions must depend on one another, allowing more of the sampling process to happen in parallel.

The proposed parallelized PixelCNN treats certain groups of pixels as conditionally independent. This modeling choice reduces the stated sampling complexity from linear to logarithmic in the number of pixels. The authors report orders-of-magnitude speedups while maintaining competitive density estimation, making the generation of 512-by-512 images practical with their model.

Evaluation covers class-conditioned image generation, text-to-image synthesis, and action-conditioned video generation. Within those evaluations, the model achieves the best results among the non-pixel-autoregressive density models that permit efficient sampling. The comparison is specific to that category. The broader contribution is a way to alter pixel dependencies so that image generation gains parallelism without abandoning competitive modeling of image distributions.
summary.tldr: A parallel PixelCNN models selected pixel groups as conditionally independent, reducing sampling complexity to logarithmic while retaining competitive density estimation.

title: Parallel Multiscale Autoregressive Density Estimation

abstract: While deep learning has led to remarkable advances across diverse applications, it struggles in domains where the data distribution changes over the course of learning. In stark contrast, biological neural networks continually adapt to changing domains, possibly by leveraging complex molecular machinery to solve many tasks simultaneously. In this study, we introduce intelligent synapses that bring some of this biological complexity into artificial neural networks. Each synapse accumulates task relevant information over time, and exploits this information to rapidly store new memories without forgetting old ones. We evaluate our approach on continual learning of classification tasks, and show that it dramatically reduces forgetting while maintaining computational efficiency.

In this study, we introduce intelligent synapses that bring some of this biological complexity into artificial neural networks. Each synapse accumulates task relevant information over time, and exploits this information to rapidly store new memories without forgetting old ones. paragraphs: Neural networks can struggle when the data they encounter changes during learning. Learning a new task may interfere with what the network previously learned, making continued adaptation difficult. This paper addresses that problem through artificial synapses that retain information about their relevance to tasks over time.

The approach takes inspiration from biological neural networks' ability to adapt continually. Each synapse accumulates task-related information and uses that history when storing new memories. The important design choice is to give individual connections a continuing record of their learning role, so that acquiring new knowledge can take previously acquired knowledge into account.

The authors evaluate the method on sequences of classification tasks and report a dramatic reduction in forgetting while maintaining computational efficiency. The stated empirical finding is reduced forgetting, rather than a demonstrated universal elimination of it. This makes the work significant as an efficient approach to continual learning: it connects information gathered during learning with later efforts to preserve useful memories while the network adapts.
summary.tldr: Synapses that accumulate task-relevant information substantially reduce forgetting in continual classification learning while remaining computationally efficient.

title: Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence

abstract: Recent studies disclose that maximizing the minimum margin like support vector machines does not necessarily lead to better generalization performances, and instead, it is crucial to optimize the margin distribution. Although it has been shown that for binary classification, characterizing the margin distribution by the first- and second-order statistics can achieve superior performance. It still remains open for multi-class classification, and due to the complexity of margin for multi-class classification, optimizing its distribution by mean and variance can also be difficult. In this paper, we propose mcODM (multi-class Optimal margin Distribution Machine), which can solve this problem efficiently. We also give a theoretical analysis for our method, which verifies the significance of margin distribution for multi-class classification. Empirical study further shows that mcODM always outperforms all four versions of multi-class SVMs on all experimental data sets.
originalAbstract: Recent studies disclose that maximizing the minimum margin like support vector machines does not necessarily lead to better generalization performances, and instead, it is crucial to optimize the margin distribution. Although it has been shown that for binary classification, characterizing the margin distribution by the first- and second-order statistics can achieve superior performance. It still remains open for multi-class classification, and due to the complexity of margin for multi-class classification, optimizing its distribution by mean and variance can also be difficult. In this paper, we propose mcODM (multi-class Optimal margin Distribution Machine), which can solve this problem efficiently. We also give a theoretical analysis for our method, which verifies the significance of margin distribution for multi-class classification. Empirical study further shows that mcODM always outperforms all four versions of multi-class SVMs on all experimental data sets.

paragraphs: A classifier's margin expresses how strongly its decision favors the correct class. Maximizing the smallest margin, as support vector machines do, does not necessarily produce better generalization. This paper studies a broader target: optimizing how margins are distributed across examples in a multiclass classification problem.

Earlier binary-classification work had shown benefits from describing the margin distribution through its mean and variance. Extending that idea to multiple classes is difficult because multiclass margins have a more complex structure. The proposed multiclass Optimal margin Distribution Machine, or mcODM, is designed to solve this optimization problem efficiently.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting the importance of the margin distribution for multiclass classification. In their empirical study, mcODM outperforms all four evaluated versions of multiclass SVMs on every experimental dataset. That consistency is a finding within the reported evaluation. The contribution provides both an efficient method and theoretical support for considering the overall pattern of margins when designing multiclass classifiers.
summary.tldr: mcODM efficiently optimizes multiclass margin distributions and outperforms four multiclass SVM variants across all reported experimental datasets.

title: Multi-Class Optimal Margin Distribution Machine

abstract: Assume we are given a set of items from a general metric space, but we neither have access to the representation of the data nor to the distances between data points. Instead, suppose that we can actively choose a triplet of items (A, B, C) and ask an oracle whether item A is closer to item B or to item C. In this paper, we propose a novel random forest algorithm for regression and classification that relies only on such triplet comparisons. In the theory part of this paper, we establish sufficient conditions for the consistency of such a forest. In a set of comprehensive experiments, we then demonstrate that the proposed random forest is efficient both for classification and regression. In particular, it is even competitive with other methods that have direct access to the metric representation of the data.

Instead, suppose that we can actively choose a triplet of items (A, B, C) and ask an oracle whether item A is closer to item B or to item C. paragraphs: This paper considers prediction when data items belong to a metric space but their representations and numerical distances are unavailable. The learner can instead choose three items and ask whether the first is closer to the second or the third. Such answers provide relative similarity information without exposing coordinates or exact distance values.

The authors construct a random forest for classification and regression using only these triplet comparisons. This extends the forest approach to a restricted information setting: the available evidence consists of chosen comparison queries rather than directly accessible features. Their theoretical analysis establishes sufficient conditions for consistency, giving circumstances under which learning from this information has a sound statistical basis.

Experiments assess both classification and regression and find the proposed forest efficient. It is also competitive with methods that receive the data's metric representation directly. The result suggests that relative comparisons can retain substantial predictive value in the evaluated settings, even when richer numerical descriptions are inaccessible. The consistency claim remains tied to the sufficient conditions established in the analysis.
summary.tldr: A random forest learns classification and regression from relative-distance comparisons alone, with conditional consistency guarantees and competitive experimental performance.

title: Comparison-Based Random Forests

abstract: We present a novel algorithm that uses exact learning and abstraction to extract a deterministic finite automaton describing the state dynamics of a given trained RNN. We do this using Angluin’s \lstar algorithm as a learner and the trained RNN as an oracle. Our technique efficiently extracts accurate automata from trained RNNs, even when the state vectors are large and require fine differentiation.
originalAbstract: We present a novel algorithm that uses exact learning and abstraction to extract a deterministic finite automaton describing the state dynamics of a given trained RNN. We do this using Angluin’s \lstar algorithm as a learner and the trained RNN as an oracle. Our technique efficiently extracts accurate automata from trained RNNs, even when the state vectors are large and require fine differentiation.

paragraphs: A trained recurrent neural network carries information through a changing internal state. This paper asks how to extract a deterministic finite automaton that describes those state dynamics. The desired output is a discrete description of the trained network's behavior, giving the extraction procedure a specific object to construct and assess.

The method combines exact learning with abstraction. Angluin's L-star algorithm serves as the learner, while the trained recurrent network serves as the oracle that the learner consults. Queries and counterexamples support the extraction process, and abstraction connects the network's state representation with the finite-state description being learned. These components place learning and state representation within a single algorithm.

The authors report that the technique efficiently extracts accurate automata even when the recurrent network has large state vectors that require fine distinctions. This matters because an extraction method must preserve behaviorally relevant differences while producing a discrete model. The stated result concerns accurate descriptions of trained networks, including cases where their internal representations are large and cannot be treated coarsely.
summary.tldr: The paper combines exact learning and abstraction to efficiently extract accurate finite automata describing trained RNN state dynamics.

title: Extracting Automata from Recurrent Neural Networks Using Queries and Counterexamples

abstract: We propose a variable selection method for high dimensional regression models, which allows for complex, nonlinear, and high-order interactions among variables. The proposed method approximates this complex system using a penalized neural network and selects explanatory variables by measuring their utility in explaining the variance of the response variable. This measurement is based on a novel statistic called Drop-Out-One Loss. The proposed method also allows (overlapping) group variable selection. We prove that the proposed method can select relevant variables and exclude irrelevant variables with probability one as the sample size goes to infinity, which is referred to as the Oracle Property. Experimental results on simulated and real world datasets show the efficiency of our method in terms of variable selection and prediction accuracy.

The proposed method approximates this complex system using a penalized neural network and selects explanatory variables by measuring their utility in explaining the variance of the response variable. This measurement is based on a novel statistic called Drop-Out-One Loss. The proposed method also allows (overlapping) group variable selection. We prove that the proposed method can select relevant variables and exclude irrelevant variables with probability one as the sample size goes to infinity, which is referred to as the Oracle Property. Experimental results on simulated and real world datasets show the efficiency of our method in terms of variable selection and prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Selecting useful predictors is challenging when a response depends on complex nonlinear relationships and interactions among many variables. The paper proposes a method for high-dimensional regression that accommodates these relationships through a penalized neural network. The network approximates the response-generating system, providing the basis for deciding which explanatory variables are relevant.

Selection uses a statistic called Drop-Out-One Loss to measure a variable's utility in explaining response variance. This connects the selection decision to how much explanatory value a variable provides within the modeled system. The method also supports selecting groups of variables, including groups that overlap, extending the selection task beyond individual inputs.

The authors prove an oracle property: as sample size tends to infinity, the method selects relevant variables and excludes irrelevant ones with probability one. This is an asymptotic result, rather than a guarantee of perfect selection at every finite sample size. Experiments with simulated and real-world datasets show effectiveness in variable selection and prediction accuracy, supporting the method's use for complex regression relationships.
summary.tldr: A penalized neural network uses Drop-Out-One Loss to select variables and overlapping groups while accommodating nonlinear interactions.

title: Variable Selection via Penalized Neural Network: a Drop-Out-One Loss Approach

abstract: Machine learning models that take computer program source code as input typically use Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. However, a major challenge is that code is written using an open, rapidly changing vocabulary due to, e.g., the coinage of new variable and method names. Reasoning over such a vocabulary is not something for which most NLP methods are designed. We introduce a Graph-Structured Cache to address this problem; this cache contains a node for each new word the model encounters with edges connecting each word to its occurrences in the code. We find that combining this graph-structured cache strategy with recent Graph-Neural-Network-based models for supervised learning on code improves the models’ performance on a code completion task and a variable naming task — with over 100% relative improvement on the latter — at the cost of a moderate increase in computation time.

paragraphs: Source code continually introduces new words through variable names, method names, and other identifiers. This changing vocabulary creates difficulties for code models built using natural language processing techniques that are not designed for such openness. The paper introduces a graph-structured cache to represent newly encountered words explicitly.

The cache creates a node for each new word and connects that node to the word's occurrences in the code. This preserves a relationship between an identifier and the places where it is used. The authors combine this structure with graph neural network models for supervised learning on code, making the cache part of a model that can reason over graph relationships.

The combined approach improves performance on both code completion and variable naming. For variable naming, the reported improvement exceeds 100% in relative terms. These improvements come with a moderate increase in computation time. The results show that explicitly linking new vocabulary to its code occurrences can provide useful information for the evaluated prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: A graph-structured cache links new code words to their occurrences, improving code completion and variable naming with moderately higher computation.

title: Open Vocabulary Learning on Source Code with a Graph-Structured Cache

abstract: The ability to perform offline A/B-testing and off-policy learning using logged contextual bandit feedback is highly desirable in a broad range of applications, including recommender systems, search engines, ad placement, and personalized health care. Both offline A/B-testing and off-policy learning require a counterfactual estimator that evaluates how some new policy would have performed, if it had been used instead of the logging policy. In this paper, we identify a family of counterfactual estimators which subsumes most such estimators proposed to date. Our analysis of this family identifies a new estimator - called Continuous Adaptive Blending (CAB) - which enjoys many advantageous theoretical and practical properties. In particular, it can be substantially less biased than clipped Inverse Propensity Score (IPS) weighting and the Direct Method, and it can have less variance than Doubly Robust and IPS estimators. In addition, it is sub-differentiable such that it can be used for learning, unlike the SWITCH estimator. Experimental results show that CAB provides excellent evaluation accuracy and outperforms other counterfactual estimators in terms of learning performance.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new decision policy from logged contextual bandit feedback requires estimating what would have happened under different choices. This counterfactual problem arises in both offline A/B testing and learning a policy from existing records. The paper develops a family of estimators that encompasses most previously proposed approaches and uses its analysis to identify Continuous Adaptive Blending, or CAB.

CAB addresses the balance between systematic estimation error and variability. The authors show that it can have substantially less bias than clipped inverse propensity weighting and the Direct Method. It can also have lower variance than Doubly Robust and inverse propensity estimators. These are possible advantages established by the analysis, rather than a claim that CAB dominates every alternative in every setting.

CAB is also sub-differentiable, allowing it to participate in optimization for policy learning, unlike the SWITCH estimator discussed in the paper. Experiments report strong evaluation accuracy and better learning performance than the other counterfactual estimators tested. Its contribution therefore covers both assessing policies and using those assessments to improve them.
summary.tldr: CAB provides a counterfactual estimator that can improve bias and variance trade-offs while supporting policy learning.

title: CAB: Continuous Adaptive Blending for Policy Evaluation and Learning

abstract: Knowledge graphs are incomplete by nature, with only a limited number of observed facts from the world knowledge being represented as structured relations between entities. To partly address this issue, an important task in statistical relational learning is that of link prediction or knowledge graph completion. Both linear and non-linear models have been proposed to solve the problem. Bilinear models, while expressive, are prone to overfitting and lead to quadratic growth of parameters in number of relations. Simpler models have become more standard, with certain constraints on bilinear map as relation parameters. In this work, we propose a factorized bilinear pooling model, commonly used in multi-modal learning, for better fusion of entities and relations, leading to an efficient and constraint-free model. We prove that our model is fully expressive, providing bounds on the embedding dimensionality and factorization rank. Our model naturally generalizes Tucker decomposition based TuckER model, which has been shown to generalize other models, as efficient low-rank approximation without substantially compromising the performance. Due to low-rank approximation, the model complexity can be controlled by the factorization rank, avoiding the possible cubic growth of TuckER. Empirically, we evaluate on real-world datasets, reaching on par or state-of-the-art performance. At extreme low-ranks, model preserves the performance while staying parameter efficient.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain observed relationships between entities but leave many facts unrecorded. Link prediction aims to infer those missing relationships. Expressive bilinear models can help, yet their parameter requirements and susceptibility to overfitting motivate more efficient ways to combine representations of entities and relations.

LowFER uses factorized bilinear pooling to perform that combination. Its factorization rank controls model complexity, allowing the authors to express richer interactions through a compact representation. The paper proves full expressivity with bounds on the required embedding dimension and rank. It also relates LowFER to the Tucker-decomposition-based TuckER model through an efficient low-rank approximation.

This construction avoids the possible cubic growth associated with TuckER while allowing complexity to be adjusted through rank. Evaluations on real-world datasets achieve performance comparable to or better than the state of the art. The reported experiments also preserve performance at extremely low ranks, supporting the practical value of controlling parameter count through factorization.
summary.tldr: LowFER uses low-rank bilinear pooling to predict missing knowledge-graph links with controllable model size and strong empirical performance.

title: LowFER: Low-rank Bilinear Pooling for Link Prediction

abstract: We prove quantitative convergence rates at which discrete Langevin-like processes converge to the invariant distribution of a related stochastic differential equation. We study the setup where the additive noise can be non-Gaussian and state-dependent and the potential function can be non-convex. We show that the key properties of these processes depend on the potential function and the second moment of the additive noise. We apply our theoretical findings to studying the convergence of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for non-convex problems and corroborate them with experiments using SGD to train deep neural networks on the CIFAR-10 dataset.
originalAbstract: We prove quantitative convergence rates at which discrete Langevin-like processes converge to the invariant distribution of a related stochastic differential equation. We study the setup where the additive noise can be non-Gaussian and state-dependent and the potential function can be non-convex. We show that the key properties of these processes depend on the potential function and the second moment of the additive noise. We apply our theoretical findings to studying the convergence of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for non-convex problems and corroborate them with experiments using SGD to train deep neural networks on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies how discrete stochastic update processes relate to a continuous stochastic differential equation. Its main results give quantitative rates for convergence to the equation’s invariant distribution, meaning a distribution that remains unchanged under its evolution. The focus is on Langevin-like processes and their connection to stochastic gradient methods.

The analysis allows additive noise to be non-Gaussian and to depend on the current state. It also permits a nonconvex potential function. Within this setting, the authors show that key properties depend on the potential and the noise’s second moment. This identifies features of the objective landscape and noise that matter for understanding the process.

The authors apply the theory to convergence of stochastic gradient descent on nonconvex problems. Experiments training deep neural networks on CIFAR-10 corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution links discrete optimization updates, their noise, and a continuous probabilistic description, providing quantitative convergence information for the analyzed processes and an application to neural-network training.
summary.tldr: The paper proves distributional convergence rates for Langevin-like processes with flexible noise and applies the theory to nonconvex SGD.

title: Stochastic Gradient and Langevin Processes

abstract: The evaluation of robustness against adversarial manipulation of neural networks-based classifiers is mainly tested with empirical attacks as methods for the exact computation, even when available, do not scale to large networks. We propose in this paper a new white-box adversarial attack wrt the $l_p$-norms for $p \in \{1,2,\infty\}$ aiming at finding the minimal perturbation necessary to change the class of a given input. It has an intuitive geometric meaning, yields quickly high quality results, minimizes the size of the perturbation (so that it returns the robust accuracy at every threshold with a single run). It performs better or similar to state-of-the-art attacks which are partially specialized to one $l_p$-norm, and is robust to the phenomenon of gradient obfuscation.

We propose in this paper a new white-box adversarial attack wrt the $l_p$-norms for $p \in \{1,2,\infty\}$ aiming at finding the minimal perturbation necessary to change the class of a given input. paragraphs: Testing a classifier's adversarial robustness often means searching for an input change that alters its prediction. Exact robustness computation does not scale well to large networks, so empirical attacks play a central role. This paper proposes a white-box attack aimed at finding a small perturbation sufficient to change an input's class.

The attack supports the l1, l2, and l-infinity norms, which provide different measures of perturbation size. It has a geometric interpretation and directly seeks to reduce distortion. Finding small perturbations is useful beyond testing one fixed budget: the results of a single run can be used to evaluate attack-based robust accuracy across perturbation thresholds.

The authors report that the method quickly produces high-quality results and performs similarly to or better than state-of-the-art attacks, including methods partly specialized to individual norms. They also report robustness to gradient obfuscation. These findings concern the effectiveness of the empirical search; the stated aim of minimizing distortion should not be read as a guarantee that every returned perturbation is the exact smallest possible one.
summary.tldr: A geometric white-box attack searches efficiently for small class-changing perturbations across three norms and supports evaluation at multiple thresholds.

title: Minimally distorted Adversarial Examples with a Fast Adaptive Boundary Attack

abstract: Individual fairness is an intuitive definition of algorithmic fairness that addresses some of the drawbacks of group fairness. Despite its benefits, it depends on a task specific fair metric that encodes our intuition of what is fair and unfair for the ML task at hand, and the lack of a widely accepted fair metric for many ML tasks is the main barrier to broader adoption of individual fairness. In this paper, we present two simple ways to learn fair metrics from a variety of data types. We show empirically that fair training with the learned metrics leads to improved fairness on three machine learning tasks susceptible to gender and racial biases. We also provide theoretical guarantees on the statistical performance of both approaches.

In this paper, we present two simple ways to learn fair metrics from a variety of data types. paragraphs: Individual fairness depends on a task-specific notion of which people should be treated similarly. That notion is encoded in a fair metric, making the metric an essential ingredient of fair learning. The paper addresses a practical barrier: many machine learning tasks lack a widely accepted metric that captures the relevant fairness judgments.

The authors present two simple approaches for learning fair metrics from data, with applicability to a variety of data types. This moves metric construction into a statistical learning problem. The learned metric can then inform fair training, linking the information used to define similarity with the behavior encouraged in the resulting predictor.

The authors provide statistical performance guarantees for both approaches and test fair training with the learned metrics on three tasks susceptible to gender and racial biases. They report improved fairness in those experiments. The contribution combines methods for obtaining a necessary ingredient of individual fairness with theoretical support and evidence that the learned metrics improve fairness in the studied applications.
summary.tldr: Two data-driven methods learn individual-fairness metrics, with statistical guarantees and improved fairness on three evaluated tasks.

title: Two Simple Ways to Learn Individual Fairness Metrics from Data

abstract: The seasonal epidemic of influenza costs thousands of lives each year in the US. While influenza epidemics occur every year, timing and size of the epidemic vary strongly from season to season. This complicates the public health efforts to adequately respond to such epidemics. Forecasting techniques to predict the development of seasonal epidemics such as influenza, are of great help to public health decision making. Therefore, the US Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has initiated a yearly challenge to forecast influenza-like illness. Here, we propose a new framework based on Gaussian process (GP) for seasonal epidemics forecasting and demonstrate its capability on the CDC reference data on influenza like illness: our framework leads to accurate forecasts with small but reliable uncertainty estimation. We compare our framework to several state of the art benchmarks and show competitive performance. We, therefore, believe that our GP based framework for seasonal epidemics forecasting will play a key role for future influenza forecasting and, lead to further research in the area.

paragraphs: Seasonal influenza returns regularly, but the timing and scale of each epidemic can vary substantially. That variability makes public health planning difficult: knowing that an epidemic will occur does not establish how it will develop. This paper proposes a Gaussian process framework for forecasting seasonal epidemics, with influenza-like illness as its demonstrated application.

The framework produces forecasts together with uncertainty estimates. This combination matters because a prediction's usefulness depends partly on how reliably its uncertainty describes what might happen. On the CDC reference data for influenza-like illness, the authors report accurate forecasts accompanied by uncertainty estimates that are small but reliable.

Comparisons with several leading forecasting benchmarks show competitive performance. The stated result therefore supports the framework as a viable forecasting approach, without establishing that it consistently surpasses all alternatives. Its contribution is a demonstrated way to combine epidemic prediction and uncertainty estimation in this setting. The authors anticipate an important future role for the approach and further research, rather than reporting that such a role has already been achieved.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process framework delivers competitive influenza-like illness forecasts with small, reliable uncertainty estimates on CDC reference data.

title: Influenza Forecasting Framework based on Gaussian Processes

abstract: We present an optimization framework for learning a fair classifier in the presence of noisy perturbations in the protected attributes. Compared to prior work, our framework can be employed with a very general class of linear and linear-fractional fairness constraints, can handle multiple, non-binary protected attributes, and outputs a classifier that comes with provable guarantees on both accuracy and fairness. Empirically, we show that our framework can be used to attain either statistical rate or false positive rate fairness guarantees with a minimal loss in accuracy, even when the noise is large, in two real-world datasets.
originalAbstract: We present an optimization framework for learning a fair classifier in the presence of noisy perturbations in the protected attributes. Compared to prior work, our framework can be employed with a very general class of linear and linear-fractional fairness constraints, can handle multiple, non-binary protected attributes, and outputs a classifier that comes with provable guarantees on both accuracy and fairness. Empirically, we show that our framework can be used to attain either statistical rate or false positive rate fairness guarantees with a minimal loss in accuracy, even when the noise is large, in two real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Fair classification becomes harder when the protected attributes used to assess fairness contain errors. The paper addresses this setting with an optimization framework that learns a classifier despite noisy perturbations in those attributes. Its goal is to retain meaningful control over both predictive accuracy and fairness when the information defining protected groups is imperfect.

The framework supports a broad family of fairness requirements expressed as linear or linear-fractional constraints. It can also handle several protected attributes and attributes with more than two categories. This flexibility matters because fairness requirements and group definitions need not fit a single binary distinction. The resulting classifier comes with provable guarantees covering both accuracy and fairness.

On two real-world datasets, the authors report achieving either statistical-rate fairness or false-positive-rate fairness with only a small loss in accuracy, including under substantial noise. The empirical result concerns these tested fairness choices and datasets. It illustrates how the framework's broader optimization machinery can translate into useful accuracy–fairness tradeoffs when protected-attribute information is unreliable.
summary.tldr: An optimization framework learns classifiers with accuracy and fairness guarantees despite noise in protected attributes.

title: Fair Classification with Noisy Protected Attributes: A Framework with Provable Guarantees

abstract: We present GNNAutoScale (GAS), a framework for scaling arbitrary message-passing GNNs to large graphs. GAS prunes entire sub-trees of the computation graph by utilizing historical embeddings from prior training iterations, leading to constant GPU memory consumption in respect to input node size without dropping any data. While existing solutions weaken the expressive power of message passing due to sub-sampling of edges or non-trainable propagations, our approach is provably able to maintain the expressive power of the original GNN. We achieve this by providing approximation error bounds of historical embeddings and show how to tighten them in practice. Empirically, we show that the practical realization of our framework, PyGAS, an easy-to-use extension for PyTorch Geometric, is both fast and memory-efficient, learns expressive node representations, closely resembles the performance of their non-scaling counterparts, and reaches state-of-the-art performance on large-scale graphs.
originalAbstract: We present GNNAutoScale (GAS), a framework for scaling arbitrary message-passing GNNs to large graphs. GAS prunes entire sub-trees of the computation graph by utilizing historical embeddings from prior training iterations, leading to constant GPU memory consumption in respect to input node size without dropping any data. While existing solutions weaken the expressive power of message passing due to sub-sampling of edges or non-trainable propagations, our approach is provably able to maintain the expressive power of the original GNN. We achieve this by providing approximation error bounds of historical embeddings and show how to tighten them in practice. Empirically, we show that the practical realization of our framework, PyGAS, an easy-to-use extension for PyTorch Geometric, is both fast and memory-efficient, learns expressive node representations, closely resembles the performance of their non-scaling counterparts, and reaches state-of-the-art performance on large-scale graphs.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph neural networks build node representations using information from neighboring nodes. On large graphs, the resulting computation can become expensive because each representation depends on further neighborhoods. GNNAutoScale addresses this growth by reusing node embeddings computed during previous training iterations.

These historical embeddings replace entire branches of the computation graph, allowing constant GPU memory consumption with respect to the number of input nodes without discarding data. Reuse introduces approximation error, so the paper provides bounds on that error and explains how to tighten them in practice. Its theoretical analysis shows that the framework can maintain the expressive power of the original message-passing network.

The implementation, PyGAS, extends PyTorch Geometric. Experiments report fast, memory-efficient operation, expressive node representations, and performance close to corresponding networks run without scaling modifications. It also reaches state-of-the-art performance on large graphs. The contribution combines a practical reuse mechanism with an analysis of why scaling need not sacrifice the original network’s ability to represent graph information.
summary.tldr: GNNAutoScale reuses historical node embeddings to scale message-passing networks while providing error bounds and preserving their expressive power.

title: GNNAutoScale: Scalable and Expressive Graph Neural Networks via Historical Embeddings

abstract: Quantization is promising in enabling powerful yet complex deep neural networks (DNNs) to be deployed into resource constrained platforms. However, quantized DNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks unless being equipped with sophisticated techniques, leading to a dilemma of struggling between DNNs’ efficiency and robustness. In this work, we demonstrate a new perspective regarding quantization’s role in DNNs’ robustness, advocating that quantization can be leveraged to largely boost DNNs’ robustness, and propose a framework dubbed Double-Win Quant that can boost the robustness of quantized DNNs over their full precision counterparts by a large margin. Specifically, we for the first time identify that when an adversarially trained model is quantized to different precisions in a post-training manner, the associated adversarial attacks transfer poorly between different precisions. Leveraging this intriguing observation, we further develop Double-Win Quant integrating random precision inference and training to further reduce and utilize the poor adversarial transferability, enabling an aggressive “win-win" in terms of DNNs’ robustness and efficiency. Extensive experiments and ablation studies consistently validate Double-Win Quant’s effectiveness and advantages over state-of-the-art (SOTA) adversarial training methods across various attacks/models/datasets. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/RICE-EIC/Double-Win-Quant.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used by neural networks, helping them run on resource-constrained devices. Robustness to adversarial attacks can complicate that efficiency goal. This paper investigates whether differences between numerical precisions can themselves help defend a model, and develops a framework called Double-Win Quant around that possibility.

The starting observation concerns adversarially trained models quantized after training: attacks associated with one precision transfer poorly to other precisions. Double-Win Quant uses random precision during both training and inference to further reduce and exploit this limited transferability. Precision therefore becomes part of the robustness mechanism as well as a means of reducing computational demands.

Experiments and ablations across attacks, models, and datasets consistently support the framework’s effectiveness relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art adversarial-training methods. The paper reports that quantized models can substantially exceed their full-precision counterparts in robustness under this framework. These findings support a joint efficiency-and-robustness benefit in the tested settings, grounded in how attacks behave across different numerical representations.
summary.tldr: Double-Win Quant randomizes precision during training and inference to exploit poor attack transfer across precisions and improve evaluated robustness and efficiency.

title: Double-Win Quant: Aggressively Winning Robustness of Quantized Deep Neural Networks via Random Precision Training and Inference

abstract: We propose a novel policy update that combines regularized policy optimization with model learning as an auxiliary loss. The update (henceforth Muesli) matches MuZero’s state-of-the-art performance on Atari. Notably, Muesli does so without using deep search: it acts directly with a policy network and has computation speed comparable to model-free baselines. The Atari results are complemented by extensive ablations, and by additional results on continuous control and 9x9 Go.

paragraphs: Muesli is a reinforcement-learning policy update that combines regularized policy optimization with model learning as an auxiliary objective. The policy determines the agent’s actions, while learning a model supplies an additional training signal. The paper studies this combination as a way to improve policy optimization and achieve strong game-playing performance.

The reported Atari result is that Muesli matches MuZero’s state-of-the-art performance. Muesli selects actions directly with a policy network and does not use deep search. Its computation speed is comparable to model-free baselines. Together, these statements describe a useful empirical combination: high Atari performance alongside direct policy execution and the reported computational profile.

The Atari evaluation is accompanied by extensive ablations, which examine the contributions of components, and additional results on continuous control and 9x9 Go. The abstract’s explicit performance-matching claim concerns Atari. The broader contribution is a policy update that combines model learning with regularized optimization, demonstrating that these ingredients can work together effectively even when actions are produced without deep search.
summary.tldr: Muesli combines regularized policy optimization and auxiliary model learning to match MuZero on Atari without deep search.

title: Muesli: Combining Improvements in Policy Optimization

abstract: Existing late fusion multi-view clustering (LFMVC) optimally integrates a group of pre-specified base partition matrices to learn a consensus one. It is then taken as the input of the widely used k-means to generate the cluster labels. As observed, the learning of the consensus partition matrix and the generation of cluster labels are separately done. These two procedures lack necessary negotiation and can not best serve for each other, which may adversely affect the clustering performance. To address this issue, we propose to unify the aforementioned two learning procedures into a single optimization, in which the consensus partition matrix can better serve for the generation of cluster labels, and the latter is able to guide the learning of the former. To optimize the resultant optimization problem, we develop a four-step alternate algorithm with proved convergence. We theoretically analyze the clustering generalization error of the proposed algorithm on unseen data. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm in terms of both clustering accuracy and computational efficiency. It is expected that the simplicity and effectiveness of our algorithm will make it a good option to be considered for practical multi-view clustering applications.

paragraphs: Late-fusion multi-view clustering combines precomputed partitions from several views of the same data. A conventional approach first learns a consensus partition matrix and then applies k-means to obtain cluster labels. Because these stages are separate, the consensus representation and final assignments cannot directly guide each other during learning.

The paper brings both stages into a single optimization problem. The consensus matrix is learned with the eventual labels in mind, while the labels help shape the consensus matrix. This makes agreement among views and the production of final clusters mutually connected parts of the objective. The authors solve it using a four-step alternating algorithm with a convergence proof.

The paper also analyzes clustering generalization error on unseen data. Experiments on multiple benchmarks report improvements in both clustering accuracy and computational efficiency. The results support jointly optimizing the intermediate consensus and final assignments. Despite the title’s reference to one pass, the stated optimization method alternates among four steps; the central unification concerns the two formerly separate learning procedures.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a consensus partition and final cluster labels improves late-fusion multi-view clustering on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: One Pass Late Fusion Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Importance sampling-based estimators for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are valued for their simplicity, unbiasedness, and reliance on relatively few assumptions. However, the variance of these estimators is often high, especially when trajectories are of different lengths. In this work, we introduce Omitting-States-Irrelevant-to-Return Importance Sampling (OSIRIS), an estimator which reduces variance by strategically omitting likelihood ratios associated with certain states. We formalize the conditions under which OSIRIS is unbiased and has lower variance than ordinary importance sampling, and we demonstrate these properties empirically.
originalAbstract: Importance sampling-based estimators for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are valued for their simplicity, unbiasedness, and reliance on relatively few assumptions. However, the variance of these estimators is often high, especially when trajectories are of different lengths. In this work, we introduce Omitting-States-Irrelevant-to-Return Importance Sampling (OSIRIS), an estimator which reduces variance by strategically omitting likelihood ratios associated with certain states. We formalize the conditions under which OSIRIS is unbiased and has lower variance than ordinary importance sampling, and we demonstrate these properties empirically.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates the performance of a target policy using data produced by another policy. Importance sampling adjusts for the difference through likelihood ratios. Its simplicity and unbiasedness make it attractive, but the resulting estimates can have high variance, particularly when the observed trajectories have different lengths.

OSIRIS reduces variance by selectively leaving out likelihood ratios associated with certain states. The organizing idea is state relevance to return: corrections attached to states that are irrelevant in the required sense can introduce variability without being needed for the value estimate. The method therefore changes which parts of a trajectory contribute to the importance weighting.

The authors formalize conditions under which OSIRIS remains unbiased and has lower variance than ordinary importance sampling, and demonstrate these properties empirically. The guarantee depends on those conditions; arbitrary omission is not the stated result. The contribution is a principled way to use state relevance when constructing an estimator, preserving correctness while reducing unnecessary variability where the analysis applies.
summary.tldr: OSIRIS selectively omits state-level importance ratios to reduce off-policy evaluation variance while retaining unbiasedness under formalized conditions.

title: State Relevance for Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: After their successful debut in natural language processing, Transformer architectures are now becoming the de-facto standard in many domains. An obstacle for their deployment over new modalities is the architectural configuration: the optimal depth-to-width ratio has been shown to dramatically vary across data types (i.e., 10x larger over images than over language). We theoretically predict the existence of an embedding rank bottleneck that limits the contribution of self-attention width to the Transformer expressivity. We thus directly tie the input vocabulary size and rank to the optimal depth-to-width ratio, since a small vocabulary size or rank dictates an added advantage of depth over width. We empirically demonstrate the existence of this bottleneck and its implications on the depth-to-width interplay of Transformer architectures, linking the architecture variability across domains to the often glossed-over usage of different vocabulary sizes or embedding ranks in different domains. As an additional benefit, our rank bottlenecking framework allows us to identify size redundancies of 25%-50% in leading NLP models such as ALBERT and T5.

paragraphs: The best balance between transformer depth and width can vary substantially across data types. This paper investigates an explanation rooted in the input representation: vocabulary size and embedding rank. It theoretically predicts a bottleneck in which embedding rank limits how much additional self-attention width can contribute to the model's expressivity.

Under this account, a small vocabulary or low embedding rank gives depth an additional advantage over width. The authors empirically demonstrate the bottleneck and its consequences for architecture design. Their analysis links cross-domain differences in preferred transformer shapes to differences in vocabulary sizes and embedding ranks that might otherwise receive little attention.

The framework also identifies size redundancies of 25%–50% in leading language models including ALBERT and T5. This result concerns redundancies revealed by the rank-based analysis. More broadly, the work argues that architecture choices should account for the information capacity of the input embedding, since wider attention layers may encounter a representational constraint imposed earlier in the model.
summary.tldr: An embedding-rank bottleneck links vocabulary properties to transformer depth–width choices and reveals substantial size redundancies in studied language models.

title: Which transformer architecture fits my data? A vocabulary bottleneck in self-attention

abstract: Transformer model with multi-head attention requires caching intermediate results for efficient inference in generation tasks. However, cache brings new memory-related costs and prevents leveraging larger batch size for faster speed. We propose memory-efficient lossless attention (called EL-attention) to address this issue. It avoids heavy operations for building multi-head keys and values, cache for them is not needed. EL-attention constructs an ensemble of attention results by expanding query while keeping key and value shared. It produces the same result as multi-head attention with less GPU memory and faster inference speed. We conduct extensive experiments on Transformer, BART, and GPT-2 for summarization and question generation tasks. The results show EL-attention speeds up existing models by 1.6x to 5.3x without accuracy loss.

EL-attention constructs an ensemble of attention results by expanding query while keeping key and value shared. paragraphs: During generation, Transformer models cache intermediate attention results to avoid repeatedly recomputing them. Those caches also consume memory and can limit the batch sizes available for faster inference. This paper targets that tradeoff by changing how multi-head attention is computed while preserving its output.

EL-attention expands the query and forms an ensemble of attention results while sharing the key and value. This avoids the heavy operations used to construct separate multi-head keys and values and removes the need to cache them. The method produces the same result as multi-head attention, so its memory savings come from reorganizing the computation rather than accepting an approximate attention output.

The authors evaluate the approach with Transformer, BART, and GPT-2 models on summarization and question generation. They report inference speedups ranging from 1.6 to 5.3 times without accuracy loss. Those measurements establish benefits in the tested generation settings. The broader significance is that attention’s computational organization can materially affect memory use and inference speed even when its result is preserved.
summary.tldr: EL-attention preserves multi-head attention outputs while reducing memory use and delivering reported generation speedups of 1.6–5.3 times.

title: EL-Attention: Memory Efficient Lossless Attention for Generation

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the workhorse in modern machine learning and data-driven optimization. Despite its popularity, existing theoretical guarantees for SGD are mainly derived in expectation and for convex learning problems. High probability guarantees of nonconvex SGD are scarce, and typically rely on “light-tail” noise assumptions and study the optimization and generalization performance separately. In this paper, we develop high probability bounds for nonconvex SGD with a joint perspective of optimization and generalization performance. Instead of the light tail assumption, we consider the gradient noise following a heavy-tailed sub-Weibull distribution, a novel class generalizing the sub-Gaussian and sub-Exponential families to potentially heavier-tailed distributions. Under these complicated settings, we first present high probability bounds with best-known rates in general nonconvex learning, then move to nonconvex learning with a gradient dominance curvature condition, for which we improve the learning guarantees to fast rates. We further obtain sharper learning guarantees by considering a mild Bernstein-type noise condition. Our analysis also reveals the effect of trade-offs between the optimization and generalization performance under different conditions. In the last, we show that gradient clipping can be employed to remove the bounded gradient-type assumptions. Additionally, in this case, the stepsize of SGD is completely oblivious to the knowledge of smoothness.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent when the objective is nonconvex and gradient noise can have relatively heavy tails. Instead of describing performance only on average, it develops bounds that hold with high probability. It also studies optimization and generalization together, connecting progress on the training objective with performance beyond the training data.

The noise belongs to the sub-Weibull family, which includes sub-Gaussian and sub-Exponential distributions while allowing heavier tails. Under this setting, the authors establish best-known rates for general nonconvex learning. A gradient-dominance curvature condition gives faster rates, and an additional Bernstein-type noise condition sharpens the learning guarantees further.

The analysis shows how optimization and generalization tradeoffs depend on the conditions imposed. It also establishes that gradient clipping can remove bounded-gradient-type assumptions. In that clipped setting, the step size does not need knowledge of smoothness. The results broaden the noise behavior covered by high-probability SGD theory while making explicit which additional assumptions support stronger conclusions.
summary.tldr: The paper gives joint high-probability optimization and generalization guarantees for nonconvex SGD with sub-Weibull noise, with stronger rates under additional conditions.

title: High Probability Guarantees for Nonconvex Stochastic Gradient Descent with Heavy Tails

abstract: We focus on analyzing the classical stochastic projected gradient methods under a general dependent data sampling scheme for constrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We show the worst-case rate of convergence $\tilde{O}(t^{-1/4})$ and complexity $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ for achieving an $\varepsilon$-near stationary point in terms of the norm of the gradient of Moreau envelope and gradient mapping. While classical convergence guarantee requires i.i.d. data sampling from the target distribution, we only require a mild mixing condition of the conditional distribution, which holds for a wide class of Markov chain sampling algorithms. This improves the existing complexity for the constrained smooth nonconvex optimization with dependent data from $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-8})$ to $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ with a significantly simpler analysis. We illustrate the generality of our approach by deriving convergence results with dependent data for stochastic proximal gradient methods, adaptive stochastic gradient algorithm AdaGrad and stochastic gradient algorithm with heavy ball momentum. As an application, we obtain first online nonnegative matrix factorization algorithms for dependent data based on stochastic projected gradient methods with adaptive step sizes and optimal rate of convergence.

While classical convergence guarantee requires i.i.d. data sampling from the target distribution, we only require a mild mixing condition of the conditional distribution, which holds for a wide class of Markov chain sampling algorithms. This improves the existing complexity for the constrained smooth nonconvex optimization with dependent data from $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-8})$ to $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ with a significantly simpler analysis.
