paragraphs: Many convergence analyses assume that each training sample is drawn independently from the target distribution. This paper studies constrained, smooth, nonconvex optimization when successive samples can depend on one another. Its main focus is stochastic projected gradient methods, with a mild mixing condition replacing independent sampling. That condition holds for a broad class of Markov chain sampling algorithms.

The authors establish a worst-case convergence rate of approximately t to the power of minus one quarter, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Reaching an epsilon-near stationary point requires approximately epsilon to the power of minus four steps, improving the previous dependence of minus eight. Stationarity is measured through the Moreau-envelope gradient and gradient mapping; the guarantee concerns approaching stationarity rather than finding a global optimum.

The analysis also yields dependent-data convergence results for stochastic proximal gradient methods, AdaGrad, and heavy-ball momentum. As an application, the authors develop online nonnegative matrix factorization algorithms using adaptive step sizes and report an optimal convergence rate. The broader contribution is a simpler analysis that accommodates dependence while substantially strengthening the stated complexity guarantee.
summary.tldr: Under a mild mixing condition, the paper strengthens convergence guarantees for constrained nonconvex optimization with dependent samples.

title: Convergence of First-Order Methods for Constrained Nonconvex Optimization with Dependent Data

abstract: Graph size generalization is hard for Message passing neural networks (MPNNs). The graph-level classification performance of MPNNs degrades across various graph sizes. Recently, theoretical studies reveal that a slow uncontrollable convergence rate w.r.t. graph size could adversely affect the size generalization. To address the uncontrollable convergence rate caused by correlations across nodes in the underlying dimensional signal-generating space, we propose to use Wasserstein barycenters as graph-level consensus to combat node-level correlations. Methodologically, we propose a Wasserstein barycenter matching (WBM) layer that represents an input graph by Wasserstein distances between its MPNN-filtered node embeddings versus some learned class-wise barycenters. Theoretically, we show that the convergence rate of an MPNN with a WBM layer is controllable and independent to the dimensionality of the signal-generating space. Thus MPNNs with WBM layers are less susceptible to slow uncontrollable convergence rate and size variations. Empirically, the WBM layer improves the size generalization over vanilla MPNNs with different backbones (e.g., GCN, GIN, and PNA) significantly on real-world graph datasets.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks can lose graph-classification accuracy when graph sizes change. This paper addresses an explanation for that difficulty: correlations among nodes can produce slow, uncontrollable convergence as graph size grows. The authors propose a different graph-level representation intended to reduce the effect of those correlations.

Their Wasserstein barycenter matching layer compares the node embeddings produced by a message passing network with learned class-specific barycenters. It represents the graph using Wasserstein distances to those barycenters, which serve as graph-level consensus references. This creates a way to summarize the collection of node embeddings through comparisons with learned references associated with classes.

The theoretical analysis shows that an MPNN with this layer has a controllable convergence rate independent of the dimensionality of the underlying signal-generating space. This makes it less susceptible to the identified source of slow convergence and graph-size variation. Experiments on real-world graph datasets show significant improvements in size generalization over standard MPNNs across GCN, GIN, and PNA backbones, supporting the usefulness of the added layer.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein barycenter matching improves graph-size generalization by comparing node embeddings with learned class references and controlling a relevant convergence rate.

title: Wasserstein Barycenter Matching for Graph Size Generalization of Message Passing Neural Networks

abstract: Projection maintenance is one of the core data structure tasks. Efficient data structures for projection maintenance have led to recent breakthroughs in many convex programming algorithms. In this work, we further extend this framework to the Kronecker product structure. Given a constraint matrix ${\sf A}$ and a positive semi-definite matrix $W\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with a sparse eigenbasis, we consider the task of maintaining the projection in the form of ${\sf B}^\top({\sf B}{\sf B}^\top)^{-1}{\sf B}$, where ${\sf B}={\sf A}(W\otimes I)$ or ${\sf B}={\sf A}(W^{1/2}\otimes W^{1/2})$. At each iteration, the weight matrix $W$ receives a low rank change and we receive a new vector $h$. The goal is to maintain the projection matrix and answer the query ${\sf B}^\top({\sf B}{\sf B}^\top)^{-1}{\sf B}h$ with good approximation guarantees. We design a fast dynamic data structure for this task and it is robust against an adaptive adversary. Following the beautiful and pioneering work of [Beimel, Kaplan, Mansour, Nissim, Saranurak and Stemmer, STOC’22], we use tools from differential privacy to reduce the randomness required by the data structure and further improve the running time.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization algorithms repeatedly use projections whose defining matrices change over time. Recomputing the relevant quantities can be expensive. This paper extends projection-maintenance data structures to matrices built with Kronecker products, targeting a structured setting in which the projection must stay useful through a sequence of updates.

The setup combines a constraint matrix with a positive semidefinite weight matrix that has a sparse eigenbasis. Two Kronecker constructions are considered, using either the weight matrix and an identity matrix or two copies of its square root. At each iteration, the weight matrix undergoes a low-rank change and a new query vector arrives. The data structure must approximately apply the current projection to that vector.

The authors design a fast dynamic structure with approximation guarantees and robustness against an adaptive adversary. They also use differential privacy tools to reduce the randomness the structure needs, improving running time further. Here, privacy techniques serve an algorithmic role in efficient, adaptive computation within the stated matrix-structure assumptions.
summary.tldr: A dynamic data structure maintains Kronecker-structured projections efficiently, using differential privacy tools to reduce randomness and resist adaptive adversaries.

title: Sketching Meets Differential Privacy: Fast Algorithm for Dynamic Kronecker Projection Maintenance

abstract: Reinforcement learning has seen wide success in finetuning large language models to better align with instructions via human feedback. The so-called algorithm, Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) demonstrates impressive performance on the GPT series models. However, the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm is complex and requires additional training for reward and value networks. In this paper, we consider an alternative approach: converting feedback to instruction by relabeling the original one and training the model for better alignment in a supervised manner. Such an algorithm doesn’t require any additional parameters except for the original language model and maximally reuses the pretraining pipeline. To achieve this, we formulate instruction alignment problem for language models as a goal-reaching problem in decision making. We propose Hindsight Instruction Relabeling (HIR), a novel algorithm for aligning language models with instructions. The resulting two-stage algorithm shed light to a family of reward-free approaches that utilize the hindsightly relabeled instructions based on feedback. We evaluate the performance of HIR extensively on 12 challenging BigBench reasoning tasks and show that HIR outperforms the baseline algorithms and is comparable to or even surpasses supervised fine-tuning. The implementation of HIR is available at https://github.com/tianjunz/HIR.

The authors evaluate HIR on twelve challenging BigBench reasoning tasks. It outperforms the evaluated baseline algorithms and performs comparably to, or better than, supervised fine-tuning. These findings support feedback-driven relabeling as a useful alternative training mechanism in the tested reasoning settings. The central idea is that feedback can improve instruction following by changing the supervised learning examples, allowing the original model to learn without additional reward or value networks.
summary.tldr: HIR turns feedback into relabeled instructions for supervised language-model alignment without additional reward or value networks.

title: The Wisdom of Hindsight Makes Language Models Better Instruction Followers

abstract: We obtain the first positive results for bounded sample compression in the agnostic regression setting with the $\ell_p$ loss, where $p\in [1,\infty]$. We construct a generic approximate sample compression scheme for real-valued function classes exhibiting exponential size in the fat-shattering dimension but independent of the sample size. Notably, for linear regression, an approximate compression of size linear in the dimension is constructed. Moreover, for $\ell_1$ and $\ell_\infty$ losses, we can even exhibit an efficient exact sample compression scheme of size linear in the dimension. We further show that for every other $\ell_p$ loss, $p\in (1,\infty)$, there does not exist an exact agnostic compression scheme of bounded size. This refines and generalizes a negative result of David, Moran, and Yehudayoff (2016) for the $\ell_2$ loss. We close by posing general open questions: for agnostic regression with $\ell_1$ loss, does every function class admit an exact compression scheme of polynomial size in the pseudo-dimension? For the $\ell_2$ loss, does every function class admit an approximate compression scheme of polynomial size in the fat-shattering dimension? These questions generalize Warmuth’s classic sample compression conjecture for realizable-case classification (Warmuth, 2003).

paragraphs: Sample compression asks whether a learning problem can be represented using a bounded amount of information from its training sample. This paper studies regression in the agnostic setting, where the chosen function class need not fit the data perfectly. Its results distinguish sharply between approximate compression and exact compression under different loss functions.

For real-valued function classes, the authors construct a general approximate scheme whose size is independent of the number of training examples. Its size grows exponentially with the fat-shattering dimension, a measure of function-class complexity. For linear regression, they obtain a stronger result: approximate compression needs size only linear in the input dimension.

Exact compression has a different boundary. For linear regression with absolute-error or maximum-error loss, the paper gives efficient exact schemes of size linear in dimension. For the other losses between these endpoints, including squared loss, bounded-size exact agnostic compression is impossible. The paper also poses open questions about polynomial-size compression for broader function classes. Together, these findings show why allowing approximation and choosing the loss function fundamentally change what compression can achieve.
summary.tldr: Approximate regression compression can avoid dependence on sample size, while bounded exact compression depends critically on the loss.

title: Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression

abstract: Inverse problems arise in a multitude of applications, where the goal is to recover a clean signal from noisy and possibly (non)linear observations. The difficulty of a reconstruction problem depends on multiple factors, such as the ground truth signal structure, the severity of the degradation and the complex interactions between the above. This results in natural sample-by-sample variation in the difficulty of a reconstruction problem. Our key observation is that most existing inverse problem solvers lack the ability to adapt their compute power to the difficulty of the reconstruction task, resulting in subpar performance and wasteful resource allocation. We propose a novel method, severity encoding, to estimate the degradation severity of corrupted signals in the latent space of an autoencoder. We show that the estimated severity has strong correlation with the true corruption level and can provide useful hints on the difficulty of reconstruction problems on a sample-by-sample basis. Furthermore, we propose a reconstruction method based on latent diffusion models that leverages the predicted degradation severities to fine-tune the reverse diffusion sampling trajectory and thus achieve sample-adaptive inference times. Our framework, Flash-Diffusion, acts as a wrapper that can be combined with any latent diffusion-based baseline solver, imbuing it with sample-adaptivity and acceleration. We perform experiments on both linear and nonlinear inverse problems and demonstrate that our technique greatly improves the performance of the baseline solver and achieves up to $10\times$ acceleration in mean sampling speed.

paragraphs: Recovering a clean signal from corrupted observations can require very different amounts of work for different samples. Difficulty depends on both the original signal and the degradation it underwent. The paper argues that reconstruction methods often fail to account for this variation, spending computation inefficiently and producing weaker results than an adaptive approach could.

The authors introduce severity encoding, which estimates corruption severity in an autoencoder’s latent representation. Their estimates correlate strongly with the actual corruption level, providing a useful indication of reconstruction difficulty. The central contribution is a way to connect an estimated property of each observation to the amount of computation used to reconstruct it.
summary.tldr: Flash-Diffusion adapts reconstruction effort to estimated corruption severity, improving tested solvers and achieving up to tenfold faster average sampling.

title: Adapt and Diffuse: Sample-adaptive Reconstruction via Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has seen substantial efforts to improve model accuracy for an unlabeled target domain with the help of a labeled source domain. However, UDA models often exhibit poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty on target data, a problem that remains under-explored and poses risks in safety-critical UDA applications. The calibration problem in UDA is particularly challenging due to the absence of labeled target data and severe distribution shifts between domains. In this paper, we approach UDA calibration as a target-domain-specific unsupervised problem, different from mainstream solutions based on covariate shift. We introduce Pseudo-Calibration (PseudoCal), a novel post-hoc calibration framework. Our innovative use of inference-stage mixup synthesizes a labeled pseudo-target set capturing the structure of the real unlabeled target data. This turns the unsupervised calibration problem into a supervised one, easily solvable with temperature scaling. Extensive empirical evaluations across 5 diverse UDA scenarios involving 10 UDA methods consistently demonstrate the superior performance and versatility of PseudoCal over existing solutions.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a model from labeled source data to an unlabeled target domain. Even when prediction accuracy improves, the model’s confidence on target examples can remain poorly calibrated. Correcting that confidence is difficult because target labels are unavailable and the target distribution can differ substantially from the source.

PseudoCal treats calibration as a problem specific to the target domain and applies it after model training. It uses mixup during inference to construct a labeled pseudo-target dataset that captures structure in the real unlabeled target data. This supplies a surrogate supervised calibration problem where direct target supervision is missing.

The resulting dataset is used with temperature scaling to adjust predictive confidence. Evaluations span five adaptation scenarios and ten adaptation methods, with consistently superior reported performance over existing calibration solutions. The findings support the versatility of constructing target-informed calibration data. The method’s role is to improve uncertainty estimates for adapted models, addressing a distinct concern from whether their predicted labels are accurate.
summary.tldr: PseudoCal creates labeled pseudo-target data from unlabeled target examples to calibrate adapted models using temperature scaling.

title: Pseudo-Calibration: Improving Predictive Uncertainty Estimation in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) ensures that training a machine learning model does not leak private data. In practice, we may have access to auxiliary public data that is free of privacy concerns. In this work, we assume access to a given amount of public data and settle the following fundamental open questions: 1. What is the optimal (worst-case) error of a DP model trained over a private data set while having access to side public data? 2. How can we harness public data to improve DP model training in practice? We consider these questions in both the local and central models of pure and approximate DP. To answer the first question, we prove tight (up to log factors) lower and upper bounds that characterize the optimal error rates of three fundamental problems: mean estimation, empirical risk minimization, and stochastic convex optimization. We show that the optimal error rates can be attained (up to log factors) by either discarding private data and training a public model, or treating public data like it is private and using an optimal DP algorithm. To address the second question, we develop novel algorithms that are "even more optimal" (i.e. better constants) than the asymptotically optimal approaches described above. For local DP mean estimation, our algorithm is optimal including constants. Empirically, our algorithms show benefits over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much auxiliary public data can improve training under differential privacy when a specified amount of public data is available. It considers both local and central privacy models, with pure and approximate privacy guarantees. The focus is the best possible worst-case error for mean estimation, empirical risk minimization, and stochastic convex optimization.

The paper then develops algorithms with better constants than those asymptotically optimal approaches. For local private mean estimation, the proposed algorithm is optimal even including constants. Experiments also report benefits over state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical and practical results together distinguish the best rate of improvement from the additional gains available through more careful use of public data.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal private-learning error rates with public data and develops algorithms that improve constants and empirical performance.

title: Optimal Differentially Private Model Training with Public Data

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the learning rate in adaptive methods, such as AdaGrad and Adam. We propose Prodigy, an algorithm that provably estimates the distance to the solution $D$, which is needed to set the learning rate optimally. At its core, Prodigy is a modification of the D-Adaptation method for learning-rate-free learning. It improves upon the convergence rate of D-Adaptation by a factor of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log(D/d_0)})$, where $d_0$ is the initial estimate of $D$. We test Prodigy on 12 common logistic-regression benchmark datasets, VGG11 and ResNet-50 training on CIFAR10, ViT training on Imagenet, LSTM training on IWSLT14, DLRM training on Criteo dataset, VarNet on Knee MRI dataset, as well as RoBERTa and GPT transformer training on BookWiki. Our experimental results show that our approach consistently outperforms D-Adaptation and reaches test accuracy values close to that of hand-tuned Adam.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as AdaGrad and Adam still face the problem of choosing a learning rate. Prodigy addresses this by estimating the distance to a solution, denoted D, which is needed to set the learning rate optimally. It builds on D-Adaptation, a method designed to avoid manual learning-rate selection.

The algorithm modifies how this distance is estimated and provides a provable improvement in convergence rate over D-Adaptation. The improvement factor scales as the square root of the logarithm of D divided by its initial estimate, d0. This connects the theoretical benefit to the relationship between the solution distance and the estimate used at initialization.

The authors evaluate Prodigy across logistic regression and neural-network training tasks involving images, language, recommendation, and MRI. Their experiments consistently outperform D-Adaptation and achieve test accuracy close to manually tuned Adam. The findings support Prodigy as a practical route toward reducing learning-rate tuning while retaining competitive predictive performance across the tested workloads.
summary.tldr: Prodigy improves distance-based learning-rate adaptation, outperforming D-Adaptation and approaching hand-tuned Adam’s test accuracy across the reported experiments.

title: Prodigy: An Expeditiously Adaptive Parameter-Free Learner

abstract: State-space models (SSMs), such as Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023), have been proposed as alternatives to Transformer networks in language modeling, incorporating gating, convolutions, and input-dependent token selection to mitigate the quadratic cost of multi-head attention. Although SSMs exhibit competitive performance, their in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, a remarkable emergent property of modern language models that enables task execution without parameter optimization, remain less explored compared to Transformers. In this study, we evaluate the ICL performance of SSMs, focusing on Mamba, against Transformer models across various tasks. Our results show that SSMs perform comparably to Transformers in standard regression ICL tasks, while outperforming them in tasks like sparse parity learning. However, SSMs fall short in tasks involving non-standard retrieval functionality. To address these limitations, we introduce a hybrid model, MambaFormer, that combines Mamba with attention blocks, surpassing individual models in tasks where they struggle independently. Our findings suggest that hybrid architectures offer promising avenues for enhancing ICL in language models.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model perform a task using information supplied in its input, without updating its parameters. This paper asks how well state-space models, particularly Mamba, support that ability compared with Transformers. The question matters because these models offer alternatives to the quadratic computational cost associated with multi-head attention.

The study compares the architectures across several kinds of in-context learning tasks. State-space models perform similarly to Transformers on standard regression tasks and better on tasks such as sparse parity learning. However, they perform worse when tasks require non-standard retrieval. This pattern shows that competitive performance on one form of contextual learning does not establish equally strong performance across other task requirements.

The authors introduce MambaFormer, a hybrid architecture combining Mamba with attention blocks. It surpasses the individual architectures on tasks where they struggle independently. The results support hybrid designs as a promising direction for improving in-context learning: different sequence-processing mechanisms can contribute useful capabilities within one model, with the observed advantages depending on the task.
summary.tldr: Mamba’s in-context learning strengths vary by task, and combining it with attention improves performance where individual architectures struggle.

title: Can Mamba Learn How To Learn? A Comparative Study on In-Context Learning Tasks

abstract: The *Rashomon Effect*, coined by Leo Breiman, describes the phenomenon that there exist many equally good predictive models for the same dataset. This phenomenon happens for many real datasets and when it does, it sparks both magic and consternation, but mostly magic. In light of the Rashomon Effect, this perspective piece proposes reshaping the way we think about machine learning, particularly for tabular data problems in the nondeterministic (noisy) setting. We address how the Rashomon Effect impacts (1) the existence of simple-yet-accurate models, (2) flexibility to address user preferences, such as fairness and monotonicity, without losing performance, (3) uncertainty in predictions, fairness, and explanations, (4) reliable variable importance, (5) algorithm choice, specifically, providing advanced knowledge of which algorithms might be suitable for a given problem, and (6) public policy. We also discuss a theory of when the Rashomon Effect occurs and why. Our goal is to illustrate how the Rashomon Effect can have a massive impact on the use of machine learning for complex problems in society.

paragraphs: The Rashomon Effect describes situations in which many different models predict equally well on the same dataset. This position paper argues that this multiplicity can be useful, especially for noisy tabular problems. When several models perform similarly, selecting a model becomes an opportunity to consider qualities beyond predictive performance alone.

The authors discuss how this flexibility relates to finding simple but accurate models and accommodating preferences such as fairness or monotonicity without sacrificing performance. They also examine uncertainty across predictions, fairness assessments, and explanations, along with the reliability of variable importance. The existence of several good models therefore affects both which model is chosen and how its behavior should be interpreted.

The paper further connects the phenomenon to algorithm selection and public policy, and discusses a theory of when and why it arises. Its position is conditional on the availability of many equally good models, a phenomenon reported for many real datasets. The proposed shift is to treat that collection as a resource for addressing practical and societal requirements.
summary.tldr: When many models predict equally well, their diversity can offer flexibility in simplicity, fairness, explanations, and practical decision-making.

title: Position: Amazing Things Come From Having Many Good Models

abstract: This paper introduces the retrieval-augmented large language model with Definite Finite Automaton (DFA-RAG), a novel framework designed to enhance the capabilities of conversational agents using large language models (LLMs). Traditional LLMs face challenges in generating regulated and compliant responses in special scenarios with predetermined response guidelines, like emotional support and customer service. Our framework addresses these challenges by embedding a Definite Finite Automaton (DFA), learned from training dialogues, within the LLM. This structured approach acts as a semantic router which enables the LLM to adhere to a deterministic response pathway. The routing is achieved by the retrieval-augmentation generation (RAG) strategy, which carefully selects dialogue examples aligned with the current conversational context. The advantages of DFA-RAG include an interpretable structure through human-readable DFA, context-aware retrieval for responses in conversations, and plug-and-play compatibility with existing LLMs. Extensive benchmarks validate DFA-RAG’s effectiveness, indicating its potential as a valuable contribution to the conversational agent.

paragraphs: DFA-RAG addresses conversations that must follow predetermined response guidelines, such as customer service and emotional support. A language model's ability to generate fluent text does not by itself provide a structured response pathway. The paper introduces an automaton learned from training dialogues to organize how the model moves through a conversation.

This automaton acts as a semantic router. Retrieval selects dialogue examples that fit the current conversational context and supports routing along a deterministic pathway. The framework therefore connects a structured representation of dialogue progression with the examples supplied to the language model, making conversational context part of both routing and response preparation.

The authors emphasize three benefits: a human-readable routing structure, context-sensitive retrieval, and compatibility with existing language models through a plug-and-play design. Extensive benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness. These findings suggest that explicit conversational structure can help guide model responses in settings with established procedures. The stated evidence supports its usefulness as a conversational framework without establishing an unconditional guarantee that every generated response will comply with every guideline.
summary.tldr: DFA-RAG combines a dialogue-derived automaton with contextual example retrieval to guide language models along interpretable conversational pathways.

title: DFA-RAG: Conversational Semantic Router for Large Language Model with Definite Finite Automaton

abstract: Predicting the mean-field Hamiltonian matrix in density functional theory is a fundamental formulation to leverage machine learning for solving molecular science problems. Yet, its applicability is limited by insufficient labeled data for training. In this work, we highlight that Hamiltonian prediction possesses a self-consistency principle, based on which we propose self-consistency training, an exact training method that does not require labeled data. It distinguishes the task from predicting other molecular properties by the following benefits: (1) it enables the model to be trained on a large amount of unlabeled data, hence addresses the data scarcity challenge and enhances generalization; (2) it is more efficient than running DFT to generate labels for supervised training, since it amortizes DFT calculation over a set of queries. We empirically demonstrate the better generalization in data-scarce and out-of-distribution scenarios, and the better efficiency over DFT labeling. These benefits push forward the applicability of Hamiltonian prediction to an ever-larger scale.

paragraphs: Predicting the mean-field Hamiltonian matrix is one way to use machine learning for molecular problems within density functional theory. A major obstacle is obtaining enough labeled training examples. This paper identifies a self-consistency principle in Hamiltonian prediction and uses it to train models without requiring labeled data.

The proposed self-consistency training is described as an exact training method. Its significance is that the task’s own consistency requirement can supply a training basis, allowing the model to use large amounts of unlabeled data. It also changes how computational effort is spent: instead of running DFT to generate a separate collection of supervised labels, the method amortizes DFT calculation across a set of queries.

Experiments show improved generalization when labeled data are scarce and when evaluation data differ from the training distribution. They also show greater efficiency than generating labels through DFT. Together, these findings support self-consistency as both a source of training information and a way to spread computation across predictions. The resulting benefit is broader applicability of Hamiltonian prediction at larger scales.
summary.tldr: Self-consistency training learns DFT Hamiltonian predictions without labels, improving reported generalization and efficiency relative to DFT label generation.

title: Self-Consistency Training for Density-Functional-Theory Hamiltonian Prediction

abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) have garnered much attention for their ability to elucidate the prediction process through a human-understandable concept layer. However, most previous studies focused on cases where the data, including concepts, are clean. In many scenarios, we always need to remove/insert some training data or new concepts from trained CBMs due to different reasons, such as privacy concerns, data mislabelling, spurious concepts, and concept annotation errors. Thus, the challenge of deriving efficient editable CBMs without retraining from scratch persists, particularly in large-scale applications. To address these challenges, we propose Editable Concept Bottleneck Models (ECBMs). Specifically, ECBMs support three different levels of data removal: concept-label-level, concept-level, and data-level. ECBMs enjoy mathematically rigorous closed-form approximations derived from influence functions that obviate the need for re-training. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our ECBMs, affirming their adaptability within the realm of CBMs.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models explain predictions through an intermediate layer of human-understandable concepts. That layer is useful only if its training information remains appropriate. Privacy requests, mislabeled examples, misleading concepts, and annotation errors can all create reasons to change a trained model. Rebuilding it from scratch becomes costly, particularly at large scale.

Editable Concept Bottleneck Models address this maintenance problem by supporting removal at three levels: individual concept labels, entire concepts, and training data. The method uses influence functions to derive mathematically grounded, closed-form approximations for the required updates. These approximations make editing possible without carrying out a new full training run.

Experiments report that the edits are both effective and efficient. The contribution extends the usefulness of a concept-based prediction system beyond its initial training, allowing corrections at different levels of its information structure. The updates are explicitly approximations, so the theoretical claim concerns the derived editing method rather than exact equivalence to retraining. The reported findings support adaptable concept models whose training information can be revised after deployment.
summary.tldr: Editable Concept Bottleneck Models use influence-function approximations to remove labels, concepts, or training data without retraining from scratch.

title: Editable Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Hypotheses are central to information acquisition, decision-making, and discovery. However, many real-world hypotheses are abstract, high-level statements that are difficult to validate directly. This challenge is further intensified by the rise of hypothesis generation from Large Language Models (LLMs), which are prone to hallucination and produce hypotheses in volumes that make manual validation impractical. Here we propose POPPER, an agentic framework for rigorous automated validation of free-form hypotheses. Guided by Karl Popper’s principle of falsification, POPPER validates a hypothesis using LLM agents that design and execute falsification experiments targeting its measurable implications. A novel sequential testing framework ensures strict Type-I error control while actively gathering evidence from diverse observations, whether drawn from existing data or newly conducted procedures. We demonstrate POPPER on six domains including biology, economics, and sociology. POPPER delivers robust error control, high power, and scalability. Furthermore, compared to human scientists, POPPER achieved comparable performance in validating complex biological hypotheses while reducing time by 10 folds, providing a scalable, rigorous solution for hypothesis validation. POPPER is freely available at https://github.com/snap-stanford/POPPER.

However, many real-world hypotheses are abstract, high-level statements that are difficult to validate directly. This challenge is further intensified by the rise of hypothesis generation from Large Language Models (LLMs), which are prone to hallucination and produce hypotheses in volumes that make manual validation impractical. Here we propose POPPER, an agentic framework for rigorous automated validation of free-form hypotheses. Guided by Karl Popper’s principle of falsification, POPPER validates a hypothesis using LLM agents that design and execute falsification experiments targeting its measurable implications. A novel sequential testing framework ensures strict Type-I error control while actively gathering evidence from diverse observations, whether drawn from existing data or newly conducted procedures. paragraphs: POPPER addresses a bottleneck in automated discovery: producing a plausible hypothesis is easier than checking whether evidence supports it. Broad statements can be difficult to test directly, and language models can generate more hypotheses than people can realistically examine. The framework turns these statements into measurable implications that agents can investigate.

Its guiding strategy is falsification. Language model agents design and execute experiments aimed at challenging a hypothesis, drawing on existing observations or newly conducted procedures. A sequential testing framework governs how evidence accumulates across these investigations while controlling Type-I errors. This statistical component matters because the system actively gathers evidence over multiple steps, rather than making a single assessment from a fixed observation.

The authors demonstrate POPPER across six domains, including biology, economics, and sociology, reporting robust error control, high power, and scalability. In their comparison involving complex biological hypotheses, it performed comparably to human scientists while taking roughly one-tenth the time. These findings support automated testing as a practical complement to automated hypothesis generation.
summary.tldr: POPPER uses language model agents and sequential statistical testing to investigate hypotheses through attempted falsification.

title: Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications

abstract: Continual Federated Learning (CFL) allows distributed devices to collaboratively learn novel concepts from continuously shifting training data while avoiding knowledge forgetting of previously seen tasks. To tackle this challenge, most current CFL approaches rely on extensive rehearsal of previous data. Despite effectiveness, rehearsal comes at a cost to memory, and it may also violate data privacy. Considering these, we seek to apply regularization techniques to CFL by considering their cost-efficient properties that do not require sample caching or rehearsal. Specifically, we first apply traditional regularization techniques to CFL and observe that existing regularization techniques, especially synaptic intelligence, can achieve promising results under homogeneous data distribution but fail when the data is heterogeneous. Based on this observation, we propose a simple yet effective regularization algorithm for CFL named FedSSI, which tailors the synaptic intelligence for the CFL with heterogeneous data settings. FedSSI can not only reduce computational overhead without rehearsal but also address the data heterogeneity issue. Extensive experiments show that FedSSI achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Continual federated learning lets distributed devices learn new concepts together as their training data changes. The challenge is to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks while adapting. Many methods revisit stored examples from previous tasks, but this rehearsal consumes memory and may create privacy concerns. The paper investigates regularization as a way to preserve knowledge without caching or replaying samples.

The authors first test existing regularization techniques in the federated setting. They find that these approaches, particularly synaptic intelligence, can work well when devices have similar data distributions but fail when those distributions differ. FedSSI adapts synaptic intelligence specifically for this heterogeneous setting, making differences between devices central to the design of its regularization algorithm.

Extensive experiments report better performance than leading existing methods. The framework also reduces computational overhead without relying on rehearsal. Its contribution is therefore tied to two interacting demands: learning sequentially without forgetting and coordinating learning across devices with different data. The findings show why a regularization approach that works under homogeneous data may need adaptation for continual federated learning.
summary.tldr: FedSSI adapts synaptic intelligence to reduce forgetting across heterogeneous federated devices without storing or replaying past samples.

title: FedSSI: Rehearsal-Free Continual Federated Learning with Synergistic Synaptic Intelligence

abstract: A common belief in the representational comparison literature is that if two representations can be functionally aligned, they must capture similar information. In this paper we focus on model stitching and show that models can be functionally aligned, but represent very different information. Firstly, we show that discriminative models with very different biases can be stitched together. We then show that models trained to solve entirely different tasks on different data modalities, and even clustered random noise, can be successfully stitched into MNIST or ImageNet-trained models. We end with a discussion of the wider impact of our results on the community’s current beliefs. Overall, our paper draws attention to the need to correctly interpret the results of such functional similarity measures and highlights the need for approaches that capture informational similarity.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes compare neural representations by testing whether they can be functionally aligned through model stitching. A common interpretation is that a successful connection indicates that the representations contain similar information. This paper challenges that inference by showing that functional compatibility can occur even when the underlying representations capture very different information.

The authors first demonstrate successful stitching between discriminative models with substantially different biases. They then extend the investigation to representations from models trained on entirely different tasks and data modalities. Even clustered random noise can be stitched into models trained on MNIST or ImageNet, making the gap between functional alignment and informational similarity especially clear.

These examples matter for interpreting what a successful stitching experiment establishes. The result shows that the ability to make representations work together does not, by itself, demonstrate shared informational content. The authors therefore call for greater care with functional similarity measures and for comparison methods that directly capture informational similarity. Their contribution concerns the conclusions researchers can draw from these experiments.
summary.tldr: Successful model stitching can connect representations with very different information, so functional alignment alone does not establish informational similarity.

title: Functional Alignment Can Mislead: Examining Model Stitching

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) excels in multimodal tasks such as image-text retrieval and zero-shot classification but struggles with fine-grained understanding due to its focus on coarse-grained short captions. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained CLIP (FG-CLIP), which enhances fine-grained understanding through three key innovations. First, we leverage large multimodal models to generate 1.6 billion long caption-image pairs for capturing global-level semantic details. Second, a high-quality dataset is constructed with 12 million images and 40 million region-specific bounding boxes aligned with detailed captions to ensure precise, context-rich representations. Third, 10 million hard fine-grained negative samples are incorporated to improve the model’s ability to distinguish subtle semantic differences. We construct a comprehensive dataset, termed FineHARD, by integrating high-quality region-specific annotations with challenging fine-grained negative samples. Corresponding training methods are meticulously designed for these data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FG-CLIP outperforms the original CLIP and other state-of-the-art methods across various downstream tasks, including fine-grained understanding, open-vocabulary object detection, image-text retrieval, and general multimodal benchmarks. These results highlight FG-CLIP’s effectiveness in capturing fine-grained image details and improving overall model performance. The data, code, and models are available at https://github.com/360CVGroup/FG-CLIP.

paragraphs: FG-CLIP targets a weakness of image-text models trained mainly with short captions: they can recognize broad correspondences while missing finer visual and semantic details. The paper improves training supervision at several levels so that the model learns both richer descriptions of whole images and more precise connections between text and individual image regions.

The approach uses large multimodal models to generate 1.6 billion image pairs with long captions. It also constructs a dataset of 12 million images containing 40 million bounding boxes paired with detailed regional descriptions. Another 10 million difficult negative examples teach distinctions between subtly different meanings. FineHARD brings together the region annotations and challenging negatives, with training methods designed for these data.

Experiments report improvements over the original CLIP and other state-of-the-art methods across fine-grained understanding, open-vocabulary detection, retrieval, and broader multimodal benchmarks. The findings indicate that more detailed supervision can improve sensitivity to small distinctions while also benefiting the wider set of evaluated image-text tasks.
summary.tldr: FG-CLIP improves image-text understanding through detailed captions, region-level supervision, and difficult examples that teach subtle semantic distinctions.

title: FG-CLIP: Fine-Grained Visual and Textual Alignment

abstract: RWKV is a modern RNN architecture with comparable performance to Transformer, but still faces challenges when deployed to resource-constrained devices. Post Training Quantization (PTQ), which is a an essential technique to reduce model size and inference latency, has been widely used in Transformer models. However, it suffers significant degradation of performance when applied to RWKV. This paper investigates and identifies two key constraints inherent in the properties of RWKV: (1) Non-linear operators hinder the parameter-fusion of both smooth- and rotation-based quantization, introducing extra computation overhead. (2) The larger amount of uniformly distributed weights poses challenges for cluster-based quantization, leading to reduced accuracy. To this end, we propose RWKVQuant, a PTQ framework tailored for RWKV models, consisting of two novel techniques: (1) a coarse-to-fine proxy capable of adaptively selecting different quantization approaches by assessing the uniformity and identifying outliers in the weights, and (2) a codebook optimization algorithm that enhances the performance of cluster-based quantization methods for element-wise multiplication in RWKV. Experiments show that RWKVQuant can quantize RWKV-6-14B into about 3-bit with less than 1% accuracy loss and 2.14$\times$ speed up.

paragraphs: RWKV offers a recurrent architecture with performance comparable to Transformers, but deploying it on constrained devices remains challenging. The paper finds that post-training quantization methods used for Transformers can substantially degrade RWKV performance. It identifies architectural and weight-distribution properties that make a direct transfer of these methods problematic.

Nonlinear operators prevent parameter fusion in smooth- and rotation-based quantization, adding computational overhead. Meanwhile, the larger quantity of uniformly distributed weights makes cluster-based quantization less accurate. RWKVQuant addresses these issues with a coarse-to-fine proxy that assesses weight uniformity and outliers to choose quantization approaches adaptively, together with a codebook optimization algorithm tailored to element-wise multiplication in RWKV.

The reported experiments quantize RWKV-6-14B to about three bits with less than 1% accuracy loss and a 2.14-fold speedup. This result supports adapting the compression method to the architecture and its weight properties. The contribution is a hybrid quantization framework designed around the specific obstacles that the authors identify in RWKV.
summary.tldr: RWKVQuant tailors hybrid quantization to RWKV, achieving about three-bit compression of RWKV-6-14B with under 1% accuracy loss.

title: RWKVQuant: Quantizing the RWKV Family with Proxy Guided Hybrid of Scalar and Vector Quantization

abstract: Detecting AI-generated images (AIGIs), such as natural images or face images, has become increasingly important yet challenging. In this paper, we start from a new perspective to excavate the reason behind the failure generalization in AIGI detection, named the asymmetry phenomenon, where a naively trained detector tends to favor overfitting to the limited and monotonous fake patterns, causing the feature space to become highly constrained and low-ranked, which is proved seriously limiting the expressivity and generalization. One potential remedy is incorporating the pre-trained knowledge within the vision foundation models (higher-ranked) to expand the feature space, alleviating the model’s overfitting to fake. To this end, we employ Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to decompose the original feature space into two orthogonal subspaces. By freezing the principal components and adapting only the remained components, we preserve the pre-trained knowledge while learning fake patterns. Compared to existing full-parameters and LoRA-based tuning methods, we explicitly ensure orthogonality, enabling the higher rank of the whole feature space, effectively minimizing overfitting and enhancing generalization. We finally identify a crucial insight: our method implicitly learns a vital prior that fakes are actually derived from the real, indicating a hierarchical relationship rather than independence. Modeling this prior, we believe, is essential for achieving superior generalization. Our codes are publicly available at https://github.com/YZY-stack/Effort-AIGI-Detection.

paragraphs: The paper connects poor generalization in AI-generated image detection to an asymmetry in learning. A detector can overfit to a limited set of repetitive fake-image patterns, compressing its feature space into a low-rank representation. The authors argue that this restricted space limits both expressiveness and the ability to generalize.

Their method uses singular value decomposition to split a pretrained vision model's feature space into two orthogonal subspaces. It freezes the principal components and adapts the remaining components to learn fake-image patterns. This preserves pretrained knowledge while explicitly maintaining separation between the preserved and adapted parts, supporting a higher-rank overall feature space.

The authors report that this construction reduces overfitting and improves generalization relative to full-parameter and LoRA-based tuning. They also interpret the method as implicitly learning a hierarchical relationship in which fake images derive from real ones. The abstract presents modeling that relationship as an important belief about better generalization, rather than establishing it as a universally necessary condition.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal feature subspaces preserve pretrained visual knowledge while learning fake-image patterns, improving detector generalization.

title: Orthogonal Subspace Decomposition for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: The AI research community plays a vital role in shaping the scientific, engineering, and societal goals of AI research. In this position paper, we argue that focusing on the highly contested topic of 'artificial general intelligence' ('AGI') undermines our ability to choose effective goals. We identify six key traps---obstacles to productive goal setting---that are aggravated by AGI discourse: Illusion of Consensus, Supercharging Bad Science, Presuming Value-Neutrality, Goal Lottery, Generality Debt, and Normalized Exclusion. To avoid these traps, we argue that the AI research community needs to (1) prioritize specificity in scientific, engineering, and societal goals, (2) center pluralism about multiple worthwhile approaches to multiple valuable goals, and (3) foster innovation through greater inclusion of disciplines and communities. Therefore, the AI research community needs to stop treating ``AGI'' as the north-star goal of AI research.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that organizing AI research around artificial general intelligence makes productive goal setting harder. The authors emphasize that the research community helps shape scientific, engineering, and societal priorities. Because AGI is highly contested, they question whether it can provide an effective shared direction for those different kinds of goals.

The paper identifies six traps aggravated by AGI discourse: Illusion of Consensus, Supercharging Bad Science, Presuming Value-Neutrality, Goal Lottery, Generality Debt, and Normalized Exclusion. These categories organize the authors' critique of how the overarching goal influences research priorities. Their concern is the quality of goal selection, including whose perspectives enter that process.

They propose three changes: state goals more specifically, recognize multiple worthwhile approaches and valuable outcomes, and include a broader range of disciplines and communities. Together, these recommendations replace reliance on a single contested destination with a more explicit and plural approach to research direction. The paper advances a position on how AI research should choose its goals, rather than reporting a technical route to AGI.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that AI research should prioritize specific, plural, inclusive goals instead of treating contested AGI ambitions as its guiding objective.

title: Position: Stop treating ‘AGI’ as the north-star goal of AI research

abstract: The infringement risks of LLMs have raised significant copyright concerns across different stages of the model lifecycle. While current methods often address these issues separately, this position paper argues that the LLM copyright challenges are inherently connected, and independent optimization of these solutions leads to theoretical bottlenecks. Building on this insight, we further argue that managing LLM copyright risks requires a systemic approach rather than fragmented solutions. In this paper, we analyze the limitations of existing methods in detail and introduce an iterative online-offline joint optimization framework to effectively manage complex LLM copyright risks. We demonstrate that this framework offers a scalable and practical solution to mitigate LLM infringement risks, and also outline new research directions that emerge from this perspective.

This position paper argues that those risks are connected, even though existing methods often address them separately. Its central claim is that optimizing individual solutions independently encounters theoretical bottlenecks because the underlying challenges interact.

The authors analyze limitations of current methods and introduce an iterative framework that jointly optimizes online and offline approaches. The key idea is to manage the connected problem through repeated, coordinated optimization. In this framing, the relationship between interventions becomes part of the design problem, alongside the performance of each intervention considered individually.

The paper presents the framework as a scalable, practical way to mitigate infringement risks and identifies research directions opened by this systemic perspective. The stated objective is risk reduction across a complex lifecycle. Its broader significance is that a collection of separately optimized safeguards may leave important dependencies unaddressed, motivating an approach that explicitly considers how the different parts work together.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that connected LLM copyright risks require iterative joint optimization of online and offline approaches.

title: Position: Iterative Online-Offline Joint Optimization is Needed to Manage Complex LLM Copyright Risks

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve strong performance in image generation but incur substantial inference costs. While prior work has reduced this cost via quantization and distillation, semi-structured sparsity—which can nearly halve FLOPs—remains underexplored. A key reason is that most existing approaches focus on weight sparsification, and pruning 50% of the weights can remove critical model capacity and degrade generation quality. Our study, however, shows that DiT activations are intrinsically sparse and significantly more robust to N:M semi-structured sparsification than weights. Motivated by this observation, we advocate a paradigm shift from weight sparsification to activation sparsification. We propose RT-Lynx, which applies N:M sparsification to activations and incorporates error-compensation techniques to mitigate accuracy loss. We further implement highly optimized CUDA kernels tailored to this setting, achieving up to a 1.55$\times$ speedup on average in linear layers. Extensive experiments across multiple diffusion models demonstrate that our method preserves the generation quality of the original models while substantially accelerating inference.

paragraphs: Diffusion Transformers can generate strong images but require expensive inference. Semi-structured sparsity offers a way to reduce arithmetic, yet removing half of a model's weights can damage its capacity and image quality. This paper investigates a different target: the activations produced while the model processes an input.

The authors find that these activations are intrinsically sparse and tolerate N:M semi-structured sparsification substantially better than weights. RT-Lynx applies that sparsification to activations and adds error-compensation techniques to limit the resulting accuracy loss. The key design choice is therefore where sparsity is introduced, guided by the observed difference between activation and weight sensitivity.

The method also includes optimized CUDA kernels so that reduced computation translates into faster execution. The authors report up to a 1.55-fold average speedup in linear layers. Experiments across multiple diffusion models preserve the original models' generation quality while substantially accelerating inference. The numerical speedup specifically describes linear layers, while the broader experimental finding is that activation sparsity can deliver useful acceleration without the reported quality degradation associated with weight pruning.
summary.tldr: RT-Lynx sparsifies diffusion-model activations and uses error compensation and optimized kernels to accelerate inference while preserving reported generation quality.

title: RT-Lynx: Putting GEMM Sparsity in the Right Place for Diffusion Models

abstract: Reward Models (RMs) are crucial for online alignment of language models (LMs) with human preferences. However, RM-based preference-tuning is vulnerable to reward hacking, whereby LM policies learn undesirable behaviors from flawed RMs. By systematically measuring biases in five high-quality RMs, including the state-of-the-art, we find that issues persist despite prior work with respect to length, sycophancy, and overconfidence. We also discover new issues related to bias toward model-specific “styles” and answer-order. We categorize RM failures as tractable or resistant to linear intervention and propose a simple post-hoc intervention to mitigate low-complexity biases that arise from spurious correlations. Our proposed mechanistic reward shaping reduces targeted biases without degrading reward quality and while using minimal labeled data. The method is extensible to new biases, model-internal, and generalizes out-of-distribution.

paragraphs: Reward models guide language-model alignment by scoring responses according to learned human preferences. When those scores contain systematic biases, a language model can learn undesirable behaviors that receive high rewards. This paper examines that problem by systematically measuring biases in five high-quality reward models, including state-of-the-art models.

The study finds persistent preferences related to response length, sycophancy, and overconfidence, despite previous work on these issues. It also identifies biases toward model-specific writing styles and answer order. The authors distinguish failures that can be addressed through linear intervention from those that resist it, making the complexity of a bias relevant to how it can be corrected.

They propose mechanistic reward shaping, a simple post-hoc intervention targeting low-complexity biases arising from spurious correlations. The method acts inside the reward model, uses little labeled data, and reduces the targeted biases without degrading reward quality. It also generalizes out of distribution and can be extended to new biases. The contribution pairs evidence that reward-model biases remain widespread with a targeted method for mitigating a tractable subset.
summary.tldr: The paper documents persistent reward-model biases and introduces a lightweight internal intervention that mitigates targeted low-complexity biases.

title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models

abstract: Multimodal learning aims to integrate multi-sensor data to exploit their complementary information, embracing a more comprehensive real-world perception and understanding. However, heterogeneous discrepancies across modalities consistently trigger imbalanced multimodal optimization, restricting the joint learning performance. Although existing methods mitigate this issue through optimization modulation and conflict alleviation, they still suffer from entangled optimization and uniform learning pace in conventional monolithic frameworks, limiting the effectiveness of multimodal learning. To address this issue, we propose a novel Multimodal Nested Learning Framework (MoNet), which reformulates the monolithic framework into nested sub-processes, decoupling and coordinating multimodal learning. To achieve this, we present a Decoupled Multimodal Stable Memory block (DMSM) as the outermost nested level, which decouples multimodal learning into independent optimization streams for semantic exploitation across modalities. Additionally, we develop an Adaptive Multimodal Coordinated Fusion block (AMCF), which constitutes the inner nested level. It attempts to coordinate multimodal information integration across multi-timescale nested memories, balancing multimodal fusion. Extensive experimental results on eight datasets across three tasks demonstrate the superiority of MoNet. Code is available at https://github.com/Yangl1nFeng/MoNet.

paragraphs: Different sensing modalities provide complementary information, but they do not necessarily learn well under one shared optimization process. The paper identifies entangled updates and a uniform learning pace as obstacles to balanced multimodal learning. MoNet restructures training into nested processes so that learning within modalities and combining them can be handled separately.

At the outer level, a Decoupled Multimodal Stable Memory block creates independent optimization streams for extracting semantic information across modalities. At the inner level, an Adaptive Multimodal Coordinated Fusion block attempts to integrate that information through nested memories operating at multiple timescales. The design pairs separation during learning with coordination during fusion.

Experiments on eight datasets covering three tasks show superior performance for MoNet in the reported comparisons. These findings support changing the organization of multimodal optimization, in addition to adjusting gradients or alleviating conflicts inside a single training process. The architecture’s intended benefit is to let modalities develop useful information through independent streams while still bringing those contributions together in a balanced way.
summary.tldr: MoNet separates modality-specific learning into independent streams and coordinates their fusion through nested memories operating at different timescales.

title: Multimodal Nested Learning for Decoupled and Coordinated Optimization

abstract: While multimodal agents can achieve strong performance through fine-tuning, their ability to generalize remains limited in complex real-world tasks such as mobile navigation, where diverse applications, frequent system changes, and customized workflows are common in practice. We argue that a fundamental bottleneck lies in whether an agent possesses sufficient task-specific procedural knowledge to accomplish a given goal. Such procedural knowledge may be provided by the general capabilities of large language models, or obtained from additional external resources such as web search when necessary. Based on this view, we propose Procedure-Aware Multimodal Agent with Meta Reasoning, a framework that explicitly represents task knowledge as natural-language procedures and trains a procedure-aware grounded agent to condition its actions on this knowledge. By learning to leverage procedural knowledge from different sources, our approach enables robust generalization across tasks, applications, interface versions, and multi-app workflows, achieving substantial improvements on challenging Android benchmarks.

paragraphs: A multimodal agent may perform well after fine-tuning yet struggle with unfamiliar applications, changed interfaces, or workflows spanning several apps. This paper argues that a key bottleneck is whether the agent has enough procedural knowledge: knowledge of the steps needed to accomplish the requested goal.

The proposed Procedure-Aware Multimodal Agent with Meta Reasoning represents that knowledge explicitly as natural-language procedures. A grounded agent is trained to choose actions conditioned on these procedures. Procedural knowledge can come from a language model’s general capabilities or, when necessary, external resources such as web search. The framework therefore gives task instructions an explicit role in connecting knowledge to interface actions.

The authors report substantial improvements on challenging Android benchmarks, with generalization across tasks, applications, interface versions, and multi-app workflows. These findings support training agents to use procedural knowledge from different sources. The practical significance is that adapting behavior can depend on obtaining and applying the relevant procedure, alongside the agent’s learned ability to act.
summary.tldr: The framework improves multimodal agent generalization by conditioning actions on explicit natural-language procedures drawn from internal or external knowledge.

title: Hierarchical Procedural Meta-Reasoning for Generalizable Multimodal Agents

abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) provide a flexible framework for generative models with strong distribution modeling capabilities. Nevertheless, their broader adoption has been limited by the difficulty of stable and efficient training. In this paper, we propose a unified and efficient latent-guided cooperative EBM that leverages informative target latent variables to guide the joint energy in capturing both data distribution and semantic structure, along with a cooperative generator designed for effective MCMC initialization. Our joint space optimization only requires MCMC sampling in the data space, and allows the energy to learn semantic data–latent relationships directly from real data. Experiments show our method improves generation quality and training stability with fewer resources, and performs effectively across multiple downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Energy-based models offer a flexible way to represent data distributions, but training them stably and efficiently remains difficult. This paper develops a cooperative approach that brings together an energy model, informative target latent variables, and a generator. The goal is to learn both the distribution of observations and meaningful relationships between observations and latent representations.

The latent variables guide a joint energy over data and latent information. A cooperating generator supplies effective initial states for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Although optimization involves the joint space, the method requires MCMC sampling only in data space. The energy can therefore learn semantic data–latent relationships directly from real examples.

Experiments show improved generation quality and training stability with fewer resources, alongside effective performance on multiple downstream tasks. These findings support the proposed division of responsibilities: latent guidance helps organize what the energy learns, while the generator helps initialize sampling. The contribution combines those roles into one training framework aimed at making expressive energy-based modeling more practical.
summary.tldr: Latent guidance and a cooperating generator improve energy-based model training while requiring MCMC sampling only in data space.

title: Latent-Guided Cooperative Energy-Based Models

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models achieve remarkable performance by sparsely activating specialized experts, yet their massive parameters in experts pose significant challenges for deployment. While low-rank quantization offers a promising route to compress MoE models, existing methods still incur nonnegligible memory overhead and inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose TileQ, a fine-tuning-free post-training quantization (PTQ) method that employs 2D-tiling structured low-rank quantization to share low-rank factors across both input and output dimensions of MoE experts. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient inference technique for TileQ that fuses multiple low-rank expert computations into a single-pass operation, significantly improving hardware utilization. Experiments show that TileQ cuts down additional memory usage up to 10x and reduces inference latency to 5% while preserving state-of-the-art accuracy.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only selected experts for a given computation, but storing their many expert parameters remains a deployment challenge. Low-rank quantization can compress those parameters, yet the compression machinery itself can add memory overhead and inference latency. TileQ addresses both costs through the way expert computations are represented and executed.

The method applies post-training quantization without fine-tuning. Its two-dimensional tiling structure shares low-rank factors across both the input and output dimensions of MoE experts. An accompanying inference technique fuses multiple low-rank expert computations into a single pass, improving hardware utilization. The representation and execution strategy are designed together so that compression also translates into more efficient computation.

The experiments report reductions of up to tenfold in additional memory usage and inference latency reduced to 5%, while preserving state-of-the-art accuracy. The memory result specifically concerns additional overhead, which is the cost highlighted by the paper. These findings support structured sharing and fused execution as complementary ways to make low-rank quantization more practical for deploying large expert-based models.
summary.tldr: TileQ combines shared low-rank factors and fused expert computation to reduce MoE quantization overhead and latency while preserving state-of-the-art accuracy.

title: TileQ: Efficient Low-Rank Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts with 2D Tiling

abstract: Salient Object Ranking (SOR) aims to study how humans visually explore complex scenes by predicting an ordered sequence of objects that attracts our attention. Existing SOR approaches typically model this ranking deterministically, assuming a single, fixed ranking sequence of attention. However, such deterministic SOR fails to capture the true nature of human attention. We observe that human attention shifts exhibit variability and stochasticity, i.e., the next object of fixation is not a definitive choice but rather a probability distribution. Yet, existing SOR methods and evaluation metrics do not account for this inherent randomness. To address this fundamental problem, we first propose ProbSOR, a novel Probabilistic Salient Object Ranking framework built upon a vision-language model (VLM) backbone. By incorporating Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), ProbSOR explicitly learns the uncertainty of attention shifts. We then propose a new metric tailored for ProbSOR, as existing SOR metrics only support deterministic rankings. We further construct a ProbSOR dataset comprising 15,000 probabilistic SOR samples, to support both model training and evaluation. Extensive experiments show that ProbSOR achieves strong performance in salient object ranking under both our proposed and traditional benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predicting visual attention often means ranking the objects a person will look at in a scene. A single fixed ordering misses the variability in those choices: several objects may plausibly attract the next fixation. This paper reformulates salient object ranking to represent that uncertainty explicitly.

ProbSOR builds on a vision-language model and uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to learn probabilistic attention shifts. The authors also introduce an evaluation metric designed for probabilistic rankings, because existing ranking metrics assume deterministic outputs. A new dataset containing 15,000 probabilistic ranking samples supports both training and evaluation of the proposed task.

Experiments report strong performance under both the new metric and traditional salient-object-ranking benchmarks. This connects the probabilistic formulation to existing evaluation while also providing a way to assess the variability that fixed rankings omit. The contribution spans the model, the measurement method, and the supporting dataset. Together, they make uncertainty in the next attended object part of the prediction target rather than forcing attention into one prescribed sequence.
summary.tldr: ProbSOR predicts uncertain attention shifts between objects and introduces a dataset and metric for evaluating probabilistic visual-attention rankings.

title: Probabilistic Salient Object Ranking

abstract: High-precision robotic manipulation requires fine-grained spatial reasoning that is often difficult to achieve with RGB-only policies due to depth ambiguity and perspective scale issues. Policies that leverage 3D information directly, such as those based on point clouds, offer a stronger geometric prior over purely image-based ones, yet their performance remains highly task-dependent. We hypothesize that this discrepancy may be due to the spectral bias of neural networks towards learning low frequency functions, which especially affects architectures conditioned on slow-moving Cartesian features. We thus propose to map point clouds from Cartesian space into high-dimensional Fourier space, effectively equipping the point cloud encoder with direct access to high-frequency features. We experimentally validate the use of Fourier features on challenging manipulation tasks from the RoboCasa and ManiSkill3 benchmarks and on a real robot setup. Despite their simplicity, we find that Fourier features provide significant benefits across diverse encoder architectures and benchmarks and are robust across hyperparameters. Our results indicate that Fourier features let policies leverage geometric details more effectively than Cartesian features, showing their potential as a general-purpose tool for point cloud-based imitation learning. We provide source code and videos on our project page: https://fourier-il.github.io/fourier-il.
