paragraphs: Precision manipulation requires a robot to respond to fine geometric differences. Point clouds provide direct three-dimensional information, but policies using them still perform unevenly across tasks. The authors hypothesize that part of this variation comes from neural networks’ preference for learning slowly varying functions, which can hinder the use of detailed spatial information.

Their proposed change maps point-cloud coordinates into a high-dimensional Fourier representation before encoding them. This gives the encoder direct access to high-frequency features, rather than requiring it to extract all fine variation from Cartesian coordinates. The intervention targets the representation supplied to an imitation-learning policy and is deliberately simple.

Experiments cover challenging RoboCasa and ManiSkill3 tasks and a real robot setup. Fourier features provide substantial benefits across different encoders and benchmarks, with robustness across hyperparameter choices. The results indicate more effective use of geometric detail and support their potential as a broadly useful tool. The spectral-bias explanation remains the motivating hypothesis, rather than a claim that every task-dependent difference has been explained.
summary.tldr: Fourier representations of point clouds help imitation-learning policies use fine geometric detail across simulated manipulation tasks and a real robot setup.

title: Fourier Features Let Agents Learn High Precision Policies with Imitation Learning

abstract: Multimodal visual object tracking can be divided into to several kinds of tasks (e.g. RGB and RGB+X tracking), based on the input modality. Existing methods often train separate models for each modality or rely on pretrained models to adapt to new modalities, which limits efficiency, scalability, and usability. Thus, we introduce OneTrackerV2, a unified multi-modal tracking framework that enables end-to-end training for any modality. We propose Meta Merger to embed multi-modal information into a unified space, allowing flexible modality fusion and robustness. We further introduce Dual Mixture-of-Experts (DMoE): T-MoE models spatiotemporal relations for tracking, while M-MoE embeds multi-modal knowledge, disentangling cross-modal dependencies and reducing feature conflicts. With a shared architecture, unified parameters, and a single end-to-end training, OneTrackerV2 achieves state-of-the-art performance across five RGB and RGB+X tracking tasks and 12 benchmarks, while maintaining high inference efficiency. Notably, even after model compression, OneTrackerV2 retains strong performance. Moreover, OneTrackerV2 demonstrates remarkable robustness under modality-missing scenarios.

paragraphs: OneTrackerV2 unifies visual object tracking across RGB and multimodal inputs. Existing approaches often require separate models for different modalities or adaptation from pretrained models, increasing the burden of training and deployment. The proposed framework uses shared parameters and a single end-to-end training process to support multiple tracking tasks within one architecture.

A Meta Merger maps multimodal information into a unified space, enabling flexible fusion. The framework then divides expert specialization into two parts. T-MoE models spatial and temporal relationships needed for tracking, while M-MoE represents multimodal knowledge. This separation is designed to disentangle cross-modal dependencies and reduce conflicts among features.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across five RGB and RGB-plus-additional-modality tracking tasks and twelve benchmarks, while maintaining high inference efficiency. Strong performance persists after model compression, and the tracker is robust when modalities are missing. Together, these findings support sharing a tracking architecture across input configurations while retaining specialized processing for motion relationships and modality information.
summary.tldr: OneTrackerV2 combines shared multimodal fusion with separate tracking and modality experts for efficient tracking across input configurations.

title: Unified Multimodal Visual Tracking with Dual Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: We study the population loss landscape of two-layer ReLU networks of the form $\sum_{k=1}^K \mathrm{ReLU}(w_k^\top x)$ in a realisable teacher–student setting with Gaussian covariates. We show that local minima admit an exact low-dimensional representation in terms of summary statistics, yielding a sharp and interpretable characterisation of the landscape. We further establish a direct link with one-pass SGD: local minima correspond to attractive fixed points of the dynamics in summary statistics space. This perspective reveals a hierarchical organisation of minima into discrete families and shows how overparameterisation changes their stability and reachability under gradient-based dynamics. In this overparameterised regime, global minima become increasingly accessible, attracting the dynamics and reducing convergence to spurious solutions. Overall, our results reveal intrinsic limitations of common simplifying assumptions, which may miss essential features of the loss landscape even in minimal neural network models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how local minima are organized in the population loss of two-layer ReLU networks. Its setting is specific: Gaussian inputs and a realizable teacher–student problem, where the student’s model class can represent the teacher. Within that setting, the authors seek an exact account of the landscape rather than a broad qualitative picture.

They show that local minima can be represented using low-dimensional summary statistics. They also connect those minima to attractive fixed points of one-pass stochastic gradient descent expressed in the same summary-statistic space. This makes the landscape and the learning dynamics part of one description: the minima correspond to states toward which the dynamics are attracted.

The analysis reveals discrete families of minima arranged hierarchically. Overparameterization changes their stability and reachability, making global minima increasingly accessible and reducing convergence to spurious solutions in the studied regime. The authors also show that common simplifying assumptions can miss essential landscape features, even in these minimal neural network models.
summary.tldr: An exact summary-statistic description links local minima to SGD dynamics in Gaussian teacher–student ReLU networks and explains effects of overparameterization.

title: Sharp description of local minima in the loss landscape of high-dimensional two-layer ReLU neural networks

abstract: Autoregressive video world models predict future visual observations conditioned on actions. While effective over short horizons, these models often struggle with long-horizon generation, as small prediction errors accumulate over time. Prior methods alleviate this by introducing pre-trained teacher models and sequence-level distribution matching, which incur additional computational cost and fail to prevent error propagation beyond the training horizon. In this work, we propose LIVE, a Long-horizon Interactive Video world modEl that enforces bounded error accumulation via a novel cycle-consistency objective, thereby eliminating the need for teacher-based distillation. Specifically, LIVE first performs a forward rollout from ground-truth frames and then applies a reverse generation process to reconstruct the initial state. The diffusion loss is subsequently computed on the reconstructed terminal state, providing an explicit constraint on long-horizon error propagation. Moreover, we provide a unified view that encompasses different approaches and introduce progressive training curriculum to stabilize training. Experiments demonstrate that LIVE achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon benchmarks, generating stable, high-quality videos far beyond training rollout lengths.

paragraphs: Action-conditioned video world models predict future visual observations one step after another. Over long sequences, small errors can accumulate because later predictions depend on earlier generated frames. Existing approaches use pretrained teachers and sequence-level matching to reduce this drift, but add computation and can still suffer error propagation beyond the training horizon.

LIVE introduces a cycle-consistency objective to constrain that accumulation without teacher-based distillation. Starting from ground-truth frames, it generates a forward rollout and then reverses the generation process to reconstruct the initial state. A diffusion loss is applied at the end of this reconstruction cycle. The return path makes the training objective explicitly sensitive to whether extended generation preserves information about where it began.

The paper also presents a unified view of different approaches and a progressive training curriculum for stability. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon benchmarks, with stable, high-quality videos extending well beyond the rollout lengths used in training. These results support cycle consistency as a way to improve extended interactive generation.
summary.tldr: LIVE uses forward-and-reverse video generation to constrain accumulated error and produce stable sequences beyond its training rollout lengths.

title: LIVE: Long-horizon Interactive Video World Modeling

abstract: Advancing complex reasoning in large language models relies on high-quality, verifiable datasets, yet human annotation remains cost-prohibitive and difficult to scale. Current synthesis paradigms often face a recurring trade-off: maintaining structural validity typically restricts problem complexity, while relaxing constraints to increase difficulty frequently leads to inconsistent or unsolvable instances. To address this, we propose Agentic Proposing, a framework that models problem synthesis as a goal-driven sequential decision process where a specialized agent dynamically selects and composes modular reasoning skills. Through an iterative workflow of internal reflection and tool-use, we develop the Agentic-Proposer-4B using Multi-Granularity Policy Optimization (MGPO) to generate high-precision, verifiable training trajectories across mathematics, coding, and science. Empirical results demonstrate that downstream solvers trained on agent-synthesized data significantly outperform leading baselines and exhibit robust cross-domain generalization. Notably, a 30B solver trained on only 11,000 synthesized trajectories achieves a state-of-the-art 91.6% accuracy on AIME25, rivaling frontier-scale proprietary models such as GPT-5 and proving that a small volume of high-quality synthetic signals can effectively substitute for massive human-curated datasets.

paragraphs: Generating useful reasoning problems involves balancing difficulty with correctness. Strong constraints can keep problems valid but restrict their complexity; loosening those constraints can produce inconsistent or unsolvable examples. Agentic Proposing addresses this tension by treating problem creation as a sequence of purposeful decisions made by a specialized agent.

The agent selects and combines modular reasoning skills, revises its work through internal reflection, and uses tools during generation. The authors train Agentic-Proposer-4B with Multi-Granularity Policy Optimization to produce verifiable training trajectories in mathematics, coding, and science. The approach makes synthesis an iterative construction process rather than a single attempt to write a difficult question and solution.

Downstream solvers trained on the generated data outperform the reported leading baselines and generalize across domains. A 30B solver trained on 11,000 synthesized trajectories reaches 91.6% accuracy on AIME25, a result the authors describe as state of the art and competitive with frontier proprietary models. This provides evidence that carefully constructed synthetic reasoning data can deliver substantial training value from a relatively small collection.
summary.tldr: A specialized agent composes reasoning skills into verifiable synthetic training data that substantially improves downstream reasoning models.

title: Agentic Proposing: Enhancing Large language Model Reasoning via Compositional Skill Synthesis

abstract: We investigate unpaired image inverse problems, a challenging setting where only independent, non-paired sets of noisy measurements and clean target signals are available for training. We propose a novel inverse problem solver based on Unbalanced Optimal Transport, called Unbalanced Optimal Transport Map for Inverse Problems (UOTIP). Our method formulates the reconstruction task—predicting clean target signals from noisy measurements—as learning a UOT Map from noisy measurement distribution to clean signal distribution by incorporating a likelihood-based cost function. By relaxing the exact marginal constraint, the UOT framework provides key advantages to our model: robustness to multi-level observation noise, adaptability to class imbalance between noisy and clean datasets, and generalizability to diverse noise-type scenarios. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that incorporating a quadratic cost term ensures the existence and uniqueness of the transport map by satisfying the twist condition, even for ill-posed inverse problems. Our experiments demonstrate that UOTIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on unpaired image inverse problem benchmarks, across linear and nonlinear inverse problems.
originalAbstract: We investigate unpaired image inverse problems, a challenging setting where only independent, non-paired sets of noisy measurements and clean target signals are available for training. We propose a novel inverse problem solver based on Unbalanced Optimal Transport, called Unbalanced Optimal Transport Map for Inverse Problems (UOTIP). Our method formulates the reconstruction task—predicting clean target signals from noisy measurements—as learning a UOT Map from noisy measurement distribution to clean signal distribution by incorporating a likelihood-based cost function. By relaxing the exact marginal constraint, the UOT framework provides key advantages to our model: robustness to multi-level observation noise, adaptability to class imbalance between noisy and clean datasets, and generalizability to diverse noise-type scenarios. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that incorporating a quadratic cost term ensures the existence and uniqueness of the transport map by satisfying the twist condition, even for ill-posed inverse problems. Our experiments demonstrate that UOTIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on unpaired image inverse problem benchmarks, across linear and nonlinear inverse problems.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction is especially challenging when training data contains separate collections of noisy measurements and clean images, with no matching pairs. UOTIP learns to map between those two distributions using unbalanced optimal transport. A likelihood-based cost connects the mapping to the measurement process, making reconstruction part of the distribution-matching formulation.

The unbalanced formulation relaxes the requirement to match the distributions’ marginals exactly. The authors identify this flexibility as providing robustness to multiple observation-noise levels, adaptation to different class proportions in the noisy and clean datasets, and generalization across noise types. These properties address mismatches that can occur when the two training collections are independently assembled.

The paper also proves that adding a quadratic cost term satisfies a twist condition that ensures existence and uniqueness of the transport map, even for ill-posed inverse problems. This guarantee concerns the learned transport formulation. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on unpaired image inverse-problem benchmarks covering both linear and nonlinear problems, supporting the approach across different measurement relationships.
summary.tldr: UOTIP uses unbalanced optimal transport to learn image reconstruction from unpaired noisy and clean datasets while accommodating distribution mismatches.

title: UOTIP: Unbalanced Optimal Transport Map for Unpaired Inverse Problems

abstract: Understanding how educational social dynamics evolve is critical for informing effective educational policies and counterfactual interventions. However, traditional methods face a fundamental dilemma: observational studies often lack causal power, while controlled experiments are frequently constrained by ethical concerns. Although LLM-based multi-agent simulations offer a scalable in silico alternative, existing approaches remain limited by weak psychological grounding and insufficient measurement of latent psychological states. To address this, we introduce EduMirror, a multi-agent simulator for the scientific study of educational social dynamics. We provide configurable education-oriented agent forms, including value-driven agents grounded in psychological needs and social value orientation, together with a dual-track measurement protocol for quantifying observable behaviors and latent psychological states. We validate the realism and usability of EduMirror through case studies on school bullying and group cooperation, as well as broader evaluations across diverse educational scenarios. The results show that EduMirror generates educational social dynamics that are realistic, theory-consistent, and measurable by empirical criteria. These properties enable structured in silico educational research, providing a computational tool for hypothesis testing and counterfactual intervention analysis in educational science. Project page: https://edumirror.net.

These properties enable structured in silico educational research, providing a computational tool for hypothesis testing and counterfactual intervention analysis in educational science. Project page: https://edumirror.net.

paragraphs: Studying educational social behavior is difficult when observational evidence has limited causal power and controlled experiments face ethical constraints. EduMirror offers a computational setting for exploring these dynamics with language-model agents. It addresses two weaknesses identified in existing simulators: limited grounding in psychology and inadequate measurement of internal psychological states.

The system provides configurable agents designed for educational scenarios, including agents whose behavior is grounded in psychological needs and social value orientation. Its measurement protocol follows two tracks, recording observable behavior and quantifying latent psychological states. This makes the simulator’s account of interaction broader than a record of outward actions alone.

The authors evaluate EduMirror through school-bullying and group-cooperation case studies, alongside a broader set of educational scenarios. They report dynamics that are realistic, consistent with relevant theory, and measurable using empirical criteria. These findings support its use as a structured computational tool for testing hypotheses and analyzing counterfactual interventions. The stated contribution is an inspectable simulation environment for educational research, with agent design and measurement developed together.
summary.tldr: EduMirror combines psychologically grounded agents with behavioral and psychological measurements to simulate educational social dynamics.

title: EduMirror: Modeling Educational Social Dynamics with Value-driven Multi-agent Simulation

abstract: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) connects visual perception with structured reasoning, but is limited by scarce annotations and the long-tailed distribution of relational predicates. Training-free methods based on vision-language models (VLMs) reduce supervision requirements, yet often rely on flat graph structures and produce hallucinated relations. We present HSGG, a training-free framework for open-world Hierarchical Scene Graph Generation, whose inference proceeds in two steps. First, bidirectional hierarchical entity perception combines top-down object expansion with bottom-up attribute reasoning to construct multi-level scene hierarchies capturing part–whole semantics. Second, geometry-guided relation reasoning infers valid relations from these structured entities: geometry-aware relation filtering first prunes spatially implausible object pairs using 2D proximity, depth cues, and object scale, and geometry-grounded contrastive relation decoding then suppresses hallucinated predicates by contrasting predictions from a visually grounded expert against a hallucination-prone geometric prior, ensuring relations are both geometrically consistent and semantically coherent. Experiments show that HSGG generalizes effectively to unseen objects and predicates without training, substantially reduces relational hallucinations, and consistently improves downstream reasoning performance.

HSGG addresses both problems through a hierarchy of entities followed by geometry-guided relation inference.

The first stage combines top-down expansion of objects with bottom-up reasoning about attributes to build multiple levels of scene structure. The second stage filters out spatially implausible object pairs using image-plane proximity, depth information, and object scale. It then contrasts predictions from a visually grounded expert with a hallucination-prone geometric prior to suppress unsupported relation labels.

Experiments show generalization to previously unseen objects and predicates without training, substantial reductions in relational hallucinations, and consistent improvements in downstream reasoning. The approach matters because it uses hierarchy to organize what is present and geometry to constrain what relationships are plausible. Together, these components improve the structured information available to later reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: HSGG builds hierarchical scene graphs without training and uses geometric constraints to reduce hallucinated relationships.

title: HSGG: Training-Free Hierarchical Scene Graph Generation with Geometry-Guided Relation Reasoning

abstract: Diffusion models have transformed image synthesis by establishing unprecedented quality and creativity benchmarks. Nevertheless, their large-scale deployment faces challenges due to computationally intensive iterative denoising processes. Although post-training quantization (PTQ) provides an effective pathway for accelerating sampling, the iterative nature of diffusion models causes stepwise quantization errors to accumulate progressively during generation, inevitably compromising output fidelity. To address this challenge, we develop a theoretical framework that mathematically formulates error propagation in Diffusion Models (DMs), deriving per-step quantization error propagation equations and establishing the first closed-form solution for cumulative error. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a timestep-aware cumulative error compensation scheme. Extensive experiments on multiple image datasets demonstrate that our compensation strategy effectively mitigates error propagation, significantly enhancing existing PTQ methods. Specifically, it achieves a 1.2 PSNR improvement over SVDQuant on SDXL W4A4, while incurring only an additional $<$ 0.5% time overhead.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization can accelerate diffusion image generation by reducing numerical precision. However, diffusion models repeatedly denoise an evolving image, so quantization errors introduced at one step can carry into later steps and accumulate. The paper studies this propagation directly to understand how small numerical errors affect the final generated output.

The authors develop a theoretical framework with equations describing error propagation at each denoising step. They also derive a closed-form expression for cumulative error, which they describe as the first such solution. Building on this analysis, they propose compensation that depends on the timestep, addressing accumulated error according to its place in the generation process.

Experiments across multiple image datasets show that the compensation improves existing post-training quantization methods by mitigating error propagation. In the reported SDXL W4A4 setting, it improves PSNR by 1.2 over SVDQuant while adding less than 0.5% time overhead. This result connects the theoretical account to a practical correction: improved fidelity in the tested setting with a very small additional time cost.
summary.tldr: The paper models accumulated quantization error in diffusion generation and uses timestep-aware compensation to improve fidelity with minimal overhead.

title: Error Propagation Mechanisms and Compensation Strategies for Quantized Diffusion Models

abstract: Learning unified road representations across diverse cities is a pivotal challenge in urban computing. However, existing approaches predominantly focus on single-city modeling, failing to handle the distribution shifts caused by heterogeneous urban layouts. We identify spectral misalignment, manifested as the significant divergence of spectral distributions across different cities, as the primary barrier preventing standard Graph Neural Networks from capturing universal patterns. To bridge this gap, we propose CoSpec, a framework that disentangles road networks into shareable low-frequency commonalities and city-specific high-frequency specificities. CoSpec employs a hierarchical dual-path architecture where the low-frequency path aligns global functional semantics via adaptive prototypes, while the high-frequency path modulates local geometric residuals to fit specific urban textures. Theoretical analysis shows CoSpec bounds the Wasserstein distance between city distributions, and extensive experiments demonstrate its superior generalization over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Road networks differ across cities, making it difficult to learn representations that transfer between urban layouts. The authors identify spectral misalignment—divergence in the networks’ spectral distributions—as the main barrier to standard graph neural networks capturing universal patterns. CoSpec addresses this mismatch while retaining information specific to each city.

The framework separates road representations into shareable low-frequency structure and city-specific high-frequency structure. Its hierarchical architecture has two paths. The low-frequency path uses adaptive prototypes to align global functional meaning across cities. The high-frequency path adjusts local geometric residuals to accommodate the particular texture of each urban network.

Theoretical analysis shows that CoSpec bounds the Wasserstein distance between city distributions, providing a formal connection to cross-city distribution alignment. Experiments report better generalization than the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The approach matters because transfer requires both a basis for sharing and a way to preserve local variation. CoSpec makes that distinction explicit in its spectral decomposition and gives the two kinds of information separate processing paths.
summary.tldr: CoSpec improves cross-city road representations by aligning shared spectral structure while preserving city-specific geometric detail.

title: Seeking Commonality, Preserving Specificity: A Spectral-Aware Hierarchical Framework for Cross-City Road Representation Learning

abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) integrate unimodal encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute complex multimodal tasks. Despite progress in the field, understanding the internal representations of these models through interpretable logic remains an open problem. To address this, we present a framework utilizing a Human-Inspired (Neuro-fuzzy) approach for learning token representations. In this method, we leverage fuzzy rules to compute activation firing strengths, which are subsequently defuzzified to extract distinct concepts. This mechanism allows for the interpretation of learned representations directly through explicit logic. Consequently, we derive "multimodal concepts" that are both semantically coherent and interpretable. We validate our approach through rigorous qualitative and quantitative experiments, demonstrating the utility of these concepts in interpreting test samples. Additionally, we evaluate the disentanglement of the learned concepts and the efficacy of their grounding in both visual and textual domains.

paragraphs: Large multimodal models combine encoders for individual modalities with language models, but understanding their internal representations through explicit logic remains difficult. This paper proposes learning token representations through a neuro-fuzzy framework so that the resulting concepts can be interpreted in terms of rules, rather than only inspected as hidden numerical features.

The method uses fuzzy rules to calculate activation firing strengths, expressing the degree to which rules activate. A defuzzification step then extracts distinct concepts from those activations. This process connects learned representations to explicit logic and produces multimodal concepts that the authors describe as semantically coherent and interpretable.

The evaluation also examines disentanglement, or how separately the concepts represent different factors, and their grounding in both visual and textual information. These checks address whether the extracted concepts provide meaningful handles on multimodal representations across the two domains. The contribution is a representation-learning mechanism that incorporates interpretable rules into concept formation.
summary.tldr: A neuro-fuzzy framework turns rule activations into interpretable multimodal concepts and evaluates their usefulness, disentanglement, and visual-textual grounding.

title: Neuro-Fuzzy Concept Learning for Interpretable Large Multimodal Models

abstract: Learning-based methods for sampling from the Gibbs distribution in finite-dimensional spaces have progressed quickly, yet theory and algorithmic design for infinite-dimensional function spaces remain limited. This gap persists despite their strong potential for sampling the paths of conditional diffusion processes, enabling efficient simulation of trajectories of diffusion processes that respect rare events or boundary constraints. In this work, we present the adjoint sampler for infinite-dimensional function spaces, a stochastic optimal control-based diffusion sampler that operates in function space and targets Gibbs-type distributions on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Our Functional Adjoint Sampler (FAS) generalizes Adjoint Sampling (Havens et al., 2025) to Hilbert spaces based on a SOC theory called stochastic maximum principle, yielding a simple and scalable matching-type objective for a functional representation. We show that FAS achieves superior transition path sampling performance across synthetic potential and real molecular systems, including Alanine Dipeptide and Chignolin.

paragraphs: Many sampling methods operate on finite-dimensional vectors, but some problems naturally ask for entire functions or trajectories. Sampling diffusion paths subject to rare events or boundary constraints is one motivation. This paper develops a learning-based sampler directly for infinite-dimensional function spaces, where theory and algorithm design have been less developed.

The Functional Adjoint Sampler targets Gibbs-type distributions on Hilbert spaces. It extends Adjoint Sampling using stochastic optimal control, with the stochastic maximum principle providing the theoretical basis. This leads to a matching-style training objective for a functional representation, connecting the function-space formulation to a simple and scalable learning procedure.

The authors evaluate transition path sampling in synthetic potential systems and molecular systems, including Alanine Dipeptide and Chignolin, and report superior performance. These results support the usefulness of extending sampling beyond a finite-vector formulation when the objects of interest are trajectories. The contribution is both a theoretical generalization of adjoint sampling and a concrete algorithm demonstrated on systems with meaningful transition paths.
summary.tldr: The Functional Adjoint Sampler extends control-based diffusion sampling to function spaces and improves reported transition path sampling performance.

title: Functional Adjoint Sampler: Scalable Sampling on Infinite Dimensional Spaces

abstract: Reward models are central to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), especially for open-ended tasks where evaluation is inherently multi-dimensional. Recent Generative Reward Models (GRMs) improve interpretability by producing natural-language rationales and task-specific evaluation principles. However, most existing GRMs generate principles after reading the actor’s response, i.e., $Q+R \rightarrow P$. We show that this coupling induces Principle Drift: when the actor performs reward hacking (e.g., verbosity, self-aggrandizement, or hallucinated self-justifications), the reward model may shift its criteria to rationalize the response, yielding inflated scores that in turn reinforce hacking during RL. We propose IP-GRM (Independent Principle GRM), a two-stage framework that first generates principles solely from the question ($Q \rightarrow P$) and then evaluates the response conditioned on $(Q, R, P)$. This decoupling keeps criteria invariant to response content, producing more objective and stable reward signals. For efficient training, we further introduce a Principle Cache strategy that reuses principles within a group, improving GRPO throughput by 23.66% while maintaining strict intra-group consistency. In GRPO training on creative writing, IP-GRM suppresses reward hacking and improves WritingBench and CreativeWriting-v3 by up to +4.6 and +7.1 points based on Qwen3-8B, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open-source models. The model and dataset are open-sourced at https://github.com/ShadeCloak/IP-GRM.

paragraphs: Generative reward models can explain their scores using task-specific evaluation principles. However, if they choose those principles after reading the response, the response can influence the standards used to judge it. The paper calls this Principle Drift: verbosity, self-praise, or invented justifications can shift criteria in ways that inflate rewards and reinforce reward hacking during training.

Independent Principle GRM separates criterion creation from evaluation. It first derives principles using only the question, then evaluates the answer using the question, response, and fixed principles. This keeps the criteria independent of the candidate’s content. They also report state-of-the-art performance among open-source models. These findings support deciding what constitutes a good answer before inspecting the answer being rewarded.
summary.tldr: IP-GRM generates evaluation principles before reading responses, reducing reward hacking and improving creative-writing training results.

title: Unbiased Principles, Robust Rewards

abstract: The characterization of histopathology with AI promises to assist clinical decision-making, but it is currently limited due to coarse-grained annotations that miss cellular identities. To overcome this gap, we bridge histopathological images, gene expression profiles, and natural-language descriptions using SpatialWhisperer, a trimodal contrastive learning model. Our training integrates community-scale datasets comprising spatially resolved gene expression profiles paired with histopathology images, as well as single-cell gene expression profiles with detailed annotations. The shared gene expression modality implies a transitive relationship between images and textual annotations, which our method leverages to enable accurate zero-shot cell type annotation directly from H&E images. SpatialWhisperer outperforms published baselines, achieving relative AUROC gains of up to 15.9% across three benchmarks spanning 19 tissues and 20 cell types. When training with data from all three modality pairs, we observe performance gains in low-data regimes. We formalize our approach and present a sufficient condition under which this transitive alignment is induced. Our work establishes transitive representation learning for fine-grained interpretation of histopathology images.

summary.tldr: SpatialWhisperer uses gene expression to connect tissue images with textual cell labels, improving zero-shot histopathology annotation.

title: Transitive Representation Learning Enhances Histopathology Annotation

abstract: Understanding the generalization behavior of learning algorithms is a central goal of learning theory. A recently emerging explanation is that learning algorithms are successful in practice because they converge to flat minima, which have been consistently associated with improved generalization performance. In this work, we study the link between flat minima and generalization in the canonical setting of stochastic convex optimization with a non-negative, $\beta$-smooth objective. Our first finding is that, even in this fundamental setting, flat empirical minima may incur trivial $\Omega(1)$ population risk while sharp minima generalizes optimally. We then demonstrate that this phenomenon extends to sharpness-aware algorithms introduced by Foret et al. (2021), namely Sharpness-Aware Gradient Descent (SA-GD) and Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM). For SA-GD we prove that it successfully converges to a flat minimum at a fast rate, but the population risk of the solution can still be as large as $\Omega(1)$. For SAM we show that although it minimizes the empirical loss, it may converge to a sharp minimum and also incur population risk $\Omega(1)$. Finally, we establish population risk upper bounds for both SA-GD and SAM using algorithmic stability techniques.

paragraphs: Flat minima are often associated with good generalization: nearby parameter changes have little effect on training loss. This paper examines that connection in stochastic convex optimization with a non-negative, smooth objective. It shows that even in this setting, flatness alone can be misleading: flat training minima may have constant-order population risk while sharp minima generalize optimally.

The authors extend this analysis to Sharpness-Aware Gradient Descent and Sharpness-Aware Minimization. For the former, they prove fast convergence to a flat minimum, yet the resulting population risk can remain large. For the latter, minimizing empirical loss may lead to a sharp minimum that also has constant-order population risk. These are possible failure behaviors, rather than claims that either method always fails.

The paper also derives population-risk upper bounds for both algorithms using algorithmic stability. Together, the results separate optimization success, local flatness, and performance on the underlying data distribution. They show why reaching a flat solution cannot by itself establish generalization, while providing another theoretical route for studying these algorithms.
summary.tldr: Even for smooth convex objectives, flat training minima can generalize poorly, so flatness alone does not guarantee low population risk.

title: Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Generative models frequently suffer miscalibration, wherein statistics of the sampling distribution—such as the fraction of generations in a given class—deviate from desired values. We frame calibration as a constrained optimization problem and seek the closest model in Kullback-Leibler divergence satisfying a calibration constraint. To address the intractability of imposing these constraints exactly, we introduce two surrogate objectives for fine-tuning: (1) the relax loss, which replaces the constraint with a miscalibration penalty, and (2) the reward loss, which converts calibration into a reward fine-tuning problem. We demonstrate that these approaches substantially reduce calibration error across hundreds of simultaneous constraints and models with up to nine billion parameters, spanning applications in protein design, image generation, and language modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/smithhenryd/cgm.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce individual outputs while getting the overall mixture of outputs wrong. For example, the fraction belonging to a particular class may differ from a desired proportion. This paper treats that mismatch as a distributional calibration problem: adjusting the statistics of what the model generates across many samples.

The authors formulate the goal as finding a model that satisfies a calibration constraint while remaining as close as possible to the original model in Kullback-Leibler divergence. Because enforcing the constraints exactly is intractable, they develop two practical fine-tuning objectives. The relax loss penalizes miscalibration directly, while the reward loss translates the calibration goal into a reward-based fine-tuning problem.

Experiments cover protein design, image generation, and language modeling, including models with up to nine billion parameters and hundreds of simultaneous constraints. Both approaches substantially reduce calibration error. The results support using surrogate objectives to adjust aggregate output statistics at scale, while the underlying optimization formulation makes preserving proximity to the original distribution an explicit part of the goal.
summary.tldr: Two fine-tuning objectives substantially reduce mismatches between desired and generated distribution statistics across many simultaneous constraints.

title: Calibrating Generative Models to Distributional Constraints

abstract: Logit-based watermarking is a widely used mechanism for identifying LLM generated content, yet its effectiveness is governed by a fundamental trade-off between detectability and semantic distortion. Existing analyses provide limited guidance for principled hyperparameter selection, leaving practical deployments reliant on heuristic tuning. In this work, we develop a power-calibrated statistical framework that establishes explicit quantitative relationships between watermark hyperparameters, detection power, and distortion. This characterization transforms watermark design into a guided optimization problem. Building on these results, we derive practical parameter selection procedures that achieve optimal trade-offs under constraints. Extensive experiments across multiple language models and datasets validate the theory and demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently identifies Pareto-optimal points.

paragraphs: Logit-based watermarking changes a language model’s token preferences to make generated text identifiable. Its central design problem is a trade-off: a stronger detectable signal can also distort the text’s meaning. The paper addresses how to select watermark settings systematically, rather than relying on trial-and-error tuning.

The authors develop a statistical framework that quantitatively connects watermark hyperparameters with detection power and semantic distortion. Detection power describes the detector’s ability to identify watermarked content. Expressing these relationships explicitly turns parameter selection into an optimization problem, where a desired detection capability or an acceptable distortion level can guide the choice.

Using this characterization, the paper derives practical procedures for choosing parameters with optimal trade-offs under constraints. Experiments across multiple language models and datasets support the theory and consistently locate Pareto-optimal settings: points where improving one objective requires worsening another. The contribution therefore concerns making the trade-off predictable and actionable. It does not claim that watermarking can achieve arbitrarily strong detection without affecting the generated content.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework selects watermark parameters by explicitly balancing detection power against semantic distortion.

title: Beyond Heuristic Tuning: Power-Calibrated LLM Watermarking

abstract: Proactive large language model (LLM) agents aim to actively plan, query, and interact over multiple turns, enabling efficient task completion beyond passive instruction following and making them essential for real-world, user-centric applications. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising solution for training such agents in multi-turn settings, allowing interaction strategies to be learned from feedback. However, existing pipelines face a critical challenge in balancing task performance with user engagement, as passive agents can not efficiently adapt to users’ intentions while overuse of human feedback reduces their satisfaction. To address this trade-off, we propose BAO, an agentic RL framework that combines behavior enhancement to enrich proactive reasoning and information-gathering capabilities with behavior regularization to suppress inefficient or redundant interactions and align agent behavior with user expectations. We evaluate BAO on multiple tasks from the UserRL benchmark suite, and demonstrate that it substantially outperforms RL baselines under controlled comparisons, while achieving comparable or even superior performance to frontier LLM agents, highlighting its effectiveness for training proactive, user-aligned LLM agents in complex multi-turn scenarios.
originalAbstract: Proactive large language model (LLM) agents aim to actively plan, query, and interact over multiple turns, enabling efficient task completion beyond passive instruction following and making them essential for real-world, user-centric applications. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising solution for training such agents in multi-turn settings, allowing interaction strategies to be learned from feedback. However, existing pipelines face a critical challenge in balancing task performance with user engagement, as passive agents can not efficiently adapt to users’ intentions while overuse of human feedback reduces their satisfaction. To address this trade-off, we propose BAO, an agentic RL framework that combines behavior enhancement to enrich proactive reasoning and information-gathering capabilities with behavior regularization to suppress inefficient or redundant interactions and align agent behavior with user expectations. We evaluate BAO on multiple tasks from the UserRL benchmark suite, and demonstrate that it substantially outperforms RL baselines under controlled comparisons, while achieving comparable or even superior performance to frontier LLM agents, highlighting its effectiveness for training proactive, user-aligned LLM agents in complex multi-turn scenarios.

paragraphs: Proactive language agents need to plan, ask questions, and interact across multiple turns. This creates a practical trade-off: too little initiative can leave user intentions poorly understood, while excessive requests for feedback can burden users. The paper develops Behavioral Agentic Optimization, or BAO, to train agents around both task performance and interaction quality.

BAO combines two parts within an agentic reinforcement-learning framework. Behavior enhancement develops proactive reasoning and information gathering. Behavior regularization discourages inefficient or redundant interactions and brings behavior closer to user expectations. Together, these mechanisms seek to improve the usefulness of an agent's initiative while controlling unnecessary demands on the user.

On multiple tasks from the UserRL benchmark suite, BAO substantially outperforms reinforcement-learning baselines under controlled comparisons. It also achieves performance comparable to, or better than, frontier language-model agents in the reported evaluations. The findings support explicitly training the balance between productive information gathering and interaction restraint, rather than treating successful task completion as the only relevant aspect of multi-turn behavior.
summary.tldr: BAO trains proactive agents to gather useful information while suppressing redundant interactions, improving reported task and engagement trade-offs.

title: Pushing Forward Pareto Frontiers of Proactive Agents with Behavioral Agentic Optimization

abstract: We introduce Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Adaptive Verifiable Environments (RLVE), an approach using verifiable environments that procedurally generate problems and provide algorithmically verifiable rewards, to scale up RL for language models (LMs). RLVE enables each verifiable environment to dynamically adapt its problem difficulty distribution to the policy model’s capabilities as training progresses. In contrast, static data distributions often lead to vanishing learning signals when problems are either too easy or too hard for the policy. To implement RLVE, we create RLVE-Gym, a large-scale suite of 400 verifiable environments carefully developed through manual environment engineering. Using RLVE-Gym, we show that environment scaling, i.e., expanding the collection of training environments, consistently improves generalizable reasoning capabilities. RLVE with joint training across all 400 environments in RLVE-Gym yields a 3.37% absolute average improvement across six reasoning benchmarks, starting from one of the strongest 1.5B reasoning LMs. By comparison, continuing this LM’s original RL training yields only a 0.49% average absolute gain despite using over 3x more compute. We release our code publicly.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs problems that provide useful feedback. A fixed training distribution can lose that value when its problems become too easy or remain too hard. RLVE uses environments that generate problems procedurally, check rewards algorithmically, and adjust their difficulty distributions as the language model's capabilities change.

The authors implement this approach in RLVE-Gym, a suite of 400 manually engineered verifiable environments. Each environment can adapt independently during training. The study also examines environment scaling: increasing the collection of environments used for learning. In the reported experiments, broader environment collections consistently improve reasoning that generalizes beyond training.

Joint training across all 400 environments improves average performance across six reasoning benchmarks by 3.37 percentage points from a strong 1.5B reasoning model. Continuing that model's original reinforcement learning produces a 0.49-point gain while using over three times as much compute. This comparison supports the combination of broader task coverage and adaptive difficulty as an effective way to maintain learning signals and improve reasoning within the tested setup.
summary.tldr: RLVE improves reasoning by training across many verifiable environments that adapt problem difficulty to the model's evolving capabilities.

title: RLVE: Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning for Language Models with Adaptive Verifiable Environments

abstract: Agent-centered scientific discovery is turning scientific models into always-on computational infrastructure. In this paradigm, AI agents coordinate tools, interpret feedback, and drive high-frequency research loops, requiring domain models that are both accurate and callable in real time. Molecular docking exposes this bottleneck: it provides essential structural feedback for drug discovery, yet current high-fidelity docking and co-folding models remain limited by iterative generative refinement and heavy computation. We present a compute-efficient co-folding framework that turns molecular docking into a sub-second structural primitive. Because docking methods operate under different levels of structural prior, we report accuracy under information-level-matched protocols, comparing blind settings with blind generative methods and interface-informed settings with surface- or interface-informed baselines. Our framework combines two ideas. First, Progressive Consistency Regularization (PCR) compresses diffusion dynamics into reliable few-step inference through reconstruction-anchored consistency tuning. Second, Residual-Safe Quantization preserves high-fidelity residual streams and geometry-sensitive operations in BF16 while quantizing selected compute-intensive linear transformations. Our model achieves state-of-the-art docking accuracy under the matched interface-informed protocol, reports blind docking performance separately under the matched blind protocol, and generates five conformations for a representative 256-token complex in 0.17 seconds on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, delivering a $>300\times$ speedup over AlphaFold3 under the benchmarked setting. Together, these results move molecular docking from an offline generative simulator toward a real-time structural primitive for agent-centered drug discovery.

paragraphs: Frequent molecular docking calls could give scientific agents rapid structural feedback, but iterative generation and heavy computation make high-fidelity models expensive. This paper presents a co-folding framework designed to make docking fast enough for such repeated use while preserving accuracy.

Progressive Consistency Regularization compresses diffusion dynamics into a few inference steps through reconstruction-anchored consistency tuning. Residual-Safe Quantization reduces precision in selected compute-heavy linear operations while keeping residual streams and geometry-sensitive operations in BF16. The evaluation separately matches blind docking methods and interface-informed methods according to the structural information they receive.

The model achieves state-of-the-art docking accuracy under the matched interface-informed protocol and reports blind performance separately. For a representative 256-token complex, it generates five conformations in 0.17 seconds on one NVIDIA H20, exceeding a 300× speedup over AlphaFold3 in the benchmarked setting. The result supports rapid structural feedback through fewer generation steps and selective quantization, with the accuracy claim specifically attached to the interface-informed comparison.
summary.tldr: Few-step diffusion and selective quantization enable sub-second docking, with leading accuracy reported under an information-matched interface-informed protocol.

title: Towards Sub-Second Molecular Docking as a Structural Primitive: A Quantized Consistency Diffusion Framework

abstract: Standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) supervises language models solely through discrete labels in the output logit space. We argue that this sparse, one-hot supervision leaves the latent representation space under-constrained, allowing hidden states to drift into degenerate and anisotropic configurations that limit generalization. To address this issue, we propose Next Implicit Token Prediction (NITP), which augments discrete prediction with dense, continuous supervision directly in the representation space. NITP requires the model to predict the implicit semantic content of the next token, using shallow-layer representations from the same model as stable self-supervised targets. Theoretically, we show that NITP regularizes the optimization landscape by mitigating under-constrained degrees of freedom and enforcing a compact, structured representation geometry. Empirically, across dense and MoE models ranging from 0.5B to 9B parameters, NITP consistently improves downstream performance with negligible computational overhead. Notably, on the 9B MoE model, NITP achieves a 5.7% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.4% on C3 and 4.3% on CommonsenseQA, with $\sim$2% additional training FLOPs and no additional inference cost. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/aHapBean/NITP.

paragraphs: Ordinary next-token training supervises a language model through the identity of the next token. The authors argue that this sparse signal leaves internal representations insufficiently constrained, allowing geometries that hurt generalization. Next Implicit Token Prediction, or NITP, adds a training signal directly to those representations while retaining discrete token prediction.

NITP asks the model to predict continuous semantic information about the next token. Its targets come from shallow-layer representations within the same model, providing self-supervision without a separate target model. The theoretical analysis describes how this objective reduces unconstrained degrees of freedom and encourages a compact, structured representation space.

Experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 0.5 billion to nine billion parameters show consistent downstream improvements. For the nine-billion-parameter MoE model, the abstract reports a 5.7% absolute MMLU-Pro improvement, plus gains of 6.4% on C3 and 4.3% on CommonsenseQA. Training requires about 2% more FLOPs, with no added inference cost. The results support improving internal representation structure through a relatively small addition to pre-training.
summary.tldr: NITP supplements next-token prediction with continuous representation targets, improving downstream results with little extra training computation.

title: NITP: Next Implicit Token Prediction for LLM Pre-training

abstract: Unifying multimodal understanding and generation is a compelling frontier that is beginning to emerge in the medical field. However, the limited existing unified medical models typically treat understanding and generation as disjoint objectives, lacking a meaningful functional synergy. In this work, we identify and address a critical question in unified medical modeling: what form of “understanding” truly benefits generation. We present SynerMedGen, a unified framework built on the proposed principle of generation-aligned understanding, which synergizes understanding objectives with generation tasks via task alignment. SynerMedGen introduces three generation-aligned understanding tasks and a two-stage training strategy that transfers generation-beneficial representations learned during understanding training to medical image synthesis. Remarkably, even with understanding training alone, our SynerMedGen achieves strong zero-shot performance across 22 medical image synthesis tasks and demonstrates robust generalization. When combined with generation training, SynerMedGen consistently outperforms state-of-the-art specialized medical image synthesis models as well as recent unified medical models. We also release SynerMed, a large-scale dataset of 1M paired synthesis samples and 2M understanding instances for studying understanding–generation synergy. Our project can be accessed at https://github.com/piooip/SynerMedGen.

paragraphs: A unified medical model can both understand multimodal inputs and generate images, but placing those capabilities in one system does not automatically make them help each other. SynerMedGen asks which understanding objectives actually benefit generation. Its central principle is to align understanding tasks with the requirements of medical image synthesis.

The framework introduces three generation-aligned understanding tasks and a two-stage training strategy. Representations learned during understanding training are transferred into image synthesis. This makes the relationship between the tasks functional: the understanding phase is designed to develop information that the generation phase can use.

The authors report strong zero-shot results across 22 medical image synthesis tasks even after understanding training alone, together with robust generalization. Adding generation training yields consistent improvements over state-of-the-art specialized synthesis models and recent unified medical models. They also release SynerMed, containing one million paired synthesis samples and two million understanding instances. The findings support choosing understanding objectives for their relevance to generation when building unified medical models.
summary.tldr: SynerMedGen aligns medical understanding tasks with image synthesis, allowing understanding training to improve generation and zero-shot performance.

title: SynerMedGen: Synergizing Medical Multimodal Understanding with Generation via Task Alignment

abstract: We present a trainable sequential-inference technique for processes with large state and observation spaces and relational structure. Our method assumes ``reliable observations'', i.e. that each process statepersists long enough to be reliably inferred from the observations itgenerates. We introduce the idea of a ``state-inference function'' (fromobservation sequences to underlying hidden states) for representing knowledgeabout a process and develop an efficient sequential-inference algorithm,utilizing this function,that is correct for processes that generate reliableobservations consistent with the state-inference function. We describe arepresentation for state-inference functions in relational domains and give acorresponding supervised learning algorithm. Experiments, in relational video interpretation, show that our technique provides significantly improved accuracy and speed relative to a variety of recent, hand-coded, non-trainable systems.

paragraphs: This paper develops a trainable method for sequential inference in processes with large state and observation spaces and relational structure. It assumes that each hidden state lasts long enough for the observations generated during that state to identify it reliably. This persistence assumption supplies the basis for the method's notion of reliable observations.

The central representation is a state-inference function that maps observation sequences to underlying hidden states. The authors build an efficient sequential-inference algorithm around this function. Its correctness applies to processes whose reliable observations are consistent with that function, so the guarantee explicitly depends on both observation reliability and the suitability of the learned representation.

For relational domains, the paper supplies a representation of state-inference functions and a supervised algorithm for learning them. Experiments in relational video interpretation report significantly improved accuracy and speed compared with several recent hand-coded systems that cannot be trained. The contribution combines a conditional correctness result with a practical route for learning the knowledge used during sequential inference.
summary.tldr: A learned mapping from observation sequences to hidden states enables efficient relational inference when states persist long enough to be reliably identified.

title: Relational sequential inference with reliable observations

abstract: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process (dHDP) is developed to model the time-evolving statistical properties of sequential data sets. The data collected at any time point are represented via a mixture representation associated with an appropriate underlying model, in the framework of HDP. The statistical properties of data collected at consecutive time points are linked via a random parameter that controls their probabilistic similarity. The sharing mechanisms of the time-evolving data are derived, and a relatively simple Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler is developed. Experimental results are presented to demonstrate the model.

paragraphs: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process models sequential datasets whose statistical properties change over time. At each time point, the observations receive a mixture representation within the hierarchical Dirichlet process framework. This provides a way to describe the data at individual times while also modeling relationships across the sequence.

Consecutive time points are connected through a random parameter controlling their probabilistic similarity. The connection allows the model to represent temporal relationships alongside the mixture description at each time. The authors derive the mechanisms through which the evolving data share information, making temporal sharing an explicit part of the probabilistic formulation.

The paper also develops a relatively simple Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for inference and presents experiments demonstrating the model. Its contribution combines a model of changing distributions with a computational procedure for working with that model. The important structural idea is that neighboring time points are related through a probabilistic similarity parameter while retaining their own mixture representations.
summary.tldr: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process links time-specific mixture models through a random parameter governing similarity between consecutive datasets.

title: The dynamic hierarchical Dirichlet process

abstract: The purpose of this paper is three-fold. First, we formalize and study a problem of learning probabilistic concepts in the recently proposed KWIK framework. We give details of an algorithm, known as the Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm, analyze its sample complexity upper bound, and give a matching lower bound. Second, this algorithm is used to create a new reinforcement learning algorithm for factoredstate problems that enjoys significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art algorithm. Finally, we apply the Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm to remove a limiting assumption in an existing reinforcement-learning algorithm. The effectiveness of our approaches are demonstrated empirically in a couple benchmark domains as well as a robotics navigation problem.

paragraphs: This paper connects a probabilistic learning problem to structure learning and feature selection in reinforcement learning. It first formalizes the problem within the KWIK framework and studies the Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm. This establishes a learning component that can then be used inside broader reinforcement-learning procedures.

The authors analyze an upper bound on the algorithm's sample complexity and provide a matching lower bound. The paired bounds give both an achievable requirement and a corresponding limit for the studied problem. They then use the algorithm to construct a reinforcement-learning method for factored-state problems, reporting a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art algorithm.

A further application removes a limiting assumption from an existing reinforcement-learning algorithm. The abstract does not identify that assumption, so the supported conclusion is that the method broadens that algorithm's applicability. Experiments in benchmark domains and a robotics navigation problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the approaches. The overall contribution links a theoretically characterized probabilistic learner to two concrete improvements in reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: The Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm has matching sample-complexity bounds and enables improvements to factored-state reinforcement learning.

title: The adaptive k-meteorologists problem and its application to structure learning and feature selection in reinforcement learning

abstract: Q-learning in single-agent environments is known to converge in the limit given sufficient exploration. The same algorithm has been applied, with some success, in multiagent environments, where traditional analysis techniques break down. Using established dynamical systems methods, we derive and study an idealization of Q-learning in 2-player 2-action repeated general-sum games. In particular, we address the discontinuous case of epsilon-greedy exploration and use it as a proxy for value-based algorithms to highlight a contrast with existing results in policy search. Analogously to previous results for gradient ascent algorithms, we provide a complete catalog of the convergence behavior of the epsilon-greedy Q-learning algorithm by introducing new subclasses of these games. We identify two subclasses of Prisoner's Dilemma-like games where the application of Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration results in higher-than-Nash payoffs for some initial conditions.

paragraphs: Q-learning has a convergence guarantee in single-agent settings with sufficient exploration, but standard analysis becomes inadequate when several agents learn together. This paper studies an idealized version of that interaction in repeated games with two players and two actions, allowing the players' interests to differ.

The authors use dynamical systems methods to analyze epsilon-greedy exploration, whose action-selection behavior introduces discontinuities. They introduce subclasses of these games and provide a complete catalog of convergence behavior for the algorithm in the studied setting. This supplies a value-based counterpart to earlier analyses of gradient-based policy search and highlights differences between the approaches.

One finding concerns two subclasses of games resembling the Prisoner's Dilemma. For some initial conditions, epsilon-greedy Q-learning produces payoffs higher than those at a Nash equilibrium. The qualification about starting conditions is central: the result identifies particular dynamics that can achieve such outcomes. The paper's catalog concerns the specified game setting and idealized learning dynamics, rather than unrestricted multiagent learning.
summary.tldr: An idealized analysis classifies epsilon-greedy Q-learning dynamics in two-player, two-action games and identifies conditional higher-than-Nash outcomes.

title: Classes of Multiagent Q-learning Dynamics with epsilon-greedy Exploration

abstract: When training a system to label images, the amount of labeled training data tends to be a limiting factor. We consider the task of learning to label aerial images from existing maps. These provide abundant labels, but the labels are often incomplete and sometimes poorly registered. We propose two robust loss functions for dealing with these kinds of label noise and use the loss functions to train a deep neural network on two challenging aerial image datasets. The robust loss functions lead to big improvements in performance and our best system substantially outperforms the best published results on the task we consider.

paragraphs: Image-labeling systems often lack enough labeled training data. This paper explores using existing maps to supply labels for aerial images. Maps offer abundant supervision, but their information may be incomplete or poorly aligned with the images. A mapped feature can therefore supply an imperfect training target even when the map is useful overall.

The authors propose two robust loss functions designed to address these kinds of label noise. A loss function determines how prediction errors influence training, so changing it changes how the learning process responds to unreliable supervision. The proposed losses are used to train a deep neural network on two challenging aerial-image datasets.

The reported experiments show large performance improvements from the robust losses, and the best system substantially exceeds the best published results for the task considered. The contribution is a way to make abundant but imperfect map labels more useful for learning. The evidence specifically concerns the incomplete and misregistered labels addressed in these aerial-image experiments.
summary.tldr: Two robust training losses help deep networks learn aerial-image labels from incomplete and misaligned maps.

title: Learning to Label Aerial Images from Noisy Data

abstract: Stochastic neighbor embedding and related nonlinear manifold learning algorithms achieve high-quality low-dimensional representations of similarity data, but are notoriously slow to train. We propose a generic formulation of embedding algorithms that includes SNE and other existing algorithms, and study their relation with spectral methods and graph Laplacians. This allows us to define several partial-Hessian optimization strategies, characterize their global and local convergence, and evaluate them empirically. We achieve up to two orders of magnitude speedup over existing training methods with a strategy that adds nearly no overhead to the gradient and yet is simple, scalable and applicable to several existing and future embedding algorithms.

We propose a generic formulation of embedding algorithms that includes SNE and other existing algorithms, and study their relation with spectral methods and graph Laplacians. This allows us to define several partial-Hessian optimization strategies, characterize their global and local convergence, and evaluate them empirically. We achieve up to two orders of magnitude speedup over existing training methods with a strategy that adds nearly no overhead to the gradient and yet is simple, scalable and applicable to several existing and future embedding algorithms.

paragraphs: Nonlinear embedding methods turn similarity information into low-dimensional representations. Stochastic neighbor embedding and related methods can produce high-quality representations, but their training cost is a substantial obstacle. This paper targets that optimization problem while working across a family of embedding algorithms.

The authors introduce a generic formulation that includes SNE and other existing methods, then study its connections with spectral methods and graph Laplacians. These relationships provide the basis for several partial-Hessian optimization strategies. Such strategies use part of the objective's curvature information to guide optimization, and the paper characterizes their global and local convergence behavior.

Empirical evaluation finds speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over existing training methods. The highlighted strategy adds almost no overhead beyond gradient computation and is described as simple and scalable. Its relevance extends to several existing and potential future embedding algorithms. The reported speedup is a best observed improvement, while the broader contribution is an optimization approach grounded in a shared formulation of embedding objectives.
summary.tldr: A shared formulation of nonlinear embeddings yields partial-Hessian training strategies with reported speedups of up to two orders of magnitude.

title: Fast Training of Nonlinear Embedding Algorithms
